articles.title: Paolo Duterte: Let Supreme Court decide if impeachment threshold rule legal
articles.summary: Davao City Representative Paolo Duterte questioned Wednesday the legality of the Senate impeachment court's decision to base the two-thirds vote to convict his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte, on…

blocks.text: Published September 23, 2026 6:56pm

Davao City Representative Paolo Duterte questioned Wednesday the legality of the Senate impeachment court's decision to base the two-thirds vote to convict his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte, on the number of senators who are capable of participating in the trial proceedings.

With 13 yes votes, one no vote, and six non-participants, the Senate impeachment court effectively set aside an earlier ruling that placed the votes needed to convict the vice president at 16. The voting threshold is still two-thirds, but absentee senators will no longer be counted.

"Is it within its authority as the impeachment court? But the bigger question remains—does that interpretation conform to the Constitution? The Constitution says conviction requires the concurrence of two-thirds of ALL the Members of the Senate," Paolo Duterte said.
The vice president's lead defense counsel, Sheila Sison, manifested before the impeachment court that her client will exhaust all legal remedies following the senator-judges' ruling.
Under the 1987 Constitution, the Senate has the sole power to try and decide on all impeachment cases.

Sharing their expert views as amici curiae as invited by the Senate impeachment court, three former Supreme Court chief justices said the meaning of two-thirds under Senate rules is not rigid to mean 16, and can be changed by senator-judges.
However, the Davao City congressman said that with the Senate voting what is meant by "all members" meant, it also raised a constitutional question.

"If the affected party chooses to bring that question before the Supreme Court, then let the High Court decide whether the Senate's interpretation is consistent with the fundamental law," Duterte said.
"At the end of the day, positions in government are temporary. The Constitution is not," Duterte said.
Senator-Judge Erwin Tulfo clarified that the threshold was not changed per se. If an absentee senator opted to show up on the day of voting, they will be counted in the computation of the two-thirds.

Senators Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada are currently detained at the Quezon City Jail for separate plunder charges. Senator Loren Legarda is on extended medical leave, while Senator Ronaldo "Bato" dela Rosa has been missing following the issuance of an arrest warrant against him by the the International Criminal Court. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Sen. Gatchalian calls for stricter gun rules after South Cotabato shooting
articles.summary: Senate President Win Gatchalian on Wednesday stricter gun regulations in the aftermath of the South Cotabato school shooting that left three students dead.

blocks.text: Published September 23, 2026 6:54pm
Senate President Win Gatchalian on Wednesday stricter gun regulations in the aftermath of the South Cotabato school shooting that left three students dead.

“I call for a review of the rules and protocols governing the issuance of firearms to government personnel. Re-examine standards for safekeeping, storage, and ensuring that access to weapons never reaches untrained hands, especially children,” Gatchalian said in a privilege speech during Wednesday’s plenary session. Gatchalian also pushed for early detection when it came to mental health struggles.

“Let us take care not to stigmatize anyone with mental health struggles, especially those who have the courage to ask for help, because they do not make a person violent. Our objective must be early detection, intervention, and support, so that qualified professional help reaches a distressed child, and that credible threats are assessed properly before anyone is harmed,” he added.
Gatchalian asked the public to remain calm amid these shootings, saying that while it is easy to get mad and look for someone to blame, there needs to be proper sharing of information.
Authorities have suspected that the shooter may have been influenced by online elements. He also urged Meta to block or stop the spreading of these types of videos on social media.
The Senate President said he also supported the passing of the Comprehensive School Safety Act and the Child Online Safety Protection Act.

The Comprehensive School Safety Act mandated every educational institution to have a School Safety Plan, and prohibited acts of violence, bullying, digital harm and more. It was passed on the third and final reading at the Senate, a few days after the South Cotabato school shooting.
Meanwhile, the Child Online Safety Protection Act aims to provide stronger protection for children against online sexual abuse and exploitation.

The school shooting in Banga National High School in South Cotabato is the third school shooting that resulted in multiple deaths. In June, two students opened fire on their classmates in a Tacloban school, killing three others.
In August, another student killed his schoolmate in Ateneo de Zamboanga before turning the gun on himself. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Macalintal: Bill postponing BSKE not yet signed by Marcos
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Election lawyer Romulo Macalintal expressed confidence that the measure postponing the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) on Nov. 2 has not yet been signed by…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Election lawyer Romulo Macalintal expressed confidence that the measure postponing the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) on Nov. 2 has not yet been signed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
He made the pronouncement on Wednesday after the Office of the President (OP) said, in an email sent to him, that it is reviewing his supplemental letter-petition for a Presidential veto.
Macalintal’s letter was transmitted and received by the OP on Tuesday, Sept. 22.

“Clearly, it indicates the bill is under deep study by the President and opens a genuine possibility for a veto. Otherwise, the Office of the Appointments Secretary would not even say that my request is under evaluation and I will be updated soon,” Macalintal said in a statement.

The House of Representatives adopted the Senate’s version of a bill, which extends the term of barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan officials to five years last Sept. 16, sending it straight to the OP for executive action.
Once signed into law, the bill would automatically postpone the BSKE and move it to the second Monday of Nov. 2028.
Macalintal maintained that the bill was “unconstitutional, vague, and defective” as it violates the constitutional right of suffrage.
According to him, Congress apparently lapsed and overlooked the distinction between the “term” and “tenure” of barangay officials.

“Indeed, postponing the polls yet again and extending the terms of incumbent barangay and SK officials on holdover capacity effectively deprives voters of their right to choose their grassroots leaders without any compelling or proper legal basis,” he expressed.
He added, “Such holdover is in the nature of a legislative appointment which is contrary to the constitutional requirement that barangay officials must be elected and not appointed.”
Macalintal said he looks forward to personally meeting the president and his legal advisers to discuss his concerns about the measure.
He did not further mention the nature and details of the said meeting. /mr

articles.title: Prosecution dismisses Sal Panelo's warning on impeachment vote threshold
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel brushed aside former presidential legal counsel Salvador Panelo's claim that senator-judges who voted to change the basis for determining the threshold to convict Vice…

blocks.text: Published September 23, 2026 6:42pm

The House prosecution panel brushed aside former presidential legal counsel Salvador Panelo's claim that senator-judges who voted to change the basis for determining the threshold to convict Vice President Sara Duterte violated the Constitution.
Panelo, who served as chief presidential legal counsel to Duterte's father, former President Rodrigo Duterte, described the impeachment court's ruling as a tragedy.

“Ang ginawa nila ay talagang nakalulungkot at isang trahedya na nilabag nila ang Saligang Batas nang lantaran. Dahil hindi talaga sila maaaring bumoto sa isang isyu na ang utos ng Saligang Batas ay hindi na nila dapat pakialaman,” he told reporters.
(What they did is truly saddening and a tragedy — they blatantly violated the Constitution. They cannot vote on an issue where the Constitution dictates that they should no longer meddle.)

The Senate impeachment court on Wednesday voted to interpret the constitutional requirement of a two-thirds vote based on the number of senators who are “legally and factually capable of participating” in the impeachment proceedings.
The ruling effectively overturned presiding officer Senator-judge Francis “Chiz” Escudero's July 6 ruling that 16 votes, or two-thirds of all 24 senators, would be needed to convict Duterte.

Thirteen senator-judges voted in favor of a motion by Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo to reconsider Escudero's July 6 ruling, following the continued absence or inability of some senators to participate in the impeachment trial.

The vote came after the Senate impeachment court heard the views of four former justices of the Supreme Court who served as amici curiae, lengthy oral arguments from both the prosecution and defense, and probing questions from senator-judges on the constitutional basis for determining the two-thirds voting threshold.
Panelo also said that senator-judges who vote under the new formula could face criminal liability.

“Pag sila ay bumoto under a new threshold, which is violative of the Constitution, they open themselves to Article 204 of the Revised Penal Code under that provision. Ang sabi po doon, if you knowingly render an unjust judgment, you are criminally liable,” he said.

(If they vote under a new threshold, which is violative of the Constitution, they open themselves up to Article 204 of the Revised Penal Code. It says that if you knowingly render an unjust judgment, you are criminally liable.)

Panelo had previously argued that the impeachment court could not alter the constitutional requirement that two-thirds of all Senate members must concur in a conviction. He also warned that senator-judges could face legal challenges and possible criminal cases if they proceeded with changing the voting requirement.
However, private prosecutors Lorna Kapunan and Amando Ligutan appeared unfazed by Panelo's comments.
“Who is he? Don't know him,” Kapunan told reporters.
“Not familiar, sorry,” Ligutan said.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Iran denies dropping preconditions amid ‘very productive’ three-hour UN talks in New York
articles.summary:
Trump says further talks possible as barrel of Brent crude falls to below $100 for first time in two weeks

Iran has pushed back on claims that it dropped former preconditions for reopening…

blocks.text: Iran has pushed back on claims that it dropped former preconditions for reopening the strait of Hormuz in surprise talks held in New York under the mediation of Qatar between Tehran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

Trump said the three-hour talks held in a room at the UN headquarters had gone very well and been very productive. He suggested further talks were possible imminently, which led to the price of a barrel of Brent crude to fall to below $100 (£75) for the first time in two weeks. Witkoff said the talks had been “encouraging, constructive and successful”.

In his speech to the UN general assembly, Trump said he had a decision to make very soon on whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” or help turn it into one of the great countries of the Middle East, the kind of bombastic threat Trump often deploys during talks with Iran.

In Tehran, the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed the talks had occurred, but appeared not to confirm any shift in the Iranian negotiating position. He said: “The interaction that took place with the American side was through Qatari mediation. This interaction was aimed at conveying Iran’s conditions, including the end of the war in all its dimensions, the cessation of American aggressive actions, the naval siege, and the economic war, the release of Iranian assets and so on.” Aware of the potential domestic backlash, he added that Iran’s conditions had been conveyed.

Iran set seven preconditions before returning to talks, and in a new development over the past 48 hours said the crucial strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met.

It is likely that the US and the Gulf states would have to accept a navigational route for shipping in the strait of Hormuz – a key waterway for transporting oil – that requires commercial shipping to enter through a sea lane mainly in Iranian waters and under Iranian rather than Omani control.

The fact that the talks lasted three hours suggests some progress was made. The US side is under pressure to leverage down oil prices and increase the availability of refined oil before the midterm elections in November. Latest published figures suggest the number of identifiable tankers making it through the strait is fewer than five a day, but estimates of the US navy are much higher.

The blockage in the strait is made worse by the uncertainty surrounding the control by the Houthis’ (the Iranian-backed Yemeni paramilitaries) of a second energy transport chokepoint, the Bab al-Mandab strait that leads from the Red Sea into the Indian Ocean.

There is little sign that Trump wants to relaunch a full-scale war with Iran or indeed with the Houthis as Republicans battle to turn the domestic political agenda away from a hugely unpopular war that the Americans think they are losing.

Iran is under ever more intense pressure from sanctions, and a US naval blockade is making it nearly impossible for Iran to export oil, depriving the country of badly needed foreign currency. Iran’s civilian aircraft on Wednesday faced a potential worldwide grounding owing to the threat of US secondary sanctions on any entity that engaged with Iran’s civilian fleet.

Iranian officials negotiated frantically with neighbouring countries to try to maintain an air bridge, but it appears Oman and Iraq have been forced to close their airspace to Iranian civilian planes.
The president of Iran, Masoud Pezeshkian, is due to address the UN general assembly on Wednesday after arriving in New York on a flight from Tehran as talks were under way.

Pezeshkian is an advocate of negotiations with the US but has not played a direct role in the talks. He has said the memorandum of understanding (MoU), agreed with the US on 17 June, remained the starting point.

Implementation of the MoU fell apart after the two sides accused one another of breaching its terms by trying to take control of the strait. Iran said the MoU clearly left Iran in control of the strait for an interim period before a long-term agreement on its management was reached, including the possibility of Oman and Iran charging fees for navigational services.

Pezeshkian is expected to condemn western double standards over what he regards as an illegal US assault on Iran that has left schoolchildren dead and infrastructure ravaged. Europe’s preparedness to call out Russia for its invasion of Ukraine, and its reticence in criticising the attack on Iran, or Israel’s treatment of Palestinians in Gaza, has been a constant theme of Pezeshkian’s remarks.

Many of the most powerful speeches on Tuesday at the UN general assembly came from European and Arab politicians who decried the inability of the west to enforce peace. In his farewell speech to the UN, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, criticised the attempt to overthrow the Iranian government by the US and Israel, arguing: “Every time a few states, sometimes even in the name of international order, have tried to replace the people in order to change a regime or a system, they have plunged those states into even greater chaos.”

He also said that the west had not imposed a peace in Gaza. “Some boast of a supposed peace. But this peace hasn’t reopened humanitarian routes for a single second. Must we stand by and watch this spectacle that shames us all? Never!”
Macron landed himself in hot water with Israel when he suggested Hamas was not present in the West Bank, as opposed to Gaza.

Netanyahu’s office responded, using the biblical name for the West Bank: “Hamas terrorists carry out attacks against Jews almost every day. They have murdered countless Israeli civilians in Judea and Samaria.”

Jordan’s King Abdullah II attacked the Israeli government for “moving the goalposts”, for continuing attacks and the destruction of civilian infrastructure in Gaza, and for refusing to withdraw from the war-torn Palestinian territory. This has forced the Palestinian population in Gaza into barely one-third of the territory, he said.
Observers must no longer treat Israeli policies as “temporary military measures” or a “consequence of war”, he said.
“Accountability begins when we call things what they are: an attempt to erase Palestinian life and impose a new territorial reality in Gaza,” he added.

image.caption: Rome's Colosseum is the largest amphitheater in the worldImage: Cecilia Fabiano/LaPresse/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Colosseum in Rome was closed on Wednesday after a worker fell to his death overnight.
Andrea Moretti, 22, died after falling while working on a new lighting installation.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she hoped that the cause of the accident would be clarified as soon as possible.

"We are deeply shocked and saddened by the news of the tragic death of Andrea Moretti, a skilled worker who lost his life last night following an accident at the Colosseum," she said. "For a person to die at the age of 22 is unacceptable and even more so when it happens in the workplace."
Italian Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli described the incident as a "tragic event that has left us shocked and stunned."
The Culture Ministry said "the second-tier section where the accident occurred" would be closed
Authorities were working on determining the circumstances of the accident, according to the statement.
The ministry said the site would be fully closed to the public for the day after all visitors leave.
The part of the site where the accident occurred had already been closed early on Wednesday.
What is Rome's Colosseum?
The ancient Colosseum is the world's largest amphitheater.
It was built in the first century under the Roman Empire. It was used to host gladiator fights, executions and animal hunts.
It is one of Rome's most iconic sites and gets up to 20,000 visitors a day at peak times.

articles.title: Judge wrong to hear case from bed while recovering from surgery, court says
articles.summary:
Richard Clayton KC had undergone operation for ruptured achilles tendon day before hearing optician’s appeal

A judge was wrong to hear a case from his bed via video link while recovering…

blocks.text: A judge was wrong to hear a case from his bed via video link while recovering from surgery, the court of appeal has said.

Richard Clayton KC, sitting as a deputy high court judge, heard an optician’s appeal against a finding of serious misconduct from bed the day after returning from hospital where he had undergone an operation for a ruptured achilles tendon.

Clayton dismissed Suleman Patel’s appeal against a nine-month suspension imposed by the General Optical Council but Patel took the case to the court of appeal. Patel claimed: “The general handling of the appeal by [Clayton] … has not been dealt with to the standard to be expected of the court such that the judgment is not reliable.”

In a judgment published on Tuesday, and first reported by the news website Legal Futures, Lord Justice Phillips, sitting with Lady Justice Falk, rejected Patel’s appeal but said Clayton should not have heard the case from bed.

Phillips wrote: “The deputy judge is to be commended on his willingness to hear a case whilst recovering from injury and his fortitude in doing so in bed, in trying circumstances. However, I consider that, save in exceptional circumstances, such as great urgency or where a matter can only be heard by a specific judge, a judge should only undertake a hearing (and a hearing should only be listed before them) when they have the essential tools to undertake the task properly and professionally …”

He added: “Although it did not cause any injustice in the present case, in my judgment the deputy judge should not have sat on the present case whilst encumbered by his injury. There was no great urgency and other arrangements could and should have been made. I do not say that a judge should never undertake a hearing whilst in bed or otherwise than at a desk or table, but it should be a last resort, where the matter cannot sensibly be listed before a judge sitting in the conventional way.”

While hearing the case, Clayton said he was “sitting prone in bed, which makes it pretty difficult, I suspect, for me to navigate some of the pdf bundles. I have, however, read all the relevant material … We will just have to see how we go.”

He later said: “This has turned out to be far more difficult, I’m afraid, than I had anticipated because I am handicapped by an ability [sic] to write anything down.” However, at several points thereafter the transcript recorded him saying he was taking a “proper note” of what was being said.

During the hearing, Clayton said the hearing was “testing my stamina significantly” and at the end apologised “for the problems at the beginning”. He explained that “it has been quite tricky but not impossible to deal with the hearing largely from a non-sitting position”.
Clayton said he had been advised he could not stand for eight days after leaving hospital, was taking paracetamol and had “cleared the position with the senior staff at the administrative court”.

articles.title: Hungary: EU Commission wants to unblock €4.2b in funding
articles.summary: The Commission's president has argued that Budapest is strengthening the rule of law with Viktor Orban finally out of office. Funds had been blocked over corruption allegations under Hungary's former…

image.caption: European Commission President von der Leyen says Hungary should be rewarded for reforms undertaken to address standing problemsImage: Omar Havana/REUTERS

blocks.text: The European Commission on Wednesday proposed unlocking some €4.2 billion ($4.8 billion) in frozen funds to be paid out to Hungary.
The cash had been blocked over allegations of corruption tied to Hungary's former government, led by Viktor Orban and his Fidesz party.
"Hungary has taken important steps to strengthen the rule of law and protect the [European] Union's financial interests," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.

A Commission press release said reforms implemented after Hungary elected Peter Magyar prime minister had addressed "shortcomings in areas such as public procurement, the anti-corruption framework, risks of conflicts of interest and the effectiveness of prosecutorial action."

Orban, a feverent critic of the EU, was often at odds with the bloc over accusations that he and his cronies had undermined rule of law and democracy in the country and that he had engaged in self-dealing and corruption — all charges that he vehemently denied.

The Commission said that steps taken by the new Magyar government to rectify prior problems should result in funds being partially unfrozen and the country once again being allowed to participate in European academic exchange and research programs.
In May, the Commission said it was prepared to unfreeze a total of €16.4 billion in earmarked funds should Budapest make good on its promises to implement all proposed reforms.
EU member states must now approve the Commission's plan.

articles.title: Mass shooting at house party in South Africa leaves 11 dead, 3 wounded: police
articles.summary: Three shooters killed at least 11 people, including a woman who was believed to be pregnant, in an attack at a house party in South Africa, police said Wednesday.

image.caption: A forensic vehicle is parked Wednesday near the scene where 11 people were killed and at least three others injured, in the township of KwaMakhutha, near Durban, South Africa. (Reuterse)

blocks.text: World·New
Three shooters killed at least 11 people, including a woman who was believed to be pregnant, in an attack at a house party in South Africa, police said Wednesday.
People had gathered in home when suspects entered and opened fire, police say
Three others were wounded in the mass shooting late Tuesday night in KwaMakhutha township, about 30 kilometres south of the city of Durban on the country's east coast.

The people had gathered at the house for a party when the suspects entered and opened fire, police said. Ten people, including the pregnant woman, died at the scene and an 11th was declared dead at the hospital.
Authorities did not immediately give out details on the condition of the three people wounded.

items: South Africa's anti-migrant protesters march nationwide after thousands flee violence

blocks.text: Police said they were searching for the attackers and no arrests had been made.

The motive for the shooting was not known, police said, but added that some of the people at the house were known to police as part of investigations into criminal activity. Police said they couldn't give out any more information on those investigations.
"Although the motive of the shooting cannot be confirmed yet, [a] feud between rival groupings cannot be ruled out," police said.

The bodies of some of the victims were laid out on the ground and covered with white sheets outside the small house where the shooting took place. Police cordoned off the larger neighbourhood with yellow tape while forensic investigators worked through the scene.
Police were also investigating if the torching of a car near the house was connected to the shooting.
Killings 'really disturbing,' says premier

Thami Ntuli, the premier of KwaZulu-Natal province, told reporters at the scene that the killings were "really disturbing." He said that there were known problems with drug dealing and illegal firearms in the community.

It's the latest in a series of mass shootings in South Africa in recent years, including one in June when multiple shooters killed 12 people in a poor neighbourhood in Johannesburg. Two mass shootings two weeks apart in December killed 21 people.

South Africa has extremely high rates of violent crime, with official police statistics recording 5,427 homicides in the latest three-month period between April and June, at an average of nearly 60 homicides a day.
Shootings are the most common form of homicide in South Africa, and police and crime experts have long said that one of the biggest problems is a high number of illegal firearms in circulation.

articles.title: Chagos Islands deal ‘can’t go ahead’ without US support, Streeting says
articles.summary: Defence secretary places annual payments to Mauritius on hold as UK government reviews deal over Diego Garcia base

blocks.text: Wes Streeting has said annual payments worth at least £120m to Mauritius are on hold as the government reconsiders its deal over the Chagos Islands, after Donald Trump refused to back the agreement.
The defence secretary said the payments would not be made “at this stage” and confirmed the deal “can’t go ahead without US support”.

Last year, the UK signed a treaty to transfer sovereignty over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, while retaining control of the joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia under a 99-year lease. Mauritius was also set to receive £165m for three years and £120m a year from the fourth year.

Asked on BBC Radio 4 Today’s programme if the payments would still go ahead, Streeting said: “Not at this stage. We’ve got to get to a point where we can agree a deal … This deal as it is currently constituted can’t go ahead without American support. So we have to get a deal to a place where it commands American support as well as the agreement of the government of Mauritius and our government.

“And the reason why that is important is because we are trying to safeguard, not just now but for the longer term, the base at Diego Garcia, and the capability it provides the United Kingdom and the United States for our national and collective security.”
Streeting said the payments would be a “price worth paying” if they secured Britain’s long-term ability to operate from Diego Garcia.

Trump doubled down on his criticism of the agreement when he met Andy Burnham at the UN general assembly in New York on Tuesday, describing the deal to transfer sovereignty over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius as “terrible”. “I don’t support it,” Trump told reporters after a bilateral meeting with Burnham on the fringes of the general assembly adding: “I think it’s a terrible deal.”
After meeting Trump, the prime minister said the government would “work hard” to find a resolution that was acceptable to the different sides.

Streeting said Trump’s criticism had not come as a surprise to ministers. “This isn’t news to us,” he said, “President Trump has been clear that he has concerns about the deal as it’s currently constituted. We will work through the detail of the US concerns and seek to reach a point that all of us can sign up to.”
The agreement can’t proceed as it is without US support because of the importance of the joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia, Streeting said.

The defence secretary also warned that Britain could not adopt an “ostrich strategy” of sticking its head in the sand and hoping the row over the Chagos Islands would go away, as he warned settling the dispute would involve “painstaking work”.

“The strategy is not to wait out President Trump. I think the approach will be to work with President Trump and his administration,” Streeting told Times Radio. “I’m not pretending that’s an easy position and that resolving this is not going to be difficult. It is difficult and necessarily painstaking work, but it is necessary.

“And the ostrich strategy of sticking our heads in the sand … , I would caution is not a wise strategy when it concerns one of the most sensitive national security assets we have anywhere in the world,” Streeting added.

He also warned ignoring that Mauritius’s claim to sovereignty posed its own risk to the military base’s future. He said the ruling from the international court of justice in 2019 is “advisory now, [but] there is a potential further course of legal action avenue open to the government of Mauritius”.

articles.title: Dolly Parton estate in feud with nephew over alleged ‘warfare’ threats
articles.summary:
Bryan Seaver, who announced Parton’s death to the world, is alleged to have intimidated her manager and others, which he denies

The estate of the late

blocks.text: The estate of the late Dolly Parton is involved in a dispute with the country star’s nephew and former head of security, and has filed for a restraining order against him amid allegations of threats.
Bryan Seaver was responsible for Parton’s security, and was tasked with announcing her death on 25 August with a video, “something Dolly asked of me years ago”, he said.

But since the singer died, her estate, which is run by Parton’s manager Danny Nozell, has reportedly fired Seaver from his security job, and has now alleged that he made “relentless” threats against Nozell and others.

According to Billboard, the lawsuit filed in a Tennessee court reads: “These were not ordinary workplace disputes or heated words; they were deliberate threats from a self-proclaimed heavily armed, former security operative with a military-contractor background. Many of [Parton’s staff members] are now afraid to come to work or have resigned entirely because they do not feel safe.”

Seaver is alleged to have written to a lawyer for Parton, “I’m a killer”, and separately told Nozell: “I’m literally an international arms dealer and mercenary. All I do is warfare. Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do.” He is also alleged to have claimed that he made a $27m arms and ammunition deal with Haiti.
He allegedly claimed he would “set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly’s brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It’s going to be great. Or fucking pay me.”

Seaver repeated some of those claims in comments to TMZ while defending his actions, saying: “I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer. However, nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by.”

Regarding the messages to Nozell, Seaver said: “I was talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend and he fancies himself a gangster. A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving.”
In another message, Seaver reportedly said: “I’m going to spend the next times I have on earth ratfucking anyone that has ever betrayed my family.”

Speaking to TMZ, Seaver said of that comment: “I was talking about people that have done bad to Dolly in business – a specific company that scared her and intimated her. Those comments were about specific, horrible business partners that have done wrong to her and I stand by that.”

Seaver’s security contract was terminated on 15 September, with a leaked termination letter saying the decision was made “for the protection of the trust and beneficiaries as a whole”, though it reassured Seaver it was “not a termination of your personal interest in the trust”.

Seaver put out a statement after the termination, saying: “We remain unshakably resolved to fulfil her final directive to protect her family, and we refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much.”
The chancery court in Nashville will now consider the restraining order filing. The Guardian has contacted Seaver and lawyers for Parton’s estate for further comment.
Parton left behind considerable financial assets: not only her songbook featuring hits such as 9 to 5, but also a broad business empire including the entertainment resort Dollywood in Tennessee.
She had no children, and her husband, Carl, died in 2025, but she is survived by other family members including six siblings and an uncle. Seaver is the son of her sister Cassie.

articles.title: Republican jitters grow as unpopular Trump fuels midterm ‘bloodbath’ fears
articles.summary:
Iran war, rising prices and president’s low ratings give Democrats advantage, but Republicans have poured cash into key races – could it be decisive?

Donald Trump pulled out all the stops at…

blocks.text: Donald Trump pulled out all the stops at the Republican party’s midterm convention two weeks ago. In speeches aimed at the voters who will soon decide whether to keep Republicans in control of Congress for the final phase of his presidency, the president dangled $5,000 checks, and warned the United States would turn into a “communist country” if Democrats are elected.

The unprecedented political gathering amounted to a hail-mary pass at retaining control of Congress, which history indicated Trump’s Republican allies had always been likely to lose in the 3 November vote. Two weeks later, with election administrators in several states already sending out mail ballots, there is no indication the gambit has worked.

Polls have continued to show Democrats with an edge on the generic ballot, a key indicator of voter sentiment in congressional races, as well as in in some key Senate contests such as North Carolina and Georgia, both states where Trump won two years ago. Forecasters have moved their ratings of other battleground races almost uniformly in Democrats’ favor, despite Republican-led states’ concerted effort to redraw House districts in the party’s favor.

Trump’s approval ratings remain low, with some surveys finding him plumbing new depths. Prices for gasoline and diesel have started climbing again amid the ongoing war with Iran, prompting the Republican Senate stalwart Chuck Grassley of Iowa to publicly encourage the president to do more for farmers, whose businesses have been particularly hard hit by the conflict’s economic shocks.

Top Republicans suddenly appear worried about the fortunes of incumbents standing for re-election in some of the reddest states in the country. Last week, vice-president JD Vance campaigned in Kansas, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly a century, but where Adam Hamilton is seen as a strong challenger to the Republican incumbent Roger Marshall.

Back in Washington, the extent of the House GOP’s jitters became clear when Democrats forced a vote on a war powers resolution to end the fighting with Iran, and three Republicans who had not backed the previous five efforts supported this one, ensuring its passage.

“This midterm is going to be a fucking bloodbath,” said Nancy Mace, the outgoing congresswoman who was among the trio of new converts, and predicted that her party would not keep control of the Senate and House of Representatives when ballots are tallied in a month and a half.
In the days that followed, more Republicans in competitive races came out against the Iran war.

“The war with Iran needs to end, and end quickly,” Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee for Michigan’s open Senate seat, said in a campaign ad released on Monday. Ashley Hinson, the congresswoman who is running to represent Iowa in the Senate, wrote on social media “the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end”. She had voted against the Democratic war powers resolution, as had John James, the congressman who is the Republican nominee for governor of Michigan, but on Tuesday, the Detroit News reported he told reporters: “We need to end this war quickly. Because war is terrible, and no one likes war.”

Democratic operatives have long maintained that Trump was leading the GOP’s congressional majorities into oblivion, and are now being joined in that prediction by veteran politics watchers, who see the toxic combination of rising prices, poor approval rating and dampening enthusiasm among voters as likely fatal for Republicans hopes of keeping control of the House, if not the Senate.

“We are seeing a dramatic souring and just overall level of anger at the broken promises of Trump and House Republicans, like, issue after issue after issue. Like, people are just unhappy right now,” said a Democratic strategist who did not want their name to be used.
Talk has even re-emerged of a “blue wave” in November that will see Republicans lose in deep-red corners of the country.
“Republicans should brace themselves: the three most plausible outcomes are that it will be bad, really bad, or truly horrible,” wrote the veteran analyst Charlie Cook.

blocks.caption: Republican attendees at the midterm convention in Dallas earlier this month. Photograph: Evan Vucci/Reuters

blocks.text: Yet not everything is necessarily going Democrats’ way. In the battle for the Senate, Republicans have grown increasingly optimistic about their Senate candidate winning in New Hampshire, which some major forecasters now view as a toss-up. The party may also have come out ahead in the mid-decade redistricting push, and definitely has more financial resources this year than the Democrats – a reversal from most midterms prior.

“House Republicans are running with a more favorable map, historic fundraising, stronger candidates, and a commonsense agenda, while Democrats are burdened by unelectable far-left nominees and deeply unpopular policies that make their path to the majority far more challenging than the pundits suggest,” said Mike Marinella, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee.

After much speculation about when he would act, Trump’s Maga Inc Super Pac has started spending its $400m war chest, buying $15m in advertisements to support the Republican Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race. Fairshake, a Super Pac connected to the cryptocurrency industry, will reportedly spend $30m against Sherrod Brown, the Democratic former senator from Ohio and cryptocurrency adversary seeking to return to the chamber, after the industry spent $40m to see him defeated in 2024.

Republicans and their allies have thus far put $384.5m into Senate races, to Democrats’ and their supporters’ $112.7m, according to data compiled by political analyst Rob Pyers. In the House, Republican supporters have spent nearly $65.7m to the Democrats’ $51.1m, but Politico has reported that much of that money has gone to districts where Trump won two years ago, a sign that the GOP is playing defense.

Winning the Senate will require Democrats to oust at least four Republicans in states that Trump won in 2024. The House seems an easier target for the party, since the GOP controls it by a low single-digit majority.

House Republican leaders including the speaker Mike Johnson nonetheless insist that voters will expand rather than disband their majority in November. They note that 23 Democrats represent districts that voted for Trump in 2024, a number that has increased due to GOP-led states’ redistricting, while only eight Republicans represent districts that backed Kamala Harris. The party also believes that voters are still too disenchanted with Democrats overall to put them back in charge in the Capitol.
“Voters might not like Trump. They might not even like Republicans. But the polling shows that they hate Democrats even more,” a Republican strategist said on condition of anonymity.

In a statement, Julie Merz, the executive director of the House Democrats’s campaign arm, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, acknowledged the party’s fundraising struggles but said they were still on track for a return to power.

“We are confident we’re poised to win the majority, and that’s why Republicans in deep red territory are running scared,” Merz said. “If Democrats want to break the Republican gerrymanders in the south and get the largest majority possible, more resources ensure we can flip those seats too. We need more cash.”

Money isn’t everything, as Democrats know – Harris and her supporters outspent Trump and his allies in 2024, a year of resounding Democratic losses. And many of the factors that will decide the election outcome may already be baked into the result, said John T Woolley, co-director of the American Presidency Project at the University of California, Santa Barbara.

“Inflation, employment rates – they’re just not going to change a whole lot. So the kind of thing that’s left, the seats, those are fixed, [you] can’t change that stuff. So the only thing that’s left is the president’s approval,” Woolley said.
“What that means is the president has to shift swing voters, independent voters, voters who don’t identify as either Republican or Democrats.”

But that group, too, appears to have soured on the GOP: a New York Times and Siena University poll released last week found 57% of independent voters were planning to vote Democratic in the midterms, and just 34% for the Republican candidate.

articles.title: [DECODED] When regulation lags, how do organizations protect their truth?
articles.summary: The more advertisers invest in truth, the more trust they build — not just for their respective organizations, but even for our information ecosystem

blocks.text: The more advertisers invest in truth, the more trust they build — not just for their respective organizations, but even for our information ecosystem

items: The Ad Standards Council (ASC) has released guidelines requiring advertisers to maintain human oversight and disclose the use of AI in ads.
Disclosures must be clear and include terms like 'AI-generated' or 'Contains AI-generated content' to promote transparency and help consumers identify AI content.
The ASC's move is seen as a step towards preserving authenticity in advertising and protecting organizations from reputational risks in an era of rapidly developing AI technology.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
In case you missed it, the Ad Standards Council (ASC) released last week its guidelines on the use of artificial intelligence in advertising. ASC’s Circular No. 2026-014 mandates that:

items: Advertisers utilize appropriate human oversight, maintaining full responsibility for all claims and depictions in their respective ads.
Ads created, generated, or materially enhanced using AI include a disclosure.
Disclosures must be clear and reasonably conspicuous, including use of words like “AI-generated,” “AI-assisted,” “Created with AI,” or “Contains AI-generated content.”

blocks.text: Hello, I am Iris B. Gonzales. I started my career in advertising back in 2018. Today, I am a Senior Brand Strategist at The Nerve and am also enrolled at the FEU Institute of Law. I chose both paths because of a growing unease about influence operations and how they affect our information landscape and, ultimately, the democratic systems we seek to uphold.

We at The Nerve have studied how influence operations in the Philippines can mislead audiences, manipulate narratives, and damage organizations’ reputations at scale. These operations now involve synthetic, AI-generated content — and the preliminary report of the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, co-chaired by The Nerve’s Head of Global Strategy Maria Ressa, points out that such content slowly erodes our ability to distinguish authentic from generated content.
That’s a slippery slope toward distrust of media that could otherwise be truthful, termed the “liar’s dividend” in the UN report.

This is why I welcome the ASC’s move to require advertisers to disclose AI use in their content. To be clear, ASC stated that the use of AI by itself doesn’t render an ad misleading or deceptive. The circular merely aims to promote transparency in AI use and compliance with existing laws.

An added benefit, in my view, is that these labels will allow us as consumers to better recognize the tell-tale signs of AI-generated content, and hopefully apply the same discipline to the other content that we consume.

But that discipline only works if the labels are honest in the first place. Advertisers play a crucial role in preserving this authenticity. The more advertisers invest in truth, the more trust they build — not just for their respective organizations, but even for our information ecosystem.

This ASC circular is just one of many discussions we should be having now that AI is developing faster than our ability to measure or govern it. When regulation lags, brands and organizations are often left to police themselves, leaving them vulnerable to reputational risks. For those navigating this shift, the question now becomes: are you ready when that risk hits your organization?

If you’re looking to protect your organization’s reputation in the age of AI, join us in our Crisis Management Masterclass on Friday, October 9. You may also join more of these discussions exploring human values during this year’s Social Good Summit. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Manitoba compensates 2 men switched at birth in 1955 with $250K each in settlement
articles.summary: Two men switched at birth in a rural Manitoba hospital in 1955 were awarded $250,000 each in the 2025-26 fiscal year, according to financial disclosure documents released by the province this week.

image.caption: Edward Ambrose holds up two picture frames. The pictures in his right hand are of his biological parents, whom he never got to meet. The picture in his left hand is a wedding photo of the parents who raised him. (Gary Solilak/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New
Two men switched at birth in a rural Manitoba hospital in 1955 were awarded $250,000 each in the 2025-26 fiscal year, according to financial disclosure documents released by the province this week.
Edward Ambrose, Richard Beauvais experienced 'a miscarriage of justice,' provincial cabinet minister says
Two men switched at birth in a rural hospital more than 70 years ago have been compensated $500,000 by the Manitoba government.
Edward Ambrose and Richard Beauvais were awarded $250,000 each in the 2025-26 fiscal year, according to financial disclosure documents released by the province this week.

"Mr. Ambrose and Mr. Beauvais are grateful to the provincial government for the public apology they received from Premier Kinew and for the resolution of their claims for financial compensation," Bill Gange, a lawyer representing both men, told CBC News in a statement.
Ambrose declined to comment when reached by phone Tuesday.
What happened to the two men was "a miscarriage of justice," provincial Justice Minister Matt Wiebe said in a written statement.
"No one can give them back the years that were lost but we hope the settlement brings some closure," he said in the statement.
The men were sent home with the wrong families in 1955 after being born at a hospital in Arborg, about 115 kilometres north of Winnipeg.
Ambrose is Métis but was raised by a Ukrainian family, and Richard Beauvais grew up believing he was of Cree and French descent when his ancestry was actually Ukrainian, Jewish and Polish.
They didn't learn the truth until Ambrose's sister took a 23 and Me DNA test that showed they weren't biologically related. The results did, however, suggest Beauvais was her sibling.

Beauvais was raised near Lake Manitoba in a Métis community. He is a residential school survivor who was removed from his home in the Sixties Scoop, a process that saw an estimated 20,000 First Nation, Inuit and Métis people taken from their families and placed with mostly white families.
Ambrose was raised on a farm in Rembrandt, about 25 kilometres north of Gimli.

"The grief of what we went through, that will always be there — you'll never walk away from that. But for now, I know who I am, and I know who my biological brothers and sisters are. So, it's a step forward to a positive," he told CBC News in 2024.
The two men wanted an apology and compensation. Gange requested both in April 2022.

The apology came in March 2024, about six months after the NDP government was elected in Manitoba and only a couple months after the health minister acknowledged the "devastating" impacts the men experienced.
As Ambrose endeavoured to connect with his biological family and cultural roots, Manitoba Métis Federation president David Chartrand personally handed Ambrose his MMF citizenship card 2½ years ago.
"He's welcomed back to his nation, and he shed tears in that perspective. And he's so pleased to be home," Chartrand told CBC by phone in Ottawa on Tuesday.

"Just imagine what Eddy and them are going through now to try to find their own cultures again and reflect their thoughts and saying, you know, 'This is what I thought I was, this is what I was supposed to have been. And yet I'm somebody else.'"
The MMF president said it was clear from his talks with Ambrose that money was not his primary concern, though Chartrand also feels it's fitting the men were financially compensated.
However, Chartrand questioned whether $250,000 was a fitting amount for what they went through.

items: For man switched at birth, path toward reclaiming lost Métis identity takes a step forward
Manitoba Premier Greg Selinger apologizes for Sixties Scoop

blocks.text: "That's not a lot of money to be somebody else for [decades], and to have never seen your family, your mom and the rest of your family," he said.
"It's definitely a matter [that] clearly still will live with them forever. And the little time they have now, they want to spend as much as they can with the family they have left."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Bryce Hoye is a multi-platform journalist with a background in wildlife biology. He has worked for CBC Manitoba for over a decade with stints producing at CBC's Quirks & Quarks and Front Burner. He was a 2024-25 Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. He is also Prairie rep for outCBC. He has won a national Radio Television Digital News Association award for a 2017 feature on the history of the fur trade, and a 2023 Prairie region award for an audio documentary about a Chinese-Canadian father passing down his love for hockey to the next generation of Asian Canadians.

articles.title: OECD says growth 'resilient' in 2026 despite Middle East war
articles.summary: The OECD group of industrialized nations put its 2026 growth forecast at 2.9%. It said investment in AI was helping drive growth, while the war in the Middle East was fueling inflation.

image.caption: The Paris-based OECD forum has raised its 2026 growth forecast despite continued inflationImage: Eric Piermont/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The OECD group of industrialized countries on Wednesday lifted its global growth forecast for 2026 despite the war in the Middle East.
It put the figure at 2.9%, an increase of 0.1 percentage points over June's estimates.
The 38-member Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) is a Paris-based forum for industrialized nations.

blocks.caption: The OECD said that 'broader financial conditions remain supportive'Image: John Angelillo/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did the OECD say about 2026 growth?
The OECD said growth remained "resilient" in 2026, and that "broader financial conditions remain supportive."
It added that the impact of the Middle East war was being softened by other factors.
"Sizeable oil inventories, additional supply from outside the Gulf economies and discretionary government support measures all helped to cushion the impact on the global economy," the group said.
It said investments in artificial intelligence could result in "stronger growth than projected," but warned that growth could still slow if investments do not pay off as expected.
Growth still threatened
However, global growth has dropped from last year's 3.4%, and the OECD has also dropped its 2027 forecast by 0.1 percentage points to 3%.
Governments around the world have begun raising interest rates to cushion inflationary pressures sparked by rising oil and gas prices.
The OECD stressed that the outlook depends on whether a lasting resolution to the conflict is found, as continued fighting would likely lead to higher inflation.

blocks.caption: The United States and Israel's war with Iran has sent oil and gas prices soaringImage: Matthew Hoen/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: The crisis has also led to an increase in government bond yields.

"Rising bond yields underline more than ever the need for enhanced efforts to contain and reallocate government spending, improve public-sector efficiency and strengthen revenues to ensure longer-term debt sustainability and maintain the ability of governments to react to significant shocks," the OECD said.
It said that other threats include weather-related risks like the El Nino pattern, which could cause supply bottlenecks and high food costs.

articles.title: Trump meets US-backed Venezuelan president for first time since Maduro seized
articles.summary: Rodriguez was handpicked by Trump as leader of Venezuela was arrested and taken to the US

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has held talks with Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodríguez at the UN General Assembly, their first face-to-face meeting since the White House backed her to take over the South American country's government.
Rodríguez succeeded Nicolás Maduro shortly after US forces conducted a raid on the Venezuelan capital Caracas and seized him.
The pair met a few kilometres from the New York jail where Maduro is awaiting trial for drug trafficking and other charges.
Rodríguez said they discussed "advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, and security".
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles also attended the meeting.

Rodríguez's government has signed an agreement allowing the US to control more than 65 billion barrels of its oil - more than a fifth of the country's reserves. It grants a US-led company 100-year concessions over 17 oilfields in Venezuela.
Trump previously called it "the biggest oil deal in world history".
During his address to the UN on Monday, Trump said the US and Venezuela control "more than 60%" of the world's oil, adding: "To the victor belong the spoils."
Rodríguez is due to address the UN on Wednesday.
She previously served as vice-president to Maduro and was sanctioned by the US in 2018, but the measures were lifted in April this year.
She was sworn in as interim president by Venezuela's National Assembly days after the US raid with the White House's blessing.
Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado has repeatedly been barred from re-entering the country.

articles.title: Leni Robredo endorses Leonen as chief justice
articles.summary: In Robredo’s letter to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. dated September 11, Robredo urged Marcos to appoint the senior magistrate to head the judiciary, citing his experience and efficiency.

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 5:47pm
Leni Robredo attends the opening of the World Teachers’ Day celebration at the CamHigh Liboton grounds.
Leni Robredo via Facebook
MANILA, Philippines — Former Vice President and now Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo has endorsed Supreme Court Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen as the next chief justice of the Supreme Court.
In Robredo’s letter to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. dated September 11, Robredo urged Marcos to appoint the senior magistrate to head the judiciary, citing his experience and efficiency.

“Justice Marvic M.V.F. Leonen is the most senior among all the justices of the Court. He has proven to be way beyond the constitutional requirements of competence, independence, probity, and integrity,” Robredo’s letter read.

Robredo highlighted Leonen’s nearly 14-year tenure in the High Tribunal since 2012, pointing out that he has authored thousands of ponencias and separate opinions characterized by legal depth, clarity, and an awareness of the nation's "postcolonial and multi-ethnic reality."
Robredo also added that despite his heavy workload, Leonen maintains one of the lowest case dockets in the Supreme Court.

The Naga City mayor also cited Leonen’s background prior to joining the bench, including his service as a public interest lawyer representing indigenous groups and marginalized sectors, his tenure as dean of the University of the Philippines College of Law, and his role in brokering the landmark peace framework agreement with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front.

"At this juncture in our political economy, we need his leadership to inspire credibility and genuine social justice—measures which we all share," Robredo added. "I have no doubt that his appointment will be acceptable to all sectors, including big business, small and medium-scale entrepreneurs, local and national government officials, and those who suffer from poverty, inequality, and disempowerment,” Robredo said.
Leonen is set to serve as an acting chief justice of the Supreme Court while the position of chief magistrate is still vacant after the retirement of Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo on November 6.
He is also included among the five Supreme Court justices invited by the Judicial and Bar Council to apply for the position of chief magistrate.

articles.title: Kayla Sanchez skips event to get better shot at Asian Games medal
articles.summary: Kayla Sanchez turns her focus on the women's 50m freestyle as she looks to deliver the Philippines its first swimming medal in the Asian Games since 1998

blocks.text: STAR. Swimmer Kayla Sanchez in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.
PSC-POC Media Pool
Kayla Sanchez turns her focus on the women's 50m freestyle as she looks to deliver the Philippines its first swimming medal in the Asian Games since 1998
MANILA, Philippines – Kayla Sanchez carries the Philippines’ best hope of ending its 28-year drought for a swimming medal in the Asian Games.

And so, national coaches opted to preserve the 25-year-old star for the women’s 50m freestyle on Thursday, September 24, at the Tokyo Aquatics Centre in Japan as she skipped the women’s 100m backstroke event on Wednesday, September 23.

“There are things we cannot control, there are things we can. Let’s focus on what we can control. So, if we can rest Kayla and prepare her better for tomorrow’s 50-meter event, where she has a very, very good chance of winning a gold, we gave her a rest,” said national coach Ryan Arabejo, a former Olympian and multi-time Southeast Asian Games champion.

Sanchez came oh-so close to becoming the first Filipino swimmer to win a medal in the Asian Games since Raymond Papa bagged a pair of bronzes in the 1998 edition as she finished fourth in the women’s 100m freestyle on Tuesday, September 22.

The Filipina-Canadian clocked 53.65 seconds, just .18 seconds behind China’s Cheng Yujie, who bagged the bronze with a time of 53.47 seconds. Hong Kong’s Siobhan Haughey (52.45) and China’s Yu Yiting (53.21) captured the gold and silver, respectively.
Freestyle is one of Sanchez’s strongest suits.
Back when she still represented Canada, Sanchez was part of the women’s 4x100m freestyle team that scored a silver in the 2020 Tokyo Olympics.
Sanchez also won the women’s 100m freestyle gold and 50m freestyle silver in the 2025 SEA Games in Bangkok, Thailand.
“Anything goes in the 50 meters. It’s anybody’s game, especially in a short-distance event,” said Arabejo.
Sanchez is expected to sit out the women’s 4x200m freestyle relay set on Thursday as well. – Rappler.com

articles.title: John Amagoalik helped found Nunavut. Now he’s fighting to age there

image.caption: John Amagoalik, who turns 79 in November, is shown in Iqaluit. The Nunavut government declined his request to provide adequate funding for his care and accessible housing, so he's going to court. (Juanita Taylor/CBC)

blocks.text: He helped found Nunavut, now he’s fighting to age there
"I'll never go back," John Amagoalik said of an assisted living facility in Ottawa, where he was sent to live by Nunavut's government in February 2025.
The territory's Department of Health transferred him to Embassy West Senior Living after an infection left no choice but to amputate part of his right leg.
"The worst part was the loneliness," Amagoalik recalled in an interview with CBC News as he sat in a wheelchair at his temporary home in Iqaluit with his wife, Evie, on Sept. 7.
"The strange surroundings. That was the worst part, being so far away from home and not ... being able to be with my many grandchildren."
Amagoalik is turning 79 in November and has multiple chronic age-related issues. He also has a difficult time talking.
He's frail, but he's still a fighter.

After a lifetime of struggle that included being forced to attend residential schools and advocating for Inuit rights and self-determination, Amagoalik is in his last fight: to age in the territory he helped create.
"It's been my life," he said, when asked what Nunavut means to him. "And I feel fortunate in being part of it."
'Father of Nunavut'
John Amagoalik is revered as the "Father of Nunavut" for his work spanning over three decades beginning in the 1970s — earning him the Order of Nunavut and the Order of Canada.

Among his many roles, he advocated for Inuit as an adviser with the Tunngavik Federation of Nunavut before it became Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. He was also on the executive council of the Inuit Circumpolar Council in the 1980s, and served as president of what was then the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada, now Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami.

Amagoalik led the land claims settlement process with Nunavut Tunngavik after ratification in 1993. He also chaired the Nunavut Implementation Commission that designed the public government of Nunavut before the territory was created in 1999.
It's the very government his Victoria-based lawyer and longtime friend, Steve Kelliher, said is now failing him. So he's helping Amagoalik take the Nunavut government to court.

items: Mounties spied on 'Father of Nunavut' in 1970s amid fears of Inuit-Dene alliance

blocks.text: Kelliher, who first worked with Amagoalik in the 1970s formulating Nunavut's future government, said his friend is still as much a force today as he was back then.

But when he and another friend, Mark Stiles of Ottawa — who first met Amagoalik in 1975 while working in the land claims office of the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada — visited Amagoalik at Embassy West in March, they felt he needed their help.
"I said, 'Well, how do you like it here, John?' And he said, 'I hate it,'" Kelliher said.
So he asked Amagoalik if he wanted help to return home. "He said, 'Do anything to get me out of here, to get me back to Iqaluit.'"
So they did.
First, they delivered a letter to the territory’s health minister, signed by Amagoalik and dated March 31, pleading to return home. Amagoalik claims he never agreed to the move being permanent.
When the minister, Janet Pitsiulaaq Brewster, didn't take any action on his request to return home, they formed the John A. Committee and brought in Iqaluit lawyer Anne Crawford.

The committee raised $30,000 for a consultant to develop Amagoalik's plan of care, buy medical equipment and supplies, and pay for eight to 10 hours of daily private home care from personal support workers.

It also secured an accessible unit at a subsidized rate of $2,000 a month that has space for his hospital bed and an elevator. The Amagoaliks' public housing unit has stairs that would be too difficult for him to use.
The committee also arranged air transportation donated by an airline to fly Amagoalik to Iqaluit. On June 12, 16 months after he arrived in Ottawa, he returned home.
An uncertain future
But despite all of the hard work to bring Amagoalik back to Nunavut, his future is still uncertain.
The funds raised by the committee were only meant to be for the short term, and Anne Crawford said the money is running out.

"Which we did tell the government at the time, this will not last forever. And therefore, can you talk to us about how and what we can do going forward to continue to support him and live in his home community?"

The request to the territorial government for $16,000 a month to cover accommodations in the accessible unit and up to 10 hours a day of support worker care was declined. However, the government can provide a maximum of two hours per week of personal support worker care.
The committee says its research shows that Nunavut was spending about $30,000 a month for Amagoalik’s care at Embassy West.

items: Coming home: Elders return to Nunavut for care after years of living in the south

blocks.text: The Health Department told CBC News that it can't comment on his care in order to protect his privacy. Brewster, the health minister, also declined to be interviewed.

But a communications manager provided a written statement saying the government has not refused to provide publicly funded health care to Amagoalik and that it continues to work in "good faith to support him."
"So we have no alternative but to appeal to the courts to compel them to do the right thing," Kelliher said, calling the situation "despicable."
"If we've got no money, we'll go beat the bushes," he said. Amagoalik "deserves better. He's earned it. He is an exception. Who treats their leaders like that? Not the Inuit. I don't believe it."
On Sept. 16, two notices of application for judicial review were filed in the Nunavut Court of Justice on behalf of Amagoalik.

"One for judicial review of the assistant deputy minister's letter, the decision not to fund John's care and housing," Kelliher said. "And an application for urgent relief to compel them to do so until the matter is fully heard, which could take months."
Lack of care facilities for seniors

Amagoalik's care situation is emblematic of a wider problem in Nunavut. The vast territory, which covers a total area of just over two million square kilometres and is home to roughly 40,000 people, has only six seniors' facilities spread across its three regions.
The government says it's expanding two more long-term care facilities in Nunavut.

items: Amagoalik among 6 northerners appointed to Order of Canada
John Amagoalik, ‘Father of Nunavut,’ honoured in Iqaluit

blocks.text: Currently, 73 elders from Nunavut are being cared for at Embassy West Senior Living, the only out-of-territory facility contracted by the government for more complex needs.

"We don't want to continue seeing our elders getting flown to Ottawa,” said Gloria Uluqsi, president of Nunavut Tunngavik. "I think they can do better. I think we as a team can do better for our elders."

articles.title: Top South African police officer charged with raping woman, 18, and grooming 16-year-old girl
articles.summary:
Arrest of Shadrack Sibiya comes as country reels from cases of femicide and alleged police corruption and criminality

One of South Africa’s most senior police officers has been charged with…

blocks.text: One of South Africa’s most senior police officers has been charged with raping an 18-year-old woman and grooming a 16-year-old girl, as the country’s police face allegations of corruption and failing to tackle violence against women and girls.

Shadrack Sibiya, who was already suspended from his role as deputy national police commissioner over allegations he interfered with political killings investigations, was arrested on Monday. He is facing charges of rape, people trafficking, promoting the sexual grooming of a child and two counts of grooming a child.

Sibiya appeared briefly in a Johannesburg court on Tuesday. He was then taken to prison in the capital, Pretoria, before a bail hearing on 29 September, as prosecutors had argued he was an escape risk.

South Africa is reeling after the discovery of nine women’s bodies across Ekurhuleni, the municipality east of Johannesburg, in September. Meanwhile, the Madlanga Commission judicial inquiry has been examining allegations of corruption and criminality within the police for the last year.

Puleng Dimpane, the acting national police commissioner, said: “Police officers are entrusted with protecting women and children. They cannot themselves be implicated in conduct that undermines this responsibility. As the country continues to confront the scourge of gender-based violence and femicide, there can be no room for anyone within the police service who is alleged to abuse their position or violate the rights of women and children.”

Sibiya is accused of raping an 18-year-old woman at a hotel in May in the Sandton business district of Johannesburg. The alleged rape took place “whilst she was passed out due to intoxication administered by the accused”, according to a copy of the charge sheet.

The alleged grooming of the 16-year-old girl took place over WhatsApp between 20 July and 3 August, according to the charge sheet. This allegedly included Sibiya sending the girl naked photos of herself, which she had not sent to him.
Sibiya did not enter a plea at the hearing on Tuesday. His lawyer told the court that they needed more time to consult with and get instructions from him, according to News24.
Firoz Cachalia, the acting police minister, said: “We strongly condemn the alleged conduct.
“Where allegations of sexual offences are made against a member of the service, they must be investigated without fear or favour.”

When Sibiya appeared before the Madlanga Commission in February he denied allegations that he had moved 121 political killings investigations from KwaZulu-Natal province to the national head office without explanation.

Sibiya also denied that he had received a gift of 20 impalas from Vusimuzi ‘Cat’ Matlala, a businessman who received an allegedly fraudulent 360m rand (£16.7m) police health services contract soon after the alleged gift.

Matlala, who has been charged with attempted murder, alongside several other charges including fraud and money laundering, declined to comment on the impalas when he appeared at the Madlanga Commission in August. He said he did not want to incriminate himself as the matter was under investigation.

articles.title: CICC extends Discord, Reddit compliance timelines after companies respond
articles.summary: CICC Executive Director Undersecretary Renato Paraiso gives Discord and Reddit further time to comply with an ultimatum after the two companies reach out

blocks.text: MEETING. Officials of the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center talk to officials of Reddit over a video call.
CICC
CICC Executive Director Undersecretary Renato Paraiso gives Discord and Reddit further time to comply with an ultimatum after the two companies reach out

items: The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) has extended the deadline for Discord and Reddit to establish a presence in the Philippines after both companies responded to an ultimatum.
Reddit officials discussed potential measures with the CICC, including the creation of 'green lanes' for reporting harmful content, and committed to opening an office in the Philippines.
Discord expressed willingness to collaborate with the CICC on user safety measures for minors and offered to present its new Teen Default Experience and Family Center tools.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) extended the time given to messaging and communications platform Discord and social discussion platform Reddit after the two companies had responded to an ultimatum to set up a presence in the Philippines within 24 hours.

According to a post on its website and on Facebook on Wednesday, September 23, CICC Executive Director Undersecretary Renato Paraiso said he gave Reddit an extension following a meeting with company officials on measures to strengthen cooperation.
Meanwhile, Discord reached out to the agency in a letter signaling willingness to discuss its current user-safety measures as it relates to teenagers.

Reddit vice president of policy Jessica Ashooh, deputy general counsel Leslie Liu, and policy and regulatory affairs manager Vijay Pamarathi talked with the agency, discussing the potential establishment of what it called “green lanes” — direct channels for Philippine authorities to flag potentially harmful content for fast review and possible removal.

According to the CICC, “These would cover content involving online sexual abuse and exploitation of children (OSAEC), child abuse and exploitation materials (CSAEM), scams, misinformation, harmful content, and materials associated with Nihilistic Violent Extremism (NVE).”
Reddit also committed to establishing an office in the Philippines, as well as creating a team to coordinate with the CICC, but did not give a timeline for this action.

Following the meeting, Paraiso said, “We decided to grant them an extension since they responded within the 24 hours and we want to give them the opportunity to work with us because what we want is accountability and a clear mechanism for government to coordinate with the platforms.”
Discord reached out to Paraiso through a letter, showing a willingness to work with the CICC to protect minors from exploitation, grooming, and exposure to violent content.

The letter said they were prepared to brief the CICC on its newly rolled out Teen Default Experience globally. According to Discord senior public policy advisor Vasundhara Singh, the new system lets users — who cannot be confidently placed into a particular age group through account-levels signals — confirm their age using privacy-preserving methods, including on-device facial age estimation. It added that biometric data would not be stored by Discord.

blocks.caption: [Tech Thoughts] Discord’s ‘Teen-by-Default’ settings are a mixed bag for users

blocks.text: Discord also offered to brief the CICC on its Family Center tools as well as its Kodex system, which allows law enforcement agencies to submit lawful takedown and data requests and get fast-tracked responses.

Tech advocacy group Democracy.net.ph on Tuesday evening called the government’s actions “performative theater” as the CICC, as a unit under the Department of Information and Communications Technology, has no mandate to ban social media platforms.
“Under our democratic system, only courts can restrict freedoms. The direction that CICC is taking is heading towards the Great Firewall of China model,” it added. – Rappler.com
