articles.title: Campus Project 2026: Georgia Takes Center Stage
articles.summary: The Beethovenfest exchange project brings German and Georgian musical traditions together. And the reasons go beyond music.

image.caption: A shared vision: German and Georgian musicians at their first meeting in TbilisiImage: Beethovenfest

blocks.text: Last June, a group of around 20 young German musicians — members of the Federal Youth Orchestra and Federal Youth Choir — arrived in Tbilisi, the capital of Georgia. They were immediately captivated by the Caucasus metropolis and its overwhelming atmosphere of relaxed freedom.
But that freedom can be deceptive. Everyone was aware of Georgia's tense political and social situation and had seen images of the pro-European protests in Tbilisi.

blocks.caption: Hand in hand: German and Georgian musicians rehearsing in TbilisiImage: DW

blocks.text: The next morning, the German musicians gathered in a simple room in central Tbilisi with an equally sized group of young Georgian musicians from the Tbilisi Youth Orchestra as well as singers from the independent music scene.
Finding a Shared Sound
The young musicians from Georgia and members of the Federal Youth Orchestra first met in June in Tbilisi to rehearse for the joint "Campus Concert" at the Beethovenfest in Bonn.
But before that, they had to find a shared sound and develop a program that would bring together two major musical traditions from the two countries.

"We Georgians are known as hot-blooded Southerners with a lot of raw emotion," says Mirian Kokhunaishvili, conductor and artistic director of the project. "Sometimes the intensity of our emotions is higher than in German music. But once you listen to German music, you understand that people are full of emotions there, too, but there's different approaches to how we express them. In music, I couldn't see any differences."

blocks.caption: Conductor Mirian Khukhunaishvili and pianist Tsotne ZedginidzeImage: Jasper Techel/Beethovenfest

blocks.text: After final rehearsals in Bonn, joint concerts will take place on Sept. 23 and 24: first at the Beethovenfest in Bonn and the following day in Berlin. DW will broadcast the concert live on the DW Classical Music YouTube channel.
A Political Message Behind the Music
The Campus project is about more than an exciting musical experiment — and not just for the Georgian participants.

"One goal is to bring the classical repertoire of Georgian music closer to an international audience," says Mirian Kokhunaishvili. "And then we want to send a message. We couldn't simply play and sing without reflecting the reality around us."

For Kokhunaishvili, the music itself is the strongest message: "Our concert is about the geopolitical reality we live in. We want to express our hope for Europe — not just the hope of joining something somewhere, but that this is our shared home. We are fighting to belong there. The core message is that in Georgia, we share Western European values of human rights."

A highlight of the program is a new synthesis arranged by Georgian composer Mika Mdinaradze. The composition combines Beethoven's choral piece "Europa steht!" ("Europe Stands!") from the cantata "The Glorious Moment" with traditional Georgian songs.

"Beethoven naturally remains unmistakable, while the Georgian polyphonic structures preserve their own identity," Mdinaradze explains in an interview with DW. "Together, they create a sonic model of Europe — a dialogue instead of forced unity — a musical declaration of where Georgia belongs."
Making a Statement Through Campus
Since 2001, the Beethovenfest Bonn has organized the Campus project, a platform for exchange among young musicians, with a focus on countries experiencing historic transformation.

"Previous projects have included Ukraine, Afghanistan, Iran and now, for the second time, Georgia — after first participating in 2003," says Thomas Scheider, who leads the Campus project team at the Beethovenfest. "These are places where culture is not simply a side effect of history, but becomes a central field where history is understood, negotiated and questioned."

blocks.caption: Standing ovations: Mirian Kukhunaishvili conducted the German National Youth Orchestra in Tbilisi, August 2026Image: Dato Shalikashvili

blocks.text: For the Federal Youth Orchestra (BJO), which has been a partner in shaping the Campus project for 10 years, the encounter also went far beyond music. "Although music is naturally at the center, the exchange showed so much more: personal connections, cultural richness, significant history, impressive nature and also the challenging current political situation," says Sönke Lentz, orchestra director of the BJO and one of the project organizers. "Pro-European artists and what is likely the vast majority of the population need our solidarity and support."

The Federal Youth Orchestra also incorporated the Campus project into this year's international tour, performing three concerts in Georgia under the direction of Mirian Khukhunaishvili and featuring soloist Giorgi Gigashvili. "Sold-out venues in Tbilisi and Kutaisi, with standing ovations, impressed us and showed us the importance of a project like this," says Sönke Lentz.
Tsotne Zedginidze: Georgian Prodigy and Campus Composer
"The new Mozart" — that is how none other than conductor Daniel Barenboim described Georgian pianist and composer Tsotne Zedginidze when he was just 16 years old.

Zedginidze has just turned 17, making him the project's youngest commissioned composer in the project's history. He composed "Chmebi: Georgian Fantasia" for piano and chamber orchestra. The Georgian word "chmebi" means "voices." The young composer himself will play piano at at the world premiere in Bonn and the subsequent performance in Berlin. "Beethoven would be completely shocked, but it would inspire him," Tsotne says with a smile about his work and the project as a whole.

In his score, Zedginidze draws on ancient, complex Georgian folk traditions for the first time, combining them with unconventional harmonies and fiery folk dance elements. "About my Georgian Fantasia, I tried not to be artificial. It resembles as much as possible Georgian music — all Genres and styles. But at the same time, it's my individual understanding, my own interpretation of Georgian music," he tells DW

blocks.caption: Supporting talent: Star violinist Lisa Batiashvili with pianist and composer Tsotne ZedginidzeImage: DW

blocks.text: Star violinist Lisa Batiashvili is eagerly awaiting the premiere of Tsotne's work. Through her foundation ((name of the foundation?)), the musician, who moved from Georgia to Germany at age 12, supports young artists in her home country. Tsotne is among the foundation's scholarship recipients.

"Over the past 20 years, I have been able to witness how the friendship between Germany and Georgia has grown and how openly and with such interest people here have approached my home country," says Batiashvili. "It is especially beautiful to see young musicians from both countries making music together, learning from each other and inspiring one another." And perhaps, Batiashvili says, something greater than music can emerge from this: a vision of a shared future.

articles.title: El Nino explained: How the weather pattern affects hurricanes and tropical storms
articles.summary: From drought to major floods and extreme heat, El Nino will have a huge impact on the world's weather. In the Atlantic, it could mean a season without hurricanes.

image.caption: Hurricane Melissa, one of the most powerful hurricanes on record, smashed across the Caribbean in October 2025Image: Ricardo Makyn/AFP

blocks.text: In a typical year, storm watchers have logged several hurricanes by late September. At this point in 2005, one of the most active years on record, five major hurricanes had already churned their way through the Atlantic Ocean — including Katrina, one of the most devastating in US history.

But 2026 has been quiet so far. As of September 23, only six tropical storms had formed over the North Atlantic, and none had intensified into hurricanes — a first since satellites began tracking storms in 1966, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) in the US.

blocks.caption: Hurricane Katrina, in August 2005, claimed some 1,200 lives and left New Orleans underwater for weeksImage: Gary Coronado/Palm Beach Post/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "In the satellite era, we have never had a year without a hurricane," said Matthew Rosencrans, lead hurricane season forecaster with NOAA's Climate Prediction Center. "This would be a first."

That's due, in large part, to the latest iteration of the El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a shifting cycle of winds and sea surface temperatures over the Pacific Ocean that shapes weather worldwide and makes it a "dominant factor in total hurricane season activity." Meteorologists have said this year's El Nino could be one of the strongest on record.
Hurricane, typhoon, cyclone — what's the difference?

NOAA's Climate Prediction Center, which tracks Atlantic storm data in the US, said the accumulated cyclone energy of this year's tropical storms — a calculation that factors in storm duration and intensity — was at a record low for so late in the season, which typically peaks on September 10.

None of the six tropical storms registered so far have reached a wind speed of at least 119 kilometers per hour (74 miles per hour) — strong enough to be considered a Category 1 hurricane with the potential to cause some minor damage to homes, trees and other infrastructure.

The name for such a catastrophic tropical storm is regional. What's known as a hurricane in the North Atlantic and eastern Pacific will be called a typhoon on the other side of the Pacific, in eastern Asia. In the Indian Ocean and the South Pacific, meteorologists will generally classify a similar storm as a cyclone.
How do tropical storms form?
How does El Nino affect Atlantic hurricanes?

NOAA's latest data showed that El Nino is still strengthening, with sea surface temperature rise in the key Pacific region now exceeding 3 degrees Celsius (5.4 Fahrenheit), creating a "very strong" El Nino over the next half year — and a "below-normal" hurricane season.

Almost all Atlantic tropical cyclone activity occurs between June 1 to November 30, though hurricanes can form at other times of the year. And meteorologists have warned that this year's calm doesn't rule out a major hurricane before the season is done.

The naturally occurring El Nino weather pattern returns on average every two to seven years, with its effects lasting up to a year. During El Nino, the regular trade winds moving east-west across the Pacific weaken and sometimes even reverse. The changes in wind in humidity and wind shift the jet stream, the strong winds in the upper atmosphere — and disrupt storm formation in the Atlantic.

NOAA's Climate Prediction Center said any hurricanes that do appear in an El Nino year tend to form along the US East Coast and near the Gulf of Mexico, giving them less time to turn into major hurricanes — but also leaving coastal communities with less time to prepare. That pattern is largely dictated by the steering currents when it forms, which typically last around a week.

"Formations deep in the tropics are hampered due to high wind shear," said Rosencrans — the strong changes in wind speed or direction at different altitudes are more likely to disrupt storm formation. "The stronger the El Nino event, the stronger the wind shear."
Pacific typhoons change track, head north

During El Nino, vertical wind shear isn't as strong in the eastern and central Pacific Ocean. Combined with the warmer waters in the Pacific, which fuel storms with heat and moisture, that tends to result in an increase in tropical cyclones in this region. This part of the Pacific has already seen several major hurricanes this year, including Polo, which this week has grown into one of the most powerful Pacific cyclones in decades — fueled in part by El Nino.

"Typically, El Nino means the storms form further east […] toward the international date line and Marshall Islands," Rosencrans told DW, anticipating an "above average" hurricane season in the Pacific. "This does mean that storms have longer life spans before reaching large land masses."

blocks.caption: The eastern Pacific off the Americas has been especially active this season, with four hurricanes in the last monthImage: CIRA/NOAA/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Anne-Claire Fontan at the World Meteorological Organization said during an El Nino event, storms on the Asian side of the vast Pacific tend to track "northward, rather than continue westwards towards East and Southeast Asia."
That meant, according to Rosencrans, that Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Japan and the Korean Peninsula "can face slightly higher odds of tropical storms and typhoons."
Strong El Nino also disrupts storms in Indian Ocean

A strong El Nino will weaken monsoon winds over the Indian subcontinent, often triggering severe drought. It also generally corresponds with a less active tropical cyclone season in the Indian Ocean, said Fontan, a scientific officer with the WMO's Tropical Cyclone Program.

Much like in the Atlantic, increased wind shear in this region can disrupt or delay the formation of storms, which Fontan said lessened the risks for countries in eastern Africa, like Madagascar and Mozambique.

"In terms of overall tropical cyclone activity in the Southwest Indian Ocean, there is a non-linear, or 'bell-shaped,' relationship with ENSO," said Fontan, highlighting El Nino and its opposite phase. "As ENSO moves towards either of its extremes — a strong El Nino or a strong La Nina — tropical cyclone activity in the basin tends to be below normal."
Are El Nino and climate change linked?

The El Nino-Southern Oscillation is a natural phenomenon, and not caused by climate change. And, as Rosencrans pointed out, "the interplay of El Nino or La Nina and the longer-lived changes is just one piece of what makes hurricane seasons active or inactive."
Among those factors is the dry, dusty air drifting out over the Atlantic from the Sahara Desert, which can also suppress hurricanes.
Powerful El Nino set to bring extreme weather

But Fontan said that the especially strong El Nino effect, combined with the warming effects of climate change from burning fossil fuels, is setting the stage for unprecedented weather extremes in the months ahead.

"El Nino is occurring in a warmer world, and this can amplify some of its impacts, including extreme heat, heavy rainfall and drought," she told DW. Already, some forecasters like the UK's Met Office have said the combined effects of El Nino and climate change could shatter heat records in 2027. A new report from the University of Chicago-based Climate Impact Lab has projected that extreme heat could cause nearly half a million more deaths worldwide during this El Nino period, especially in the Global South.

"We are already seeing the disruption and devastation caused by droughts and floods, and we expect these impacts to worsen as El Nino intensifies," said Celeste Saulo, head of WMO, in early September, in a stark warning for governments and humanitarian organizations.

articles.title: Sara Duterte's team may appeal lower impeachment voting threshold to SC
articles.summary: The defense team of Vice President Sara Duterte said Wednesday it is mulling over appealing to the Supreme Court the ruling of the Senate impeachment court that lowered the voting threshold to…

blocks.text: Published September 23, 2026 5:14pm

The defense team of Vice President Sara Duterte said Wednesday it is mulling over appealing to the Supreme Court the ruling of the Senate impeachment court that lowered the voting threshold to convict her.
Michael Poa, spokesperson of the defense panel, said he would talk to Duterte first regarding the matter.

"Well, siyempre tayo pa rin ay lumahok sa oral arguments kanina, para maipakita lang natin, di lang naman sa impeachment court kundi sa publiko, kung ano ang posisyon ng defense sa usapin ng voting threshold. Ganun pa man, you know, that was the decision of the impeachment court," he said in a press briefing.

(Well, of course we still participated in the oral arguments earlier, just to show—not only to the impeachment court but also to the public—what the defense's position is on the issue of the voting threshold. Be that as it may, you know, that was the decision of the impeachment court.)
"Siyempre, hindi ko naman ide-deny na 'yung pag-akyat sa Supreme Court is a real possibility. As to when, we will have to discuss the matter with our client," Poa added.
(Of course, I won't deny that bringing the matter to the Supreme Court is a real possibility. As to when, we will have to discuss the matter with our client.)
Senator-judges voted 13-1-6 to set the conviction threshold at two-thirds of those who are legally allowed to participate in the proceedings.
This means that Duterte can be convicted with fewer than 16 votes as several senators are facing charges, remain in hiding, or on medical leave.
When asked if they believe the Vice President is being treated unfairly, the defense said they do not want to speak badly about the impeachment court.

"I don't want to say anything negative against the court. But sa amin, ayan po 'yung naging pasya ng bawat senator-judge, and we really have to respect that. But that doesn't mean that we don't have any legal remedies; isa nga 'yung pag-akyat sa Supreme Court," said Poa.

(I don't want to say anything negative against the court. But for us, that was the decision made by each senator-judge, and we really have to respect that. But that doesn't mean that we don't have any legal remedies, one of which is taking it up to the Supreme Court.)
After the senator-judges made the ruling, Duterte's defense team said that the Vice President would now participate in the trial with caution.

Lead defense counsel Sheila Sison said that the Vice President is not trying to evade accountability amid the ongoing impeachment trial against her. But she noted that Duterte has the right to pursue all legal remedies in the wake of the ruling.—AOL, GMA News

articles.title: COA flags OVP over relief operations, documentation lapses
articles.summary: In its consolidated audit report on the country's disaster risk reduction and management funds, state auditors reported that the OVP’s relief operations suffered from inconsistent reporting,…

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 5:14pm

MANILA, Philippines — The Commission on Audit (COA) has flagged the Sara Duterte-led Office of the Vice President (OVP) over a series of control and documentation deficiencies in its disaster relief operations, raising concerns over the reliability and verifiability of its distribution records.

In its consolidated audit report on the country's disaster risk reduction and management funds for calendar year 2025, state auditors reported that the OVP’s relief operations suffered from inconsistent reporting, unauthorized operational deviations, “issuance of open-ended mission orders,” and incomplete documentation.

“Control and documentation deficiencies were observed in the implementation of Relief Operations, such as: (a) inconsistencies between Situational Report (SitReps) from the agencies/LGUs concerned and Office of the Vice President (OVP) SitReps; (b) deviations from approved Mission Orders during actual operations; (c) issuance of open-ended Mission Orders; (d) deficiencies in beneficiary documentation and distribution records; and (e) incomplete, missing, or non-submission of required documents, contrary to Section 9.0 of the Policy Manual on Disaster Operations Program dated June 26, 2024 and Section G of OVP Office Order No. 2025-74. These deficiencies reduced assurance on the completeness, reliability, and verifiability of relief distribution records and weakened controls over Relief Operations. (OVP).”

State auditors discovered significant discrepancies between the Situational Reports (SitReps) prepared by local government units or affected agencies and those drafted by the OVP. These inconsistencies involved welfare goods valued at P19.67 million.
The COA noted differences in the reported number of affected families, while some local reports completely lacked beneficiary counts.

“Although management attributed these to evolving disaster conditions and subsequent validation, supporting documents for the revisions were not consistently attached. Consequently, the reliability of the SitReps used as basis for planning relief operations and issuing Mission Orders was diminished,” the COA’s report read.
The COA also called out the OVP for deviating from its own approved Mission Orders during actual field deployments.

State auditors identified 24 relief operations, involving P39,009,054.98 worth of welfare goods, that altered schedules, distribution sites, and the volume of relief items and rice without securing documented approvals.

“The deviations included changes in schedules, distribution locations, quantities of relief items, and the amount of rice distributed. While management cited operational adjustments due to changing field conditions, the absence of documented approvals weakened assurance that the changes were properly authorized and supported,” the COA said.

Furthermore, the OVP issued eight open-ended Mission Orders for distributions totaling P84.12 million. Because these orders failed to specify target beneficiaries, auditors noted that the OVP lacked a concrete basis for determining the exact quantity of goods requested and distributed.
The audit further exposed widespread deficiencies in beneficiary documentation and distribution records.
State auditors also flagged uncertified Master Lists, unsigned Relief Distribution Sheets (RDS), duplicate entries, and incomplete beneficiary information.

In 11 relief operations involving more than 200 beneficiaries, the OVP inappropriately applied documentary requirements meant for individual crises rather than the procedures mandated by its Disaster Operations Policy Manual, leading to inconsistent practices and a lack of verifiability.

Compounding these issues, relief operations serving 33,980 beneficiaries and utilizing P25.27 million in welfare goods completely lacked vital pre-operation documents, such as verified Master Lists and SitReps.

Citing one instance, the COA said that the OVP could not produce the required RDS, claiming the records were lost during Typhoon Kristine, and instead substituted them with explanatory certifications.
Recommendations
The COA has directed the OVP management to implement stricter review procedures over its liquidation and operational documents.
State auditors recommended that the OVP require its satellite offices and disaster personnel to properly document and attach all field adjustments to their Requisition and Issue Slips.

“The Audit Team recommended that OVP Management: a. strengthen the review procedures over Relief Operations to ensure completeness, consistency, and accuracy of operational and liquidation documents; b. require concerned Satellite Offices (SOs) and Disaster Operation Center (DOC) personnel to ensure that adjustments in SitReps, Mission Orders, beneficiary lists, and distribution records are properly documented, supported, and attached to the RIS and that beneficiary documentation, including Master Lists and RDS, are complete, verified, signed, and supported with appropriate authorization when representatives receive relief goods and further strengthen the documentation of operational adjustments and corresponding approvals through activity logs, memoranda, incident reports, or other appropriate records whenever practicable;
Additionally, the OVP was instructed to clearly define the scope of future Mission Orders and ensure that any relief operation exceeding 200 beneficiaries strictly

articles.title: OPAPRU flags online extremist recruitment at ASEAN peace forum
articles.summary: The Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity (OPAPRU) on Wednesday flagged reports of online recruitment into extremist groups, as international delegates gathered for…

blocks.text: Published September 23, 2026 5:13pm

The Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity (OPAPRU) on Wednesday flagged reports of online recruitment into extremist groups, as international delegates gathered for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Peace Education Conference.
Speaking to GMA News Online, Presidential Peace Adviser Secretary Mel Senen Sarmiento described online recruitment into extremist groups as a “modern” and “emerging” threat.

“It’s actually an emerging threat. There are recruitment efforts linked to modern extremism. There is a threat of exposure even on social media, as well as incidents happening in schools nowadays,” Sarmiento said in an interview.
“It’s alarming because it seems that something happens almost every month in the Philippines, among other things, of course,” he added.

According to the United Kingdom government, extremism can contribute to the “radicalization of individuals,” denial of people’s rights and opportunities, incitement of hatred, erosion of democratic institutions, social capital and cohesion, and acts of terrorism.
Sarmiento made the statement following the school shooting in Banga, South Cotabato, where at least three students were killed and eight others were injured.
The student shooter was reportedly part of a “true crime community,” which Banga Mayor Albert Palencia said may have influenced him to copy other shooting incidents.
Challenge to new BARMM Parliament
This year’s ASEAN Peace Education Conference is themed “Peace Education for Shared Futures and Enduring Cooperation.”

Sarmiento underscored the significance of the international forum, saying it allows delegates to engage in dialogue and learn from the peace-related experiences and challenges faced by different countries.
“It’s good because we learn from each other, such as how others addressed a particular problem and how lessons learned from that experience could possibly be applied in other places,” he said.

With regard to the peace process in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), Sarmiento challenged the newly elected Parliament members to set aside their personal interests and work together to advance the region’s development.

“I hope those who won — this is my personal prayer — will set aside, so to speak, their individual thoughts and concerns for the meantime. I hope they all unite because we are always behind and need to catch up,” he said.
“But if all their leaders unite and focus first on strengthening the economy and advancing the development of the BARMM, that would be better,” Sarmiento added.

Sarmiento said OPAPRU will hold a meeting with stakeholders over the weekend as part of the normalization process under the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro (CAB) to address remaining details.
OPAPRU oversees the implementation of the government’s peace agreements with various groups in Mindanao, including the normalization track under the CAB.

The normalization process includes the decommissioning and reintegration of former Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) combatants, as well as other measures intended to help former combatants and their communities transition to peaceful civilian life.
The BARMM held its first parliamentary elections on Monday, September 14, with a final voter turnout of 84.34%, representing 2.02 of the region’s 2.39 million registered voters.

The 80 newly elected Parliament members will assume office on October 30 and elect the region’s chief minister. The first elected officials will serve a five-year term until June 30, 2031.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Diokno: Prosecution's job is the same amid threshold vote
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel said its aim to secure the conviction of Vice President Sara Duterte remains just as tough regardless of the Senate impeachment court's vote on the threshold.

blocks.text: Published September 23, 2026 5:10pm

The House prosecution panel on Wednesday said that its target to secure the conviction of Vice President Sara Duterte remains just as tough regardless of the Senate impeachment court's vote that the threshold to convict depends on the senators who are qualified to vote.

“It never gets easier. Dati nabanggit ko na rin ito, 'yung trabaho ng prosecution and 'yung mismong pinakamalaking hamon sa amin ay magtayo ng bahay ng ebidensya. Mas, in a way, mas madali nga ang trabaho ng defense dahil ang nais lang nila ay sirain ang bahay,” Akbayan Representative and House prosecutor Chel Diokno said in a press conference.
(I have said this before, the prosecution’s job and biggest challenge is building a sturdy house of evidence. In a way, the defense’s job is easier because what they want is to destroy that house.)

“That challenge is the same with whatever numbers are needed [for conviction]. Kaya para sa amin, ‘yung ang focus namin ay talagang mag present ng pinakamaayos at pinaka-solid na evidence. Anuman ang pinal na numero, tuloy ang prosecution sa paglalatag ng mga ebidensya para sa pananagutan at hustisya,” Diokno added.
(That is why our focus is to present a compelling, solid evidence. No matter the threshold, we will soldier on in presenting evidence for accountability and justice.)
The Senate court also determined that the following will be disqualified from voting:

items: detained and/or suspended or otherwise legally restrained from exercising the functions of a senator;
persons sought by authorities whose whereabouts are unknown;
those suffering from a physical or medical incapacity;
those beyond the coercive processes of the Senate; and
others similarly situated.

blocks.text: Asked if the prosecution is worried that the six Senator judges who did not vote on the threshold would also boycott the the voting on the final question whether to convict or acquit the Vice President, Diokno said it is up for the Senate impeachment court to decide and prosecution’s focus is to present airtight evidence against the Vice President.
“We expect that the process that is commanded by the Constitution will continue, at ipagpapatuloy po namin ang aming tungkulin din bilang mga prosecutor,” he said.
(We will proceed with our duties as a prosecutor.)

It was Diokno who argued for the prosecution’s position, saying that an acquittal cannot be secured by default. Heargued that the case must be decided based on evidence, not by the inclusion of Senators who are absent in the denominator in determining the two-thirds of all the members of the Senate.

“There's no substitute for being here in person. In fact, I believe that that would be fair to the respondent. that everyone would be present here and physically able to assess the evidence. Sa tingin ko po, as far as whether the question of participation of the judges is concerned, is really meant to safeguard the respondent,” Diokno said during the questioning of Senator judge Alan Peter Cayetano.

“And that is why we believe that it's important that all the members of the court who will decide and vote on this case should be able to hear and see the evidence right here, inside the courtroom,” Diokno added. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: A ‘grubby rumour’ and a $5m extortion attempt: former Toplace executive gives Icac evidence
articles.summary: Sharangan Maheswaran also told inquiry his bid for story on unsubstantiated rumour about then-Liberal minister David Elliott was ‘not a serious offer’

blocks.text: A purported $5m extortion attempt of fugitive property developer Jean Nassif was actually a genuine request for his company Toplace to pay a contractor, a lawyer assisting the New South Wales anti-corruption watchdog has argued.

Former Toplace lawyer and executive Sharangan Maheswaran told the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Wednesday he had not “dishonestly conveyed” to the building commissioner, David Chandler, that someone had attempted to extort Nassif on Chandler’s behalf.

Icac is investigating the allegation that Liberal figures Christian Ellis, Jeremy Greenwood and Charles Perrottet took $2m in illegal donations from Nassif or Toplace in exchange for political outcomes.

Greenwood and Perrottet have denied payments were for political outcomes. Ellis has moved overseas and is not expected to give evidence. Nassif, in an appearance from his Beirut bedroom, insisted he was “not corrupt”. Maheswaran, who is named in a separate allegation by Icac, has denied any wrongdoing.

The alleged outcomes include damage to the political career of Liberal minister, David Elliott, who had opposed Toplace developments, and the removal of the building commissioner, David Chandler, who had been scrutinising defects in Toplace apartments.

The commission has previously heard that Nassif claimed two individuals had asked him for $5m on Chandler’s behalf to lift prohibition orders on Toplace developments. Maheswaran subsequently passed on details of the alleged extortion attempt to Charles Perrottet.
Chandler is not named as a person of interest in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of any wrongdoing.

On Wednesday, the commission heard a phone call recorded by Nassif with one of the alleged individuals, contractor Navid Ardestani, who is not named in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of any wrongdoing.

“Navid mate,” Nassif began the call. “I didn’t know you were so fucking powerful, mate”, he continued, accusing Ardestani of sending a “report” to the building commissioner. Earlier on Wednesday, the commission heard that Nassif had become suspicious of Toplace contractors after a report about apartment defects had been passed on to Chandler.
In the call, Ardestani responded, “which report you talking about, sir?”, subsequently requesting a face-to-face meeting with Nassif.
“You can’t see me. You’re a fucking lying cunt. Bye,” Nassif ended the call.

Maheswaran was taken to messages between Ardestani and Nassif after a subsequent meeting between the two men, in which Ardestani wrote that “purpose of this meeting was to get my mate, the builder, to come and fix the issues that the building commissioner requested to be fixed”.

Maheswaran accepted counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer’s suggestion there was “nothing threatening about that”. She put it to him that this was “clearly a request for payment so that remediation works can take place on Jean Nassif’s building”.
He rejected this, saying it was inconsistent with an audio recording of the meeting, which the commission is expected to hear on Thursday.

The commission heard that Maheswaran had already met with Chandler about the alleged extortion attempt, with the building commissioner suggesting they go to the police. Chandler himself subsequently reported it to his departmental head, and was cleared by an internal audit.
Asked why he did not share details of the people allegedly involved in the extortion attempt with Chandler, Maheswaran said he did not think it was relevant.
“Mr Nassif was taking this very, very seriously, was contemplating paying $5m to these people and from my perspective this was obviously not something that was real.”
“The best way to dispel that illusion in Mr Nassif’s mind [was] to raise it with the commissioner with whom we had a good relationship”.

Dwyer later said: “I’m suggesting to you, I want to put it straight, that you dishonestly conveyed to Mr Chandler that there had been a genuine extortion or shakedown attempt from an anonymous person,” he said.
after newsletter promotion
“I absolutely deny that,” said Maheswaran.
A ‘grubby rumour’

On Wednesday morning, Maheswaran accepted he had given a private investigator, “Mr Nanetti”, Elliott’s address in 2020 to investigate a rumour that the MP was breaching Covid-19 restrictions to conduct an extramarital affair. Maheswaran accepted he now knew the rumour to be untrue.

In a statement and evidence to the commission, Elliott has strongly rejected the allegation of an extramarital affair or breach of Covid-19 restrictions. Multiple witnesses have accepted there was no evidence for the allegation.
He said Nanetti initially made “observations” at Elliott’s address as a favour, but he subsequently paid him $1,000 to return to Elliott’s address, where he took photographs.
Dwyer asked him if he had offered Greenwood $1,000 to place a story with a journalist.

Maheswaran said he had, but told the commission it was “not a serious offer”. Dwyer took him to the messages: “You say: ‘1000 bucks if you can get the yarn up’, and Greenwood says ‘Hahaha’, and you reply, ‘Not joking!’”.

The commission heard the men unsuccessfully tried to place the story with the Daily Telegraph, including providing photos of Elliott in a car with a woman who was not his wife and a draft statutory declaration by the private investigator. Elliott has said photographs show him signing documents for work purposes.
Dwyer, who described the story as a “grubby rumour” to which there was no truth, suggested that Maheswaran was “persistent” because he was pursuing a political outcome sought by Nassif.

Maheswaran rejected that, saying he had a “decade of track record pitching stories that are adverse to Liberal National MPs, ministers”. He said Nassif was the source of the rumour about Elliott, but had not requested the story be placed.
Maheswaran is expected to continue giving evidence to the commission on Thursday and Friday. He is the final scheduled witness across nine weeks of public hearings.
Icac’s inquiry continues.

articles.title: A battery fire at a P.E.I. solar farm is finally out. Canada may not be ready for more
articles.summary: The solar farm battery fire in Summerside, P.E.I., is now deemed out, but fire experts say what happened there should concern communities far beyond the Island.

image.caption: Fire and explosion investigation expert Richard Meier says lithium‑ion battery fires are hard to put out because you can’t just smother them. The batteries can create their own oxygen‑like chemicals, so cutting off air doesn’t work the way it does with a typical fire. (Richard Meier)

blocks.text: PEI·New
The solar farm battery fire in Summerside, P.E.I., is now deemed out, but fire experts say what happened there should concern communities far beyond the Island.
'We’re a bit behind the eight ball,' says Canadian Volunteer Fire Services Association vice-president
Summerside solar farm fire is out after 2 weeks, city says
The blaze at the Summerside Sunbank is believed to have started on Labour Day, Sept. 7, in a battery bank.
It led to a shelter in place order and a voluntary evacuation notice for nearby residents because of the potential risk from toxic smoke. The city deemed the fire to be out on Monday after two weeks.

items: Summerside deems solar farm fire to be out as response moves into recovery phase
Life in Summerside returning to normal after 'volatile few days' of solar farm fire

blocks.text: Fire and explosion investigation expert Richard Meier said these kinds of fires can last a long time and don't behave the way most people imagine.
"You can’t really put it out in the traditional sense of you’re starving it of oxygen," Meier told Mainstreet P.E.I. host Mitch Cormier.

Across Canada, large lithium-ion battery systems are being added to the grid to store renewable energy, including in rural areas and small communities protected by volunteer fire departments, just like Summerside.

The fire in P.E.I.’s second-largest city is now out, but it has raised a bigger national question: are Canadian fire services prepared to handle the long-lasting, difficult battery fires that can come with the clean energy transition?
'Coming out like a flamethrower'
Meier said large lithium-ion battery fires can be difficult to control because tightly packed cells can keep setting one another off.
"We're dealing with a fire of lithium-ion batteries in … what's basically essentially a shipping container. So we're talking about a lot of large batteries," he said.
If a battery cell overheats, is damaged or is overcharged, a separator inside can fail, causing a short circuit and a rapid rise in temperature.
That can trigger what's called thermal runaway — a chain reaction in which one failing cell generates enough heat to ignite or damage the cells around it.
Meier said the batteries also contain a flammable liquid electrolyte.

"It’s similar in consistency to kerosene," he said. "If you have a battery that goes into thermal runaway, now you’re superheating this flammable material.… It’s basically coming out like a flamethrower."
And when these batteries break down, they can make their own chemical that behaves like oxygen, meaning firefighters can't simply smother the fire by cutting off the air, he said.

Instead, Meier said, firefighters may have limited access to the individual cells and have to focus on cooling the batteries enough to stop the chain reaction. That was the approach used during the Summerside fire.

items: Firefighter safety is getting more costly. Some P.E.I. stations are going into debt to keep up
No money for new full-time firefighters in Charlottetown budget draws union criticism

blocks.text: For Paul Maynard, vice-president of the Canadian Volunteer Fire Services Association, Summerside’s ordeal points to a growing challenge across the country.

"We know there have been a number of incidents across the country that involve everything from battery storage facilities to even smaller equipment," Maynard said, pointing to electric and hybrid vehicles, e‑bikes, scooters and power tools.
The challenge can be particularly significant in rural areas, where departments often rely heavily on volunteers.
"Most of Canada relies on, in our rural areas, volunteers," he said. "These incidents can be very time consuming and resource heavy."
Maynard said departments are being asked to handle complex calls of long duration with limited people and equipment.
He also said there are gaps in training and preparation on a national level.
"The technology seems to be evolving faster than what … the public safety system can kind of keep up to," he said.
Maynard said Canada needs a national strategy for dealing with these fires, covering everything from how sites are marked and identified to common training and tactics.
That would bring together emergency management co-ordinators, firefighters, manufacturers and other stakeholders, he said.

He said fire services also need to understand what is in their communities — from battery storage and solar sites to EV charging stations and residential solar installations — and be equipped and trained accordingly.
"We’re a bit behind the eight ball for sure," Maynard said.
'I don’t think the technology is going away'
Meier said physical design changes can also reduce the risk that a failing battery container triggers others nearby.
"If you want to keep it safe as possible, put enough room between these that they’re not sitting next to each other," he said.
"Just treat it like you would explosives in a depot: you put space between them, you put berms between them so that one doesn’t cause the other to go off."
Here's what P.E.I. firefighters are learning about battling ever-evolving types of fires
Maynard said manufacturers also need to involve firefighters much earlier, not just after their systems are already in the field.
"Manufacturers really have to view firefighters as almost design stakeholders, not simply end users of emergency information," he said.
At the end of the day, Maynard said, he is not arguing against clean energy.
"I don’t think the technology is going away," he said. "It’s just going to continue to grow and grow.… So we have to figure out ways to support that."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Thinh Nguyen is a digital reporter with CBC P.E.I. He can be reached at thinh.duc.nguyen@cbc.ca

articles.title: UNGA: World leaders discuss AI, global conflicts
articles.summary: As the UN General Assembly starts its second day, much attention will turn to the war in Iran, artificial intelligence and climate change. Follow live.
articles.byline: Wesley Dockery, Mark Hallam, Felix Tamsut, Jon Shelton

image.caption: The annual UN General Assembly runs until September 28Image: David Dee Delgado/REUTERS

blocks.text: September 23, 2026
UNGA day 2: AI, Iran war, climate to dominate debate

blocks.caption: World leaders still have plenty to talk about as the UN General Assembly begins its second dayImage: Charles Guerin/ABACA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Beyond speeches by the presidents of Syria, Iran and Ukraine, artificial intelligence (AI), the US-Israeli war in Iran and the still-pressing issue of climate change are set to dominate the agenda at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Wednesday.

On day 2 of this 81st UNGA session, tech industry leaders Sam Altman (OpenAI), Dario Amodei (Anthropic) and Clement Delangue (Hugging Face) will brief an emergency meeting of the 15-member UN Security Council. Their attendance comes as international concerns — raised from within the industry — prompt debate over slowing AI development before the new technology potentially spins out of control with unknown consequences.
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday blasted calls to slow the technology as part of a "globalist scheme," brushing aside warnings that it could wipe out humanity within years if left unchecked.

After Trump used his General Assembly speech on Tuesday to threaten the annihilation of Iran and to drive its people to hell, the Islamic Republic's President Masoud Pezeshkian will directly address world leaders for the first time since the start of the war against Iran in February.
The conflict in Iran has settled into a hot stalemate, directly impacting neighboring states militarily and the entire globe economically.

Iranian and US representatives have met on the sidelines of the General Assembly in New York, but, as has been the case for months, a peace deal remains elusive and the flow of oil through the blockaded Strait of Hormuz stunted.

Russia's more than four-and-a-half-year full-scale assault on Ukraine will also be the topic of diplomatic debate on Wednesday, with a Security Council session scheduled for the morning and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy set to address the General Assembly in the afternoon.
Lastly, climate urgency is on the slate, with outgoing UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres blasting fossil fuel giants for treating the Earth's atmosphere like an "open sewer" for emissions.
He further chided "big oil" for its greed as the world grapples with armed conflict.

"Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, five major Western oil companies have pocketed nearly half a trillion dollars in profits," he said, noting that at the same time just $34 billion (€29.8 billion) had been invested in helping developing countries adapt to a warming world.
Editing:Sean Sinico

articles.title: China's new travel rules unsettle tech giants and talent
articles.summary: Beijing is locking the gates to stop expertise and capital in strategic industries from fleeing. The country accused of industrial-scale intellectual property theft now fears the West will take its…

image.caption: China wants its best minds to stay, while adding extra scrutiny for foreign expertsImage: Wang Yu/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: For decades, China has faced accusations from the United States and the European Union of stealing their technology.

From robotics and advanced semiconductors to precision engineering and automotive parts, Chinese firms have recruited top engineers, allegedly spied on Western rivals and been linked to cyberattacks aimed at gaining access to valuable trade secrets.
It is perhaps ironic, then, that Beijing is now taking steps to prevent its own high-end technologies and talent from escaping abroad.
How China is upping pressure on German businesses
China's Great Wall around its top brains

Last week, new entry-exit rules took effect, giving Chinese authorities the power to stop engineers, founders and other specialists from leaving the country if their expertise in batteries, rare earths or artificial intelligence (AI) is judged a threat to "industrial and technological security."
Recently, Beijing has also tightened outbound-investment rules, cracked down on Chinese nationals holding their wealth offshore and restricted the posting of technical staff overseas.
Henry Gao, a law professor at Singapore Management University (SMU), believes that, taken together, the curbs "offer a rare glimpse into the true state of China's economy."

"These measures suggest that Beijing is deeply concerned about economic weakness and substantial capital outflows," Gao told DW, adding that authorities are also determined to stop "entrepreneurs and skilled personnel from leaving the country."

The strain on China's economy is increasingly hard to hide. While demand for exports remains strong — especially for high-tech goods — the country's property crash has severely weakened domestic consumption, with bank lending falling to a record low over the summer and new car sales in August dropping nearly a quarter year-on-year.

blocks.caption: China blocked Meta's takeover of AI startup Manus and stopped its founders from leaving the countryImage: VCG/IMAGO

blocks.text: Beijing blocks deals, founders seek exit

The same anxiety now extends to people and money leaving. The most prominent recent example is Manus, an AI startup created by two Chinese nationals in Beijing. Last year, the company moved its headquarters to Singapore, partly to avoid US investment curbs and expand into global markets.
When Facebook owner Meta tried to acquire Manus last December for $2 billion (€1.74 billion), Beijing blocked the move and barred the firm's two founders from leaving the country.
Just this month, Chinese social media has been awash with rumors that Huawei founder and CEO Ren Zhengfei and his daughter, CFO Meng Wanzhou, may have left the country.

The claims were picked up by Taiwanese and Indian media outlets, but have not been confirmed by the tech giant and Chinese authorities. At least one family member has since appeared in public in Beijing.
Wealthy Chinese struggle to get capital out
Bloomberg Intelligence estimated that some $1 trillion in Chinese wealth had exited the country last year — the largest amount of "hot money" leaving since 2006, when records began.

Beijing has not tightened its annual $50,000 foreign-exchange quota that households may take out of the country. What has tightened, says Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for Asia-Pacific at French investment bank Natixis, are the unofficial routes the wealthy used around that cap.
"They haven't changed the $50,000 quota. They are now squeezing the people and agents that money usually travels with," Garcia-Herrero told DW.

An entire industry has grown up, in China and abroad, to help people get themselves and their capital out. Emigration agents arrange visas and relocations, while offshore brokers and trusts help Chinese nationals to park wealth overseas.
Companies sometimes use a foreign subsidiary, a listing or a staff posting to take money and know-how out together.
AI's expanding power alarms China's intelligence agency
New rules may spur workarounds

SMU's Gao believes the new curbs may prove counterproductive, as the more difficult it becomes to move capital or people abroad, the greater the incentive for those with the means to find other ways out.
"Over time, that could further erode confidence, accelerate capital flight and deepen the very economic problems the measures are intended to contain," Gao told DW.
Garcia-Herrero, meanwhile, thinks the block on talent will matter more than the squeeze on capital.

"You can still move money slowly, with approvals," she told DW. "You cannot easily replace a process engineer who cannot board a plane — or who will not take an overseas job because of an indefinite ban."
AI talent now needs permission to fly
The risk is already hitting China's AI firms, which are fast catching up with their US rivals in the race to produce the most advanced AI systems.
In May, Bloomberg reported that Chinese authorities now required top AI researchers, founders and executives at firms like Alibaba and DeepSeek to obtain approval before traveling abroad.
Last year, some DeepSeek staff were asked to hand in their passports, according to tech news site The Information. Beijing has neither confirmed nor denied the practice.
Bloomberg reported in January last year that other tech engineers face similar pressure, including those helping foreign firms cut their reliance on China by building factories in Vietnam and India.

blocks.caption: Trips to China by foreign nationals are increasingly being watchedImage: Rafael Ben-Ari/Chameleons Eye/Newscom/picture alliance

blocks.text: Lawyers and officials tighten legal advice

For foreign nationals, both Chinese and foreign firms sometimes disguise a working visit to China to avoid scrutiny and visa delays. They may suggest a trip is for tourism, business meetings or a factory tour rather than actual work.

Ahead of the new curbs, international law firms like DLA Piper advised companies to keep visa filings "truthful" and "complete," warning that a mismatch between the paperwork and the actual work could now mean an entry ban of up to five years.

The new rules state that a visitor should, in principle, be told if they are banned. However, Chinese authorities may withhold notification if it "may affect national security or the investigation of criminal cases."

In an updated travel advisory earlier this month, the US State Department went further, warning Americans to "exercise increased caution in mainland China due to ... the use of exit bans without a fair and transparent process under the law, and the risk of unjust arrest or detention."

articles.title: Jonvic Remulla admits error on Harry Roque’s asylum status
articles.summary: In an interview with reporters on Tuesday, September 22, Remulla said that Roque's status is currently "in limbo.”

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 4:44pm
In a video uploaded on Nov. 25, 2025, Harry Roque says he will file a motion for reconsideration after a court approved the Philippine government’s request to cancel his passport.
Harry Roque via Facebook / Philstar.com's screenshot
MANILA, Philippines — Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla admitted he was mistaken regarding his previous claims that former presidential spokesperson Harry Roque’s asylum application had been denied.
In an interview with reporters on Tuesday, September 22, Remulla said that Roque's status is currently "in limbo.”
“I was wrong...status now is in limbo,” Remulla said.
According to Remulla, while a decision on an asylum application is normally handed down within six months, Roque's case remains unresolved despite nine months having passed since he applied.
“In his case, it's neither denied nor accepted. So under the eyes of the law, he still does not have asylum,” Remulla said.
(In his case, it is neither denied nor accepted. So in the eyes of the law, he still does not have asylum.)
Remulla also said they are assessing whether an individual granted asylum would be immune from an Interpol red notice.
“We think that there is no reason not to bring him in,” he said.
On September 15, Remulla claimed that Roque’s asylum bid had been denied, which was disputed by the former human rights lawyer.
Roque is currently facing non-bailable qualified human trafficking charges tied to the raided Lucky South 99 POGO hub in Porac, Pampanga, and remains in Austria, where he is seeking asylum.
An Angeles City court ordered his arrest in May 2025, following his undocumented departure from the Philippines in 2024 as law enforcement began hunting for him.

articles.title: DOLE sets guidelines for workers’ protection from air hazards
articles.summary: The guidelines in assessing workers’ exposure to “elevated air pollutants” were outlined in Labor Advisory No. 15 released on Monday, September 21.

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 4:40pm

This aerial photo taken from a commercial plane shows haze from Indonesian forest fires blanketing a residential district in Kuching, the capital city of Sarawak state on the island of Borneo on September 5, 2026.
AFP / Mohd Rasfan
MANILA, Philippines — Private sector employers are directed to implement safety protocols to protect workers from air hazards under the Department of Labor and Employment’s (DOLE) new labor advisory.
The guidelines in assessing workers’ exposure to “elevated air pollutants” were outlined in Labor Advisory No. 15 released on Monday, September 21.

Under the directive, employers are required to conduct a Hazard Identification, Risk Assessment, and Control (HIRAC) to determine their workers’ exposure to smoke, haze and other air pollutants and to prevent potential health dangers.

The Air Quality Index Matrix and Action Points (AQIMAP) issued by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) and the Department of Health (DOH) was recommended to be used as the basis in conducting the assessment.

“The HIRAC shall be reviewed and updated periodically and whenever there is a material change in the AQIMAP level, workplace conditions, nature or extent of workers' exposure, or other circumstances that may affect the assessed risk,” DOLE’s advisory reads.
The labor agency’s advisory came after reports of poor and unhealthy air quality in Metro Manila earlier this month, as smoke and haze from forest fires in Indonesia reached the Philippines.
Implementation
The labor agency also laid out the specific ideal responses of employers for each air quality index (AQI) level.

For unhealthy levels, employers are advised to monitor the air quality levels, provide personal protective equipment in case outdoor work is unavoidable, improve ventilation in enclosed areas, and limit or reschedule outdoor activities.
“Personal protective equipment shall not be used as a substitute for feasible engineering or administrative controls,” the advisory read.

Meanwhile, for acutely unhealthy air quality, employers are urged to implement flexible work arrangements. Workers who are required to report to work physically must be provided with appropriate protective equipment.
In times of emergency, employers are advised to suspend work.
Those who are involved in public utilities and health services are encouraged to maintain a skeleton force, or minimum personnel, to continue operations.

articles.title: Famine threatens the Ukrainian town of Oleshky in the southern Kherson region as Russia delays creating a humanitarian evacuation corridor
articles.summary: Food supplies to the town of Oleshky in the occupied part of the southern Kherson region have been cut off since May. Efforts by Kyiv to negotiate the evacuation of civilians with Moscow have been…

image.caption: The town of Oleshky has been cut off from food deliveries since May, prompting famine for the around 6,000 residents left in the townImage: VALENTYN OGIRENKO/REUTERS

blocks.text: A man sends a photo of "Oleshky borsch," a vegetable soup he has made from leftovers. To make the soup more filling, he says he has added millet and two eggs.

"Today, we have a delicacy in our borsch. My mother traded 2.5 kilograms (5.5 pounds) of sugar for 10 eggs," he tells the recipient of the photo, Tetiana Hasanenko, the head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, which is based in territory controlled by Kyiv. "There's no cabbage in it, but there is asparagus," he adds.

Hasanenko says she's used to getting such messages. "I receive reports like this every day," Hasanenko told DW. "People want to be given some kind of hope, but there is no hope." She said food was last delivered to the town at the end of May. "The situation is critical," she said, warning that "you can't just call this starvation — it's a famine."

Oleshky is located in Ukraine'ssouthern Kherson region on the left bank of the Dnipro River. The city has been occupied since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion.Russia's full-scale invasionin February 2022.
In June 2023, the town was almost completely flooded after a blast at the Kakhovka Power Plant and the breach of the Kakhovka Dam.

Hasanenko said the situation worsened last winter. She said there were about 6,000 people left in the area, including 180 children. They have already become accustomed to living without electricity and gas and have to fetch water from wells. Now, they have to prepare for another harsh winter.

blocks.caption: The destruction of the Kakhovka Dam in southern Ukraine has flooded Oleshky and left many basements full of food inaccessible for monthsImage: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: 'One kilo of zucchini for 1,000 rubles'

"To be honest, I haven't eaten anything yet," resident Halyna (whose name has been changed for security reasons) told DW by phone at around lunchtime. "My best option for today is a flatbread made of water and flour, as there's still some left. I spread apple sauce on it and make myself some tea without sugar. That's about it."

People only go out between 7 a.m. and 9 a.m., she explained, adding that they tended to gather in the market square to hear the latest news and would trade or sell food from their supplies or gardens.

"Today, there were a few zucchinis for 1,000 rubles (€10 or $11.4) per kilo," she said, adding that someone had sold a large sack of flour for 200,000 rubles. She speculated that he was probably going to try to leave Oleshky, which is why the price was so high.

Minibuses used to run from Oleshky to Skadovsk about an hour south and then to Crimea or Russia. They also transported food to Oleshky for sale. After they were attacked by drones, two ambulances were deployed instead. "But for the past month and a half, none of the ambulances have been running, because one of the drivers was killed on a trip," Halyna reported.
She explained that people are now stocking up on food in the village of Radensk, located 20 kilometers (12.4 miles) to the south. People walk there or ride their bikes.

Anyone who wants to be evacuated must reach the village of Tarasivka, which is another 20 kilometers away. From there, you can get to Skadovsk by minibus or by hitchhiking. However, the route is heavily mined. "You set out and could die along the way," Halyna said, adding that two women who were trying to get food died that way.
According to Halyna, scores of people in Oleshky have been injured by mines and explosive devices. But they can't count on medical help.

"If your leg is blown off, you're as good as dead. There's a surgeon at the hospital, but no anesthesiologist and no medicine," she said. Conditions are also deteriorating for inpatients. "Last winter, they still got some soup and two pieces of baked dough," she said, adding that now there's one and a half spoonfuls of semolina porridge cooked in water and cold tea.
Moreover, evacuating from Oleshky is difficult not only because of the danger of landmines. Many residents have neither a Russian nor a Ukrainian passport. In addition, people lack cash.

blocks.caption: Ukrainian authorities say that Russia has been slow in creating a humanitarian evacuation corridor for the trapped civiliansImage: Metin Aktas/Anadolu Agency/picture alliance

blocks.text: Moscow lacks evacuation willingness

"There is only one solution: A 'green corridor' must be established and the people evacuated. The occupying authorities must move the people deeper into the temporarily occupied territory," says Tetiana Hasanenko of the Ukrainian military administration.

Talks about an evacuation from Oleshky have been ongoing since last spring. At that time, at the initiative of the Ukrainian parliamentary human rights commissioner, Dmytro Lubinets, city officials compiled a list of residents who wish to leave the municipality of Oleshky.

"358 people need to be evacuated urgently," he wrote on social media. "These are only the ones we've heard about," he emphasized, noting that the town of Oleshky currently has more than 6,000 residents. "These people must be rescued because the town has become a death trap," the ombudsman said.

According to him, preliminary agreements had been reached between Kyiv and Moscow. The Ukrainian military was to ensure a ceasefire, and the International Committee of the Red Cross was to assist with the evacuation. But Russia "has not reaffirmed its willingness" to carry out the evacuation "for quite some time," Lubinets said.

Meanwhile, the residents of Oleshky are desperate, says Tetiana Hasanenko. "They had hoped that the evacuation would begin at any moment. But what now? I can't give them any hope at all," she laments.
Russia steps up drone attacks on Ukraine's Kherson
This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

articles.title: Malacañang dismisses 'presidential pork barrel' claim on LGSF as intrigue
articles.summary: Malacañang on Wednesday again defended the proposed P58.53-billion allocation for the Local Government Support Fund (LGSF) in the 2027 national budget after critics, led by Caloocan City Rep. Edgar…

blocks.text: Published September 23, 2026 4:22pm

Malacañang on Wednesday again defended the proposed P58.53-billion allocation for the Local Government Support Fund (LGSF) in the 2027 national budget after critics, led by Caloocan City Rep. Edgar Erice, described it as a “presidential pork barrel.”
Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said describing the LGSF as a presidential pork barrel was merely “pang-intriga” (for intrigue).

“Karapatan niyang tumakbo kahit saang korte pero dapat siguraduhin lamang po niya na mayroong basehan dahil kung mabibigyan lamang siya o aaralin po niya ang proseso kung paano nairi-release ang LGSF sa mga LGU (local government units), malamang ay maliwanagan po siya,” Castro said, referring to Erice.

(It is his right to go to whatever court, but he should make sure that there is a basis because if he is given [the information], or if he studies the process of how the LGSF is released to LGUs, he will likely be enlightened.)

Castro made the statement in response to Erice’s questioning of the proposed LGSF allocation under the 2027 National Expenditure Program and his suggestion that he could bring the matter before the Supreme Court if necessary.

Erice said granting the executive department the power to decide on LGSF allocations effectively gives the President a “blank check” and amounts to Congress abdicating its constitutionally mandated power of the purse.

Erice has repeatedly cited the LGSF allocation granted to Naga City for the rehabilitation of the Jesse Robredo Coliseum. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. personally presented the allocation to Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo, which Erice said gave the impression that the administration was courting her as a potential candidate.
Castro said that although she did not want to mention Robredo’s name again in the issue, the Naga City mayor had already explained how the local government applied for the LGSF.

“As soon as I assumed office in 2025, I tried to look for funding already for its rehabilitation. It was difficult because of the big amount that is required. Senator Kiko Pangilinan advised me that we could apply for LGSF funding because of the nature of the project, which we did,” Robredo wrote in a Facebook post.
Castro also pointed to the Supreme Court’s ruling in Belgica v. Executive Secretary, which she said did not prohibit the LGSF.
“Hindi po ipinagbabawal ng Supreme Court ang LGSF,” Castro said.
(The Supreme Court does not prohibit the LGSF.)

The Supreme Court, in its 2013 ruling in Belgica v. Ochoa, declared the Priority Development Assistance Fund (PDAF) and similar congressional pork barrel mechanisms unconstitutional, saying they allowed lawmakers to intervene in the post-enactment stages of budget execution.
The Court also struck down provisions granting broad discretion to the President over certain lump-sum funds for failing to meet the constitutional requirement of sufficient standards.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Mark Villar, facing graft complaints, breaks from minority on VP Sara threshold vote
articles.summary: Sen. Mark Villar twice strayed from the Senate minority bloc on Wednesday, September 23, by abstaining from his bloc's bid to block the threshold vote, then joining the majority in lowering the bar…

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 4:22pm
Senator-judge Mark Villar attends Day 2 of the impeachment trial at the Senate in Pasay City.
Mark Villar via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Mark Villar twice strayed from the Senate minority bloc on Wednesday, September 23, by abstaining from his bloc's bid to block the threshold vote, then joining the majority in lowering the bar for convicting Vice President Sara Duterte.

Villar was the only minority senator to take part in the second vote that sought to settle the question raised by Sen. Erwin Tulfo whether the 16-bar threshold for conviction should still hold given four senators' absence from the trial.
Thirteen senators including Villar voted in favor, while Presiding Officer Sen. Chiz Escudero cast the lone vote against overturning the ruling he himself issued when the trial opened in July.

The rest of the minority bloc members chose to boycott the proceedings and keep out of the chamber during the vote, namely Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano, Sen. Pia Cayetano, Sen. Bong Go, Sen. Imee Marcos, Sen. Camille Villar and Sen. Robin Padilla.

Cayetano earlier raised a point of order in an attempt to prevent the court from holding a vote at all. He argued the court had no authority to reopen the threshold in the middle of the trial and that the question belonged to the Supreme Court.

To address Cayetano's point of order, Escudero divided the house and called for a vote. Thirteen senator-judges voted to shoot down Cayetano's appeal, while the five other minority senators present backed Cayetano. Villar abstained.
Legal issues

Both Mark and Camille Villar are among the members of their family facing criminal and administrative complaints the Ombudsman filed last Friday over PrimeWater Infrastructure Corp.'s water district deals.

The agency found the joint ventures grossly disadvantageous to the government. It identified the senator, who served as public works secretary from 2016 to 2021 under then-President Rodrigo Duterte, as the company's beneficial owner.

It was against this backdrop that Camille made a rare emotional interjection earlier Wednesday to urge her colleagues to stop invoking the criminal cases of the senators who have missed the trial. Two of the four, Senators Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada, are detained on nonbailable plunder charges.

"Lahat naman po ng wala dito, hindi naman po sila napatunayan na may sala. Hindi po sila plunderer. Hindi po sila magnanakaw," she said. (Those who are not here have not been proven guilty. They are not plunderers. They are not thieves).

She was answering Sen. Erwin Tulfo, who had argued that the framers of the 1987 Constituion never anticipated senators facing plunder charges, since those in their time faced subversion, sedition and rebellion.
Tulfo later said he had called no one a convicted plunderer and was merely speaking of the reality that four senators cannot take part in the trial.
Hours later, Camille left the chamber with the rest of the bloc. After the lunch break, she was seen briefly returning to the Chamber and conversing with her brother before leaving.
The court ruled on Wednesday that the two-thirds needed to convict will be computed only from senators legally and factually capable of taking part when the verdict is called.
Excluded are senators who are detained, suspended, medically incapacitated or beyond the Senate's coercive processes and others similarly situated.

articles.title: Sara Duterte trial: Prosecution gets more viable conviction path after threshold ruling
articles.summary: There are no premature celebrations though for the prosecution, which believes securing a guilty verdict against the Vice President remains a challenging task

blocks.text: PROSECUTOR. Rep. Chel Diokno makes a manifestation during Day 7 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on July 20, 2026.
Senate Social Media Unit
There are no premature celebrations though for the prosecution, which believes securing a guilty verdict against the Vice President remains a challenging task

items: The impeachment court's ruling prevents absentee senators from voting, potentially aiding the prosecution in securing a conviction against Vice President Sara Duterte.
Prosecutors acknowledge that while the ruling may change the voting dynamics, their task remains challenging as they must build a strong case against the defense.
The new ruling reduces the voting denominator from 24 to 20, affecting both the conviction and acquittal thresholds, which could have implications for both the prosecution and defense.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The impeachment court ruling that barred absentee senators from voting in the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte effectively gives the prosecution a more feasible path to securing her conviction.
But there are no premature celebrations for the prosecution, which believes the challenge remains the same.

“The prosecution’s job is to build a house of evidence. In a way, the defense’s job is actually easier because they only want to tear down the house,” prosecutor Chel Diokno said in a press conference after Wednesday’s trial, September 23. “It never gets easier.”

blocks.caption: Sara Duterte trial: Prosecution gets more viable conviction path after threshold ruling

blocks.text: “We don’t view it in terms of whether the job has become harder or not. What’s more important for us at this point is to properly lay out the evidence and continue the proceedings until the end,” prosecutor Terry Ridon added.
The new decision overturns presiding officer Chiz Escudero’s July 6 ruling, which had kept the conviction threshold at 16 votes.

Under the latest ruling, the impeachment court won’t count in the voting total those who are detained, suspended, legally restrained from voting, have unknown whereabouts, and/or are suffering from physical and medical incapacity.
The descriptions fit at least four senators: jailed plunder defendants Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta, fugitive Bato dela Rosa, and Loren Legarda who has been on medical leave.
This could bring down the new denominator from 24 to 20. Two-thirds of that, which is the constitutional conviction threshold, is equivalent to 14.
But the prosecution pointed out that a reduced voting denominator also benefits the defense, because it will also lower the acquittal threshold.
“It’s a two-way consequence for both the defense and the prosecution,” Luistro said.

blocks.caption: Sara Duterte trial: Prosecution gets more viable conviction path after threshold ruling

blocks.text: Diokno, who represented the prosecution during the oral arguments, insisted that absentee senators should not be able to vote because it will be tantamount to an acquittal by default.

“Their inability to participate is beyond dispute. And yet, if the denominator is fixed at twenty-four, conviction would always require sixteen votes. This is absurd,” Diokno told the court on Wednesday morning. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Minority member Mark Villar votes for lower threshold
articles.summary: Senator Mark Villar on Wednesday voted "yes" to lower the threshold to convict Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial, despite being a member of the senate minority.

blocks.text: Published September 23, 2026 4:04pm
Senator Mark Villar on Wednesday voted "yes" to lower the threshold to convict Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial, despite being a member of the senate minority.
He was the lone senator from the minority to do so as Senate minority leader Alan Peter Cayetano, and five others from the group did not participate in the voting.
Among them, Senators Pia Cayetano, Christopher "Bong" Go, Imee Marcos, Robin Padilla, and Mark's sister, Camille Villar.
Senator Mark Villar has yet to give an explanation on his vote. His sister, Camille, has also yet to issue a statement.
GMA News Online has reached out to Mark Villar for comment, but he has yet to reply as of posting time.

The Senate impeachment court on Wednesday has voted to lower the threshold required to convict Duterte in her impeachment trial by setting it to two-thirds of the senator-judges who are legally allowed to participate in the proceedings.

Thirteen senator-judges voted in favor of the motion put forward by Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo, who sought reconsideration of the July 6 ruling that set the voting threshold at 16 which is two-thirds of the 24-member Senate.

“It means that for purposes of determining the two-thirds concurrence vote required for conviction under Article 11, Section 3.6, the phrase 'All members of the Senate' shall refer only to those members who, at the time of the vote, remain legally and factually capable of participating in the impeachment proceedings," Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero said.
He said excluded members are those:

items: detained and/or suspended or otherwise legally restrained from exercising the functions of a senator,
persons sought by authorities and whose whereabouts are unknown,
suffering from a physical or medical incapacity,
beyond the coercive processes of the Senate, and
others similarly situated.

blocks.text: “The remaining [qualified] members shall then constitute the denominator from which the required two- thirds concurrence shall be computed. When the computation of two-thirds results in a fraction, the number of votes required for conviction shall be rounded up to the next higher whole number, even if the fraction is less than 0.5,” Escudero added.
Tulfo sought consideration since four of their colleagues have not been present in the impeachment trial proceedings.

Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta are detained on plunder and other related charges due to their alleged involvement in flood control projects and undeclared campaign donations, respectively.

Senator Ronald dela Rosa, on the other hand, is nowhere to be found amid a standing warrant of arrest issued against him by the International Criminal Court due to his alleged involvement in the drug war deaths.
Senator Loren Legarda, for her part, is on an extended medical leave abroad due to a lung ailment.
The 1987 Constitution states that "no person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate." —VAL, GMA News
