articles.title: Sara Duterte now participating in impeachment trial 'with caution'
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte is now participating in her impeachment trial with caution after the Senate voted to lower the voting threshold for her conviction, her defense team said Wednesday.

blocks.text: Published September 23, 2026 4:02pm
Vice President Sara Duterte is now participating in her impeachment trial with caution after the Senate voted to lower the voting threshold for her conviction, her defense team said Wednesday.

Lead defense counsel Sheila Sison made the manifestation on Day 29 of Duterte's impeachment trial, shortly after senator-judges voted 13-1-6 to set the conviction threshold at two-thirds of those who are legally allowed to participate in the proceedings.

"Even as we understand that this tribunal will proceed as it deems fit, we nonetheless are constrained to place on record, na mula sa araw na ito, the respondent's participation or any participation that the respondent will have in this trial ay may tahasang pag-iingat or with ad cautelam," said Sison, referring to the Latin phrase which means "with caution."

(Even as we understand that this tribunal will proceed as it deems fit, we nonetheless are constrained to place on record that from this day forward, the respondent's participation or any participation that the respondent will have in this trial will carry outright caution or with ad cautelam.)
Sison stressed that the vice president is not trying to evade accountability amid the ongoing impeachment trial against her.

"Let it be clear that the respondent does not shrink from accountability nor does she fear the outcome of this impeachment trial. She asks for nothing spectacular from this court. Only the most essential and basic guarantees due to every individual: fairness and impartiality," Sison said.
With the new decision on the voting threshold, Duterte can be convicted with less than 16 votes as several senators are facing charges, remain in hiding, or remain on medical leave.
The interpretation of the phrase "All members of the Senate"—referring to the base number to compute the two-thirds requirement—has been the subject of debate.
Sison said Duterte has the right to pursue all legal remedies in the wake of the ruling.

"She reserves every right to exhaust all legal remedies available sa ilalim ng ating batas at Konstitusyon na may pagtatangi sa esensya ng isang tunay na malayang, demokratikong institusyon. At karapatan ng bawat mamamayan na madinig sa isang hukuman na walang kinikilingan o kinakatakutan," she added.

(She reserves every right to exhaust all legal remedies available under our law and Constitution, with due regard for the essence of a truly free, democratic institution. And it is the right of every citizen to be heard in an impartial court that fears no one.)

Thirteen senators voted in favor of the motion put forward by Senator-Judge Erwin Tulfo, who sought reconsideration of the July 6 ruling that the voting threshold is set at 16, or a fixed two-thirds computation of the complete 24-member Senate.
Six minority senators, on the other hand, did not participate in the voting.

In early September, the impeachment court invited retired Supreme Court Chief Justices Artemio Panganiban, Reynato Puno, and Hilario Davide Jr. and Associate Justice Adolfo Azcuna as amici curiae or friends of the court to share their views on the matter.
Panganiban, Puno, and Davide said that the voting threshold should be based on the number of senator-judges who actively participated in the impeachment trial.

However, Azcuna, one of the framers of the 1987 Constitution, offered a different view that the two-thirds concurrence requirement should relate to the entire membership of the Senate; hence, a conviction by 16 senator-judges is needed. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: ‘Ghost patient’ policy wrongly removing at-risk people from GP lists, doctors say
articles.summary:
NHS England initiative to reduce cut-off period to three months ‘disproportionately affecting’ most deprived areas

An NHS policy to remove “ghost patients” from GP lists is inadvertently…
articles.byline: Tobi Thomas Health and inequalities correspondent

blocks.text: An NHS policy to remove “ghost patients” from GP lists is inadvertently leaving some of the poorest people in England without vital healthcare, analysis has found.

Under previous NHS rules, inactive patients at risk of being removed from their GP practice were given six months to respond to outreach. But under NHS England’s accelerated list validation timeline, introduced last October, patients now have only three months to reply.

According to analysis by Healthtech-1, registered GP lists in English practices declined by 483,019 patients between October 2025 and July 2026, with the most deprived fifth of practices accounting for about 138,400 of the net decline – just under 30% of the national decline.

While GP lists need reviewing as people move away or die, GPs have said the accelerated timeline has inadvertently led to patients from deprived areas being incorrectly removed, creating barriers to receiving treatment.
Consequently, GPs and practice managers have reported having to re-register vulnerable and elderly patients, creating an additional administrative burden.

De-registering patients can also cause gaps in care and disruption to treatment. Since GP practices’ income also depend on the number of registered patients, a drop can leave practices struggling to pay for running costs.

A GP at a university practice in Southampton said the accelerated timeline was causing problems because patients were being incorrectly removed from their list and were struggling to access their prescriptions and treatment.

“If you give prescriptions out to people, they’re on repeat and once they get kicked off the lists they can no longer access any prescriptions,” he said. “The risk is that if you’re unable to access your repeat prescriptions, your treatment will be affected.”
He added: “If you’re narrowing the window from six to three months, more people are going to be kicked off and therefore more people will be put into the position where they cannot access treatment.”
The GP also warned that, besides reducing a practice’s income, the policy change was hitting patients from deprived and vulnerable backgrounds hardest.
“In our case, we had around 100 people who were taken off our list who didn’t leave at all. That worked out as around £10,000 in lost income for our practice,” he said.
“We were later contacted by these patients telling us that they couldn’t access their prescriptions and that they hadn’t gone anywhere.
“The money we’ve lost hasn’t been compensated, and I know of another practice locally that has lost £100,000 that they also won’t be compensated for.
“For those who have been erroneously taken off, we’re being penalised. We’re going to have to make cuts somehow to make up the shortfalls.”

Dr Clare Bannon, the chair of the British Medical Association’s GP committee, said GPs across England support the principle of keeping patient lists accurate but the current list-cleansing process is “seriously flawed”.

Bannon said: “We have called on NHS England to pause the exercise. The approach is overly aggressive, leading to practices losing tens of thousands of pounds in income and causing active patients, including vulnerable individuals, to be removed in error.
“It is essential that active patients are not deprived of access to a GP through no fault of their own.”

An NHS spokesperson said: “There are robust checks in place to ensure that vulnerable groups are not removed from GP lists – people are contacted through multiple different channels with the thorough processes lasting up to five months before any action is taken.

“This process ensures that patient contact details are correct so that they receive vital information about screening and vaccination appointments, while ensuring NHS funding resources are allocated fairly with money no longer spent on people who do not live in England.”

articles.title: Robert Pattinson's Primetime hates Chris Hansen
articles.summary: Primetime is a chaotic, spiralling dark comedy is off-putting and strange. But more than that, it attempts to take down Chris Hansen.

image.caption: Robert Pattinson appears as Chris Hansen in a still from A24's Primetime. Director Lance Oppenheim and writer Ajon Singh aim to expose a deep rot at the centre of the NBC crime series To Catch a Predator. (Elevation Pictures)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Primetime is a chaotic, spiralling dark comedy is off-putting and strange. But more than that, it attempts to take down Chris Hansen.
Lance Oppenheim directed takedown of Chris Hansen's To Catch a Predator pulls no punches
It's 9 p.m. on a Wednesday. Do you know where your children are?

If you're the fictionalized version of To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen portrayed by Robert Pattinson in A24's Primetime, you're convinced you do — at least, you've convinced your network you know where everybody else's are.

This Hansen explains, drink in hand, to his airplane seatmate: it's what got his show greenlit in the first place. As he tells his executives, children aren't off roaming the streets or falling down wells. They're alone in their rooms. But outside, Hansen says, is a man standing on the porch, genitalia in hand. And in movie-Hansen's shockingly vulgar description that we're not going to fully quote here: he's about to charge up to that bedroom.
But if his audience just watches To Catch a Predator tonight on NBC, Hansen pitches, he'll tell them how to stop him.

The value of that advice he's offering is obvious to anyone familiar with what happened on that 2004 show. The Dateline series had Hansen pop out of closets and bedrooms to confront alleged child predators his team had lured there — and that infamously led to failed prosecutions, dangerous copycats and at least one death.

But Primetime is anything but a strait-laced critique. What spins out from the movie charting this fraught history is a whirligig of obscenity and oddity. It's a chaotic, spiralling dark comedy. And one so off-putting (it is produced by The Strange Thing About the Johnsons' Ari Aster, after all) you're not even shocked when it pairs that offhand humour with stomach-churning horror.

We see Tony Revolori (Spider-Man: Homecoming) making bug-eyed, intentionally ridiculous faces at the camera along with images of butchered children's bodies abandoned in a nameless jungle. We see Pattinson's Hansen inexplicably projectile-spitting mouthwash into a sink — while standing in a bent-arms, leaned-forward pose that looks less like a journalist, and more like an attacking goose.

And then, later, we see that same goose-man chasing down an actual monster, a personification of what is supposedly lurking outside of society. But as he keeps looking for that evil outside of himself, and stares into the face of evil, we stare right back into his.

There's a high-wire act of unself-conscious commitment-to-the-bit that Pattinson so often brings to his roles: a seeming incapability to feel embarrassment that allows him to dive completely into accents, impersonations and general absurdity.

Here, that's a campy, elevated, Spirit Halloween version of Chris Hansen: one that drawls "Why don't you take a seat" with a gravelly self-seriousness that, in anyone else's hands, would just read as ridiculous.

As director Lance Oppenheim and writer Ajon Singh would have us believe, all those over-the-top affectations are really meant to expose a deep rot at the centre of the real man. Because based as it is on the blistering article "Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die," about a shocking outcome to one of his stings, Primetime is not exactly a fan of Hansen's Dateline series. Echoing criticism — and even court rulings — against the ensuing "Creep Catcher" groups that would copy To Catch a Predator's modus operandi, this screenplay offers deep and obvious condemnations.
Which makes it evident as to why the real Chris Hansen hasn't exactly made himself a friend to the project.

Instead, he says he bought his own trailers ahead of the movie, to say the story you're about to see is completely fabricated. Like the Church of Latter-day Saints did in the Playbill for The Book of Mormon, he'll point audiences toward his own tome of content where, he says, the true story lies.

The true-crime streaming network he's since built continues to release content around sexual offences. An unending slew of new shows follow the format of, and capitalize on audiences' insatiable appetite for, the public-shaming vigilantism of To Catch a Predator.

items: Documentary on aftermath of Windsor, Ont.'s Creeper Hunter to premiere at Toronto's Hot Docs Festival
6 teens charged after string of assaults linked to 'Catch a Predator' trend, police say

blocks.text: The critical read of Primetime's funhouse-mirror interpretation is right there. Instead of giving Predator's seemingly righteous goals even a tiny bit of credit, Oppenheim makes it his rhetorical aim to deliberately deconstruct Hansen's assumed self-interest while unreservedly humanizing his targets.

Throughout Hansen's interactions with a harried and hapless producer (Merritt Wever), a clearly traumatized and exploited "decoy" actor used for luring these alleged criminals (Skyler Gisondo) and the empathetically depicted subjects themselves, Primetime's message is clear.

Glassy-eyed, preening and frantic Hansen does not run Predator as some sacred calling, the film says. He does not manipulate local police forces into bypassing laws around search and seizure, wake up his barely grade-school sons in the middle of the night to watch his latest catch or stare hatefully at NBC reporter Stone Phillips reporting on "real" news because he's performing some sacred calling.
In the eyes of Primetime, he's doing it because he wants just that: to be on prime time.

That alone wouldn't be enough. The idea that respectability died first on the airwaves is obvious to the point of insulting; it wasn't enough to float the sci-fi commentary on capitalism The Running Man last year, and it's not enough to float the Rupert Murdoch/Larry Lamb biopic Ink that showed at this year's TIFF.

Neither is it enough to merely acknowledge the existential fear around stranger danger that has fuelled political campaigns and platforms of the past 50 years. From the genuinely moving, loosely inspired adaptation of six-year-old Etan Patz's disappearance in Without a Trace to the abysmally exploitative child-trafficking film Sound of Freedom, the blinding fear around the vulnerability of children already clearly motivates us.

What Primetime gets at is more probative, and more unsettling. A question not necessarily about self-delusion, but about how a lack of humanity seems justified, even encouraged, when dealing with Hansen's subjects.
It's a topic raised by that same airplane seatmate, who asks Hansen whether he ever wants to skip the justice system and just "bleed" the men he catches.
And it's a proposition Hansen considers, then says that just maybe, what he's doing is worse. And then he smiles.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: UK to launch military squadron to protect satellites in space
articles.summary:
New RAF unit will warn of incoming missile attacks, and support offensive and defensive operations

A new military unit dedicated to defending satellites, protecting services people need on…

blocks.text: A new military unit dedicated to defending satellites, protecting services people need on Earth and potentially supporting offensive operations is being launched by the UK.
The No III Space Effects Squadron will be announced on Wednesday, with the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, warning that Britain needs to “keep pace in the new space race”.
“Control of the waves was the essential ingredient in 19th-century deterrence,” he will tell the Space Power conference.

“That is why Britain built the finest naval power in history. In the 20th century it was control of the skies, and so we built a world class air force to protect us. This century will depend on control of space.”

blocks.caption: The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, will say at a conference on Wednesday that Britain must ‘keep pace in the new space race’. Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PA

blocks.text: The new Royal Air Force (RAF) squadron will protect satellites used to warn of incoming missile attacks, provide communications and help guide ships, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) said.
It will bring together specialist personnel from across the armed forces to counter hostile activity in orbit and defend satellites the nation depends on every day.
Two existing units – No I Space Operations Squadron and No II Space Warning Squadron – already allow the RAF to watch and warn of threats in space.
The MoD said the new squadron would act against those threats, using advanced technology, including electronic warfare, “to disrupt, degrade and deny hostile actions”.
It is intended to support offensive and defensive space operations and will expand over time as new capabilities enter service.

The chief of the air staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, will say on Wednesday: “Space no longer supports operations from the sidelines. It’s a domain of direct competition, where our military advantage can be won or lost.”

The UK has formally ruled out destructive anti-satellite missile testing and the government said on Wednesday that it continues to work through the UN committee on the peaceful uses of outer space to promote norms, rules and principles of responsible space behaviours.
Smyth and Streeting are speaking at the conference in London which being promoted by the Space Command wing of the RAF.

The moves come after warnings that other nations have been building up military capabilities in space. The UK Space Command said last year that Russia was attempting to jam UK military satellites on a regular basis.
after newsletter promotion
The US, which established the United States Space Force in 2019 as the sixth branch of the its armed forces, said earlier this month that it had deployed weapons in space for the first time.

Responding to the US announcement, China’s foreign ministry said Washington was “preparing for war in outer space”, and warned against turning space “into a battlefield, as well as an arms race there”.
The UK announcement on Wednesday comes weeks after the release of a government strategy designed to strengthen defences against threats from space.
The SaxaVord Spaceport, on the island of Unst, Shetland, at the northernmost point of the UK, is to receive a further £30m as part of the plans.
The strategy sets out funding of £7.8bn across the space sector up to 2030.
The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, has previously said that the UK wanted to strengthen the UK’s ability to launch satellites.

articles.title: Chiz Escudero explains how to compute for two-thirds vote in Sara Duterte impeachment trial
articles.summary: Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis "Chiz" Escudero on Wednesday said that two-thirds of all members of the Senate qualified to vote will be the voting threshold needed to convict Vice…

blocks.text: Published September 23, 2026 3:56pm

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis "Chiz" Escudero on Wednesday said that two-thirds of all members of the Senate qualified to vote will be the voting threshold needed to convict Vice President Sara Duterte.

Escudero made the explanation after the Senate court approved the motion put forward by Senator Erwin Tulfo to lower the threshold needed for conviction, given that four of the 24 senator-judges have been constantly absent from the proceedings.
Escudero said that the following Senators will be excluded from the senator-judges qualified to vote:

items: detained and/or suspended or otherwise legally restrained from exercising the functions of a senator;
persons sought by authorities whose whereabouts are unknown;
those suffering from a physical or medical incapacity;
those beyond the coercive processes of the Senate; and
others similarly situated.

blocks.text: Escudero, however, said that such determination of who are the senator-judges qualified to vote for the conviction or acquittal of Duterte will come at a later time.

“The impeachment court shall determine on the basis of competent and sufficient evidence whether a member falls within any of the five circumstances mentioned in the new controlling ruling. The remaining members shall then constitute the denominator from which the required two thirds concurrence shall be computed,” Escudero said.

When the computation of two-thirds results in a fraction, Escudero said the number of votes required for conviction will be rounded up to the next higher whole number, even if the fraction is less than 0.5.

“For example, if the denominator is 20, two thirds is 13 and one third or 13.33. If we round it down to 13, 13 votes would fall short of the constitutionally required two-thirds concurrence, which is 13.33. Since a fraction of a vote is impossible, as there is no fraction of a senator, 13.33, again by way of example only, [the threshold] must be rounded up to 14 votes, the next higher whole number, to ensure that the votes for conviction constitute at least two-thirds of the relevant membership,” Escudero said.

Likewise, Escudero said that the lowered threshold is only applicable for the impeachment trial of Duterte, given that a decision of an impeachment court does not bind the impeachment court that will convene in the future, unlike in regular court proceedings.

“This ruling and interpretation of the court shall operate pro hac vice, or for this occasion only. It shall not constitute a binding precedent in any future impeachment proceedings. This is a ruling, not an amendment of the rules. As such, it has no binding but merely persuasive effect on future impeachment proceedings, the hands of whom we cannot shackle as there is no stare decisis as between impeachment courts,” Escudero said.
“Further, the circumstances that gave rise to this ruling [of lowered threshold] are extraordinary. Before and the chair hopes that it shall never happen again,” he added.
The Constitution, however, does not state a number but reads “no [impeachable] person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the members of the Senate.”
Article 11, Section 6 of the Constitution states that "No person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate."
The same constitutional provision also states that "The Senate shall have the sole power to try and decide all cases of impeachment."
Absent judges
Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta are detained on plunder and other related charges due to their alleged involvement in flood control and undeclared campaign donations, respectively.

Senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa, on the other hand, is nowhere to be found amid a standing warrant of arrest issued against him by the International Criminal Court due to his alleged involvement in the drug war deaths during the Rodrigo Duterte administration.
Senator Loren Legarda, for her part, is on an extended medical leave abroad due to a lung ailment. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: PM’s new anti-disinformation unit won’t target ‘domestic politcal dissent’, defence secretary says – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Wes Streeting told GB News: ‘We’re not interested in policing domestic political dissent’

Good morning. Andy Burnham delivered his speech to the United Nations in what…

blocks.text: Good morning. Andy Burnham delivered his speech to the United Nations in what felt like the middle of the night in UK time and he announced that he is setting up what he is calling a National Centre for Information Defence.

Burnham said this was necessary because “over the last decade we have given too much ground to those who want to run a negative, corrosive narrative about life in Britain, which bears no resemblance to reality”.

Over at GB News they seem a bit worried this morning about the prospect of a crackdown on corrosive narratives about Britain which bear no resemblance to reality, and it is running a story with a headline referencing “free speech fears” and a quote from a rightwing commentator claiming the Burnham speech was all “talk of control and censorship – exactly the kind of messaging that the Trump administration absolutely hates”.

But close reading of the speech makes it clear that Burnham is not aiming his fire at any parts of the UK media. Burnham said he was concerned about hostile state actors waging disinformation warfare, especially Russia. He told the UN:

double quotation markIn recent years we have seen an industrial-scale assault by hostile actors on the information environment in the UK and that of many of our allies. Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people’s fears. They’ve used bots and fake websites. Falsified newspaper articles. Forged the branding of 28 British organisations – including universities and the BBC. They’ve amplified far-right narratives. And we have evidence that they tried to interfere with the 2019 general election.

(Burnham did not address the fact that there are some within the Trump administration who have also been amplifying far-right narratives with claims about the UK which certainly count as misinformation, and arguably meet the disinformation threshold too.)

Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, has been giving interviews this morning and, speaking to GB News, he was asked about claims that Burnham’s new unit could be used against Britons who” simply disagree” with the government. That would not happen, he said.
He told the programme:

double quotation markOne of the great things about Britain, and one of the things that I have a responsibility to defend, is the freedom and democracy that we all enjoy. And that includes the freedom to disagree, the freedom for people to challenge their government, to challenge government policy, to criticise robustly what we are doing and then to have the opportunity to choose a different government. That is a stark contrast to the position that our friends the Russian people endure under the political system that they suffer under. Russia is just one of a number of malign state and non-state actors that seek to threaten and disrupt our democracy, including through misinformation and disinformation.
Streeting added:
double quotation markWe’re not interested in policing domestic political dissent.
You can read Burnham’s UN speech in full here. I will be posting more from it soon.

The Commons is still in recess, and most people in government are getting ready for the Labour conference next week, and so there is almost nothing in the Westminster diary. But there was enough news at the UN yesterday to pad out the week, and so I’m sure there will be enough to cover.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: World lagging on key UN biodiversity targets
articles.summary: Hundreds of nations signed on to a goal to protect 30% of the world's land and sea by 2030. As the timeline reaches the halfway point, activists say the current protection estimates are way behind.

image.caption: Only 10% of global oceans are currently designated for conservation and could only reach 12% by 2030, the research revealsImage: DW

blocks.text: World governments are off track to meet a historic United Nations target to protect at least 30% of the planet's land and seas by the year 2030, according to a new study published Wednesday.

The research by environmental groups Campaign for Nature and Together for the Ocean shows that about 20% of land and inland waters are designated as protected or conserved, following the signing of the 30×30 goal in 2022.
If nations fully deliver on existing quantified commitments, the estimate could increase to 27% by the turn of the decade, the report said.

The 30x30 goal was adopted under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework at COP15 and was signed by nearly 200 nations that pledged at least $200 billion (about €175 billion) annually to reduce biodiversity loss.
Only 'a third' of target reached in ocean protection
For the world's oceans, the study says protection is "lagging."
The coverage is currently at 10% of global ocean and could only reach 12% by 2030, the research revealed.

"The ocean is emerging as one of the defining implementation challenges of 30×30," Together for the Ocean said, adding that important marine ecosystems, like offshore and deep-sea habitats, remain "vulnerable."
Last month, the Convention on Biological Diversity, the UN treaty dedicated to the global nature goals, also cautioned that countries were not on track.
Funding gap
The report singled out finance for conservation as "one of the greatest barriers" to reaching global targets.
The research said that between $100 billion and $180 billion was needed each year to make the 2030 target. Current annual spending, however, amounted to just $24 billion.
"The gap is particularly stark for the ocean, where approximately $16 billion is needed annually, but only an estimated $ 1.8 billion is currently spent," the study said.
From October 19, the UN biodiversity summit in Yerevan will see the nations address the progress shortfall and assess ways of getting back on target.

blocks.text: What you need to know

items: A rule allowing gas stations to raise prices only at noon has not achieved its objective of lowering them, motoring association ADAC says
The number of entry-level jobs has dropped by two-thirds since 2022, an online job exchange says
Traces of explosives have been found near a German military base close to where drone parts were discovered last week, security sources say

blocks.text: Here is a roundup of headline stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, September 23, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click hereClick here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
September 23, 2026
ADAC calls to drop once-a-day price rise rule for fuel

The ADAC motoring association has said that a rule in force since April 1 allowing gas stations to raise fuel prices only once a day, at noon, has not brought down prices and "should therefore be abolished."
Although the rule had greatly reduced the number of price changes throughout a day and made increases easier to predict, the gap between the highest and lowest prices had increased, the ADAC said.
It also said motorists who needed to buy gas shortly after noon, when gas stations have typically jacked up prices, were faced with unjustifiably higher costs.
An economic research institute, ZEW, also found in April that prices were higher on average after the rule was introduced, with fuel prices generally going up after noon and cheaper in the morning.
Fuel prices in Germany and Europe in general have skyrocketed amid the war in the Middle East.

The ADAC reported that average gas prices in Germany hit a record high on Thursday, reaching €2.308 for a liter of super E10 and €2.471 for a liter of diesel ($9.98/US gallon and $10.69/US gallon, respectively)

In its statement, the ADAC, however, welcomed the government's temporary reduction in the energy tax that is planned to go into force on October 1, saying it was the most realistic way to lower the burden on motorists.

articles.title: Gus Lamont’s parents make emotional plea as $1m reward offered for information about disappearance
articles.summary:
No trace of Gus has been found since he went missing from his family’s South Australian farm on 27 September last year

The parents of missing four-year-old Gus Lamont have made an emotional…

blocks.text: The parents of missing four-year-old Gus Lamont have made an emotional plea for any information about their “unique little boy” as authorities offered a $1 million reward over the disappearance.
No trace of Gus has been found since he went missing from his family’s enormous sheep farm in the South Australian outback almost a year ago.
Gus’s parents, Joshua Lamont and Jessica Murray pleaded with the public to come forward with any information, no matter how small.
It had been “the most devastating and inexplicable event we have ever experienced”, Murray said in a video message released on Wednesday.
“Our memories of Gus are of a beautiful, sweet, and unique little boy who loved music, listening to stories, and playing in the natural world.
“During the time Gus has been missing, he should have celebrated his fifth birthday and his little brother’s first birthday with us.”
A tearful Lamont said they were desperate for answers.
“We believe that someone knows something. Someone knows what happened to Gus, and may even know where he is,” he said.

South Australian police Det Supt Darren Fielke described the eleven painstaking ground searches in inhospitable territory, which have so far turned up no useful clues – although some “anomalies” in aerial images may prompt yet another search.
Officials are hoping the state government reward of up to one million dollars for anyone with information leading to a conviction or a body will help move the investigation forwards.
Gus, described as both shy and adventurous, was last seen playing outside at 5pm on Saturday 27 September. Half an hour later, when his family went to check on him, he was gone.
His disappearance sparked one of the biggest searches the state has ever undertaken, with new searches launched as new information or theories came to light.

Volunteers, police, emergency services and defence personnel, along with dogs, divers and drones, aircraft and Aboriginal trackers scoured the 60,000 hectare Oak Park Station, about 300km inland from Adelaide.
One of the biggest moments in the search came in February this year, when Sapol declared his disappearance a major crime, and said they had identified a suspect.
Fielke said at the time they had effectively ruled out Gus wandering off or being abducted, and that they were now investigating someone in his household.
The suspect was not one of his parents, Fielke said, something he emphasised on Wednesday.

Fielke said Task Force Horizon had covered more than 700 sq km and undertaken “a painstaking, methodical, forensically detailed manual search of the aerial imagery”, which “identified some anomalies”. Those anomalies will be reviewed before any decision to start a new search is made.
Premier Peter Malinauskas said there had been “no sign of Gus”, so the government was offering the $1m reward in hopes of solving the case.
Previous state governments have offered the same amount in cases of missing children, including the three Beaumont children who disappeared without a trace from an Adelaide beach in 1966.
“We put this in place because … we spare no expense. Justice needs to be done here one way or another,” Malinauskas said.
“We will not tolerate, as a state, any circumstances where children go missing and are not able to be accounted for.”
Anyone with information relating to the disappearance of Gus Lamont is urged to contact crime stoppers.
“We’re going to continue to thoroughly and meticulously investigate the disappearance of Gus until we get a resolution,” Fielke said.

articles.title: Trend Intel: In this economy?! Why young Filipinos choose to live alone
articles.summary: As more Filipinos move out of their homes and live alone, content creators grab the opportunity to ease the journey and make it less lonely

blocks.text: Hello Trendsetters,

For a lot of us Filipinos, moving out of our parents’ house is basically an achievement unlocked by marriage — and sometimes, not even then. Staying in our childhood homes well into adulthood has long been the norm, whether it’s for practical, financial, or very Filipino-family reasons. But something’s shifting. More young Filipinos are getting curious about what it actually means to live on their own — paying their own bills, making their own rules, and figuring out adulthood.
In this Trend Intel piece, we find out who these young people are and what’s making them rethink what being an adult is supposed to look like.

The Philippine Institute for Development Studies in 2024 reported that the percentage of one-person households in the country more than doubled within three decades — from 2.9% in 1990 to 9.1% in 2020.

A 2023 study in the Journal of Population Research also cited an increase in separation between couples, an increase in marriage delays or non-marriage, and a rise in internal migration in the country due to employment.

blocks.caption: Chart, Bar Chart

blocks.text: This particular rise in solo living among younger age groups reflected a similar phenomenon online: the rise of vloggers who romanticized solo living and created its accompanying aesthetic.

If you’ve scrolled through TikTok, chances are you’ve been hit by videos of young professionals restocking their pantries, bringing you along to their mid-day coffee runs or “get ready with me” morning routines. This kind of content has proven to be effective as more creators are riding the trend.

Data consultancy The Nerve analyzed TikTok videos related to solo living from 2020 to 2026 through its video content and narrative analysis solution, Probe Video — observing a spike in 2023 and a continued rise since 2025.

blocks.caption: Bar Chart, Chart, First Aid

blocks.text: What did these videos tackle? The Nerve found three key themes in solo living content on TikTok: vlogs, expenses, and guides.
Vlogs took up more than half of solo living content on TikTok at 61%. There’s a sense of comfort seeing what living alone can look like, based on the videos I’ve watched online.

Steph Ambroce, for example, started posting user-generated content on TikTok in 2023. She shifted to solo living content in 2025, documenting her escape from chaotic households and her journey living alone. She pursued the content niche full-time after one of her videos garnered more than a million views shortly after it was published.
“It’s so easy to make,” she said. “You only need to take videos of your everyday life and upload them to social media, then viewers will flock to your videos not long after.”

@ang.elu let's talk non negotiables!! 🫢📝 here are my deal breakers when i was looking for an apartment as someone living alone 🏠🚽🔨 #livingalonephilippines #sololivingph #apartmentphilippines ♬ Chill Vibes – Tollan Kim
Insurance manager Clark Macasio also saw the potential of posting solo living vlogs.

“When I put out something on social media, I want to be real with my audience. I didn’t want to continue posting engineering content even when it was doing really well because if I want my content creation to be sustainable, I have to be true to what I post,” he shared.
Now based in Metro Manila, Macasio shared guides on solo living. Similar guides took up 15% of solo living content on TikTok, according to The Nerve’s analysis.

“I think audiences appreciate when we don’t sugarcoat the reality of living alone. It’s not just going out on solo dates drinking matcha — it’s also buying groceries, paying the bills, and taking out the trash,” Macasio said.

@clarkmacasio 2x meal/day plan for living alone with ₱1,500 weekly budget🥗🏠 FULL RECIPE on my latest vlog—follow for PART 2+ 🏷️: #livingalone #sololiving #clarkmacasio #mealplan #budgeting ♬ original sound – ig/yt: clarkmacasio👨🏻‍💻

Writer and editor Angelu Zafe became renowned on TikTok also for her solo living guides. “There was so much aesthetic, aspirational solo living content, but there was an absence of practical information you need to live alone,” she said.
Zafe’s solo living guides include what those planning to live alone need to prepare before taking the leap, how much to save, and what to ask landlords when hunting solo living spaces, among others.
While transparent guides and honest takes were appreciated, talking about money and expenses had mixed reactions, as the topic is still taboo in the Philippines.

She was met initially with so much backlash, with comments calling her out for sharing something too “personal.” This was disappointing to find out, as it was actually the content that tackled expenses that was most helpful to me in my upcoming solo living journey.
Zafe thought the same, saying these posts made living alone doable.

“You get to have action steps, unlike before when there were no posts like this,” she expounded. “But now that there are more people generous enough to share what they know, people now have a point of reference to rely on.”

With all three creators forecasting continued growth for this niche, it is clear that this trend is more than just a passing algorithm spike. It is a shared survival guide. And in the pursuit of solo living, this just goes to show that you’ll never be alone.
Godspeed and good luck with your journey!
From Rappler’s Culture Desk
All quotes in this story were translated to English for brevity.

articles.title: Jesse Baird ‘petrified’ of Beau Lamarre-Condon and kept repeating ‘he has a gun’, court hears
articles.summary: Friend sobs in witness box and tells Sydney murder trial Baird was scared to go to the police

blocks.text: Before he was fatally shot, Jesse Baird became “petrified” of Beau Lamarre and kept repeating that the police officer had a gun, a court has heard.
Lamarre-Condon has been accused of fatally shooting Sydney couple Jesse Baird, 26, and Luke Davies, 29, with a police service weapon at Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.
The 31-year-old pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
Lamarre-Condon developed an “obsession and infatuation” with Baird, which manifested in compulsive actions during their brief relationship, the prosecution alleged.
By the time Baird decided he wanted to end things in November 2023, the behaviour had escalated.
Corey-Dean Thorpe, who had previously been in a years-long relationship with the 26-year-old and remained close friends, began sobbing in the witness box as he told the trial how Baird felt.
“He was petrified,” Thorpe told the New South Wales supreme court.
“I’d never heard him so scared in his voice before.
“He just kept repeating, ‘he has a gun’.”
Baird told Thorpe he was “extremely scared” of Lamarre-Condon because he had a gun and was a member of the police force, the court heard.
Asked by crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC if the 26-year-old had said he was scared to go to the police because Lamarre-Condon was a police officer, Thorpe agreed.
Baird was also worried Lamarre-Condon would make a false allegation against him that would “ruin his career”, Thorpe said.
Because he was a television presenter on children’s show Totally Wild and an AFL umpire, he needed a certification to work with children, the court heard.

During their relationship, Baird told Thorpe that Lamarre-Condon would go through his phone when he was asleep, find other men Baird had been talking to, and block their numbers before deleting their chats.
Lamarre-Condon would also use his own close friends story on Instagram to target “romantic rivals”, the prosecution alleged.
Damon Wilson, who had been casually seeing Baird, told the court about an incident in November 2023 when the TV presenter had to go to Melbourne for work.
Lamarre-Condon added Wilson to his close friends story on Instagram before posting a photo of a bouquet captioned “when he’s in Melbourne but still sends you these” with a heart-eyes emoji.
Baird later told his work colleague Briony Blackstone that he had not sent Lamarre-Condon any flowers, the court heard.

He found out the police officer had created a close friends list that included only one person so Lamarre-Condon could imply he and Baird were in a more serious relationship, Blackstone told the court.
This wasn’t the first time he had done this, the prosecution alleged.
Earlier in 2023, Lamarre-Condon had told his work colleague Rubina Shrestha that he had created a close friends group which had only one person: a Canberra man who had been seeing Baird.
He then posted a photo of Baird or himself with Baird to “send out a message that they’re together and Jesse’s not available,” Shrestha told the court.
When he told her about the bouquet close friends story, Shrestha told him: “that’s crazy” before Lamarre-Condon replied, “it works”.
After seeing the flowers in Lamarre-Condon’s story, Wilson messaged Baird, who confirmed he was not in a relationship with Lamarre-Condon.

Wilson said to Baird in a message: “I was a little confused why he added me to his close friends as soon as we met then starting posting photos of you guys … you getting him flowers. Glad we are on the same page.”
after newsletter promotion
A week later Wilson received a protracted message from Lamarre-Condon warning him about Baird’s supposed “gaslighting”.
“He literally destroyed me,” Lamarre-Condon said in messages read to the court.
“It took me so long to recover from all the manipulation.
“He has tried to make me look like the bad guy.”
Around this time, Baird asked Thorpe for advice on how to break up with Lamarre-Condon.
Baird told Thorpe he was worried about what would happen when he ended things “because of the gun and because the accused had stalked and controlled him”, the prosecutor alleged.
But he pushed ahead with the break-up and confronted Lamarre-Condon about the flowers in the close friends story.
The officer responded by claiming the flowers were sent by his stepdad, who was living in Melbourne, to his mother, the court heard.
Lamarre-Condon later told his colleague Shrestha he “would do anything to get him back”.
On 3 February 2024, months after the break-up, one of Baird’s best friends, Matthew Edwards, asked if he had heard from Lamarre-Condon.
Edwards said Baird had replied: “No, thank fuck, I’m so done with him.”
“Once I move house, this will be the last piece of me that Beau knows.”
Baird confirmed his new relationship with Davies to Edwards soon after during their last phone call together.
“He was almost falling in love with him,” Edwards told the court.
“I’d never seen Jesse as happy with Luke as what I’d seen him ever. There was something about Luke that just lit Jesse up: they were the real deal.”
Lamarre-Condon’s defence team has claimed the police officer was acting in self-defence when he disguised himself as an Uber Eats driver and entered Baird’s home on 19 February.
Defence lawyer John Stratton SC argued a struggle had ensued which led to the shots that killed Davies and Baird.
The trial before justice Natalie Adams continues.

articles.title: Eleven killed in mass shooting at house in South Africa
articles.summary: One of those killed is believed to be a pregnant woman, police said.

blocks.text: At least 11 people have been killed in a mass shooting in a residential building near the South African city of Durban.

Gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township late on Tuesday and opened fire on 14 people. Ten were killed at the scene and four were taken to hospital, where one later died from their injuries, police said.
Police said some of the victims were on their watch in connection with illegal activities, which they could not "divulge at the moment to protect investigations which have been launched".
While the motive of the shooting has not yet confirmed, the police said they could not rule out a "feud between rival groupings".

"Information available at this stage suggests that 13 men and one woman, who is believed to be pregnant, were reportedly having a party inside a house when three men arrived and opened fire on them," the police said in a statement. The woman is among those who died.
A local TV reporter from the eNCA channel at the scene said the gunmen had set fire to a vehicle belonging to one of the victims before fleeing, with footage showing the burnt-out car.
The police say they have launched a manhunt for the suspects.
South Africa has one of the world's highest murder rates, with police data showing a murder rate equivalent to more than 60 deaths a day.
In recent weeks, the gruesome discovery of at least nine murdered women, with some of the bodies dumped by the roadside, has heightened fears in the country.
Last year, nine people were killed in a mass shooting at a tavern in Johannesburg.
Rivalry among criminal gangs amid turf wars, drug trafficking and illegal mining is common in the country, often driving violence within communities.

In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa said organised crime was "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development", as he announced that he would be deploying the army to support the police.

articles.title: Vince Dizon testifies in Zaldy Co flood control case
articles.summary: Department of Public Works and Highways Secretary Vince Dizon has testified before the Sandiganbayan in the case of fugitive former lawmaker Zaldy Co.

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 3:00pm

Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon joins Presidential Communications Office undersecretary and Palace press officer Atty. Claire Castro in a press briefing with the Malacañang Press Corps on Sept. 1, 2025.
The Philippine STAR / Ryan Baldemor
MANILA, Philippines — Department of Public Works and Highways Secretary Vince Dizon has testified before the Sandiganbayan in the case of fugitive former lawmaker Zaldy Co.
Dizon testified before the anti-graft court’s Fifth Division on Wednesday, September 23, in the P289.5-million flood dike project in Naujan, Oriental Mindoro, where Co faces a graft charge.

In an ambush interview with reporters on Wednesday, Dizon confirmed that he verified information showing the sheet piles used in the project were only three meters long instead of the required 12 meters.

He described the construction work done by Co-owned Sunwest Corporation as substandard, noting that during his personal visit to the site, he observed areas where erosion and excavation were already occurring after just a single rainfall.
“Pagka talaga substandard 'yung pundasyon, eh talagang 'yun ang mangyayari. So para sa'kin klarong-klaro 'yung ebidensya dito sa kaso na 'to,” Dizon said.
(When the foundation is substandard, that is inevitably what will happen. So for me, the evidence in this case is crystal clear.)
Co, who is hiding in Europe, is currently facing graft and malversation charges over the Oriental Mindoro flood control project. All of his co-accused are currently detained.

The former lawmaker is also facing a plunder charge, along with former House Speaker Martin Romualdez, for allegedly “repeatedly receiving, directly or indirectly, on at least fifteen occasions, commissions, shares, percentages, kickbacks, ‘commitments’ and/or other pecuniary benefits” worth at least P7.44 billion linked to flood control projects.

articles.title: Will PH see funding boost for early childhood care in 2027?
articles.summary: A lower budget for the Early Childhood Care and Development Council is seen to ‘greatly affect’ the upgrade of existing daycare centers to child development centers in 2027

blocks.text: EARLY CHILDHOOD. Inside a national child development center, which serves as a convergence point for efforts related to early childhood care and development.
Early Childhood Care and Development Council's website
A lower budget for the Early Childhood Care and Development Council is seen to ‘greatly affect’ the upgrade of existing daycare centers to child development centers in 2027

items: The proposed 2027 budget significantly cuts the Early Childhood Care and Development Council's funding by 65%.
Concerns were raised about the lack of financial assistance for local government units and the reduced budget for feeding programs.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – In his 2027 budget message, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. acknowledged the importance of investing in the development of young Filipinos, especially in their formative years.

“The journey toward quality education begins long before a child enters the classroom. Strong foundations in early childhood development are essential to improving learning outcomes, reducing inequality, and enabling every learner to succeed throughout life,” Marcos said.

But it seems such a pronouncement did not fully materialize in the proposed 2027 budget, as the government is set to cut by more than half the budget of the Early Childhood Care and Development (ECCD) Council.
According to the National Expenditure Program, the ECCD Council was allocated P123.84 million for next year.
That is 65% lower than the P356.79 million given in the 2026 General Appropriations Act (GAA) or the national budget.

The ECCD Council, which is the lead agency in implementing programs for health, nutrition, early education, and social services provided to children aged 5 years old and below, originally proposed P1.06 billion as its 2027 spending plan.
No exact reason was given during budget deliberations at the House of Representatives regarding the lower allocation.
Among the differences between the 2027 NEP and the 2026 GAA is the lack of financial assistance for local government units (LGUs) lodged with the ECCD Council next year.

Last year’s aid was for the repair, rehabilitation, and conversion of existing daycare centers into child development centers (CDCs) in fourth- and fifth-class municipalities or low-income and remote areas.
CDCs have a more structured system, where professional child development workers and child development teachers provide care and services to children.

Republic Act No. 12199 or the ECCD System Act, which was enacted into law in May 2025, requires a CDC in every barangay. The law also transferred the ECCD Council from the Department of Education (DepEd) to the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG).

“The conversion of these daycare centers [into] child development centers will be affected greatly,” ECCD Executive Director Teresita Inciong said in a House briefing on the DILG’s budget on August 27.
The ECCD Council’s original proposal earmarked P881 million for the provision of learning materials, furniture and fixtures, and other essential components in upgrading existing facilities to CDCs.
According to the Second Congressional Commission on Education, 96.9% of existing daycare centers have yet to be converted into CDCs.
Inciong also said there are still 3,743 barangays without CDCs in the country.
She said that under the new law, funding for the establishment of CDCs will be lodged with LGUs already. The LGUs can tap the Local Government Support Fund for this matter.

“‘Yan ang malaking butas ngayon sa ating national budget. Sabi natin palalakasin natin ang ECCD System, pero bakit pagdating sa pondo lahat ngayon ay nakaasa sa LGU?” Gabriela Representative Sarah Elago said during the plenary deliberations on the DepEd’s budget on Tuesday, September 22.
(That’s a big gap in our national budget. We said we would strengthen the ECCD System, but why are we placing all funding concerns in the hands of the LGUs?)
Elago has been signaling that she would propose a special provision in the 2027 GAA to fund the CDCs of low-income areas, something that was also seen in previous national budget laws.
Another issue related to ECCD is the slashed budget for feeding programs next year.
The DepEd’s school-based feeding program is set to have P11.43 billion next year, which would force it to be scaled down, according to a lawmaker.

“The implementation will be affected if we approve only the proposed allocation. The implementation will be shortened to 120 days and limited to kindergarten learners,” Davao de Oro 1st District Representative Maria Carmen Zamora, the DepEd’s budget sponsor, said in a mix of English and Filipino.
The DepEd is seeking an additional P19.30 billion to set the universal coverage of the school-based feeding program to 180 days for both kindergarten and Grade 1 learners — the same coverage in 2026.

Funding for the Department of Social Welfare and Development’s Supplementary Feeding Program, which provides milk and hot meals in CDCs, may also decrease from P9.56 billion in 2026 to P6.36 billion in 2027, based on the latest NEP.
According to the ECCD Council, only around a third of Filipino children aged 3 to 4 years old were enrolled in CDCs for school year 2025-2026.
For 2027, much of the budget of the ECCD Council will go to maintenance and other operating expenses.
Here are the proposed allocations for the council’s programs:

items: Capacity-building and institutional development of intermediaries and other partners – P55.58 million
General management and supervision – P41.23 million
Accreditation of ECCD service providers – P25 million
Development of policies, standards, and guidelines – P2.36 million

blocks.text: Meanwhile, Marcos said the government will set aside P227 million for the scholarship program for child development workers next year. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Trump administration accuses banned media outlets of 'falsehoods' ahead of court hearing
articles.summary: The US Justice Department's response to a lawsuit filed by CNN, Politico and MS NOW also cites national security.

blocks.text: The US Justice Department has filed documents that accuse three media outlets banned from the White House of "trafficking in verifiable falsehoods" and reporting which "threatened national security" as it prepared to defend the move in court.
Last week, President Donald Trump barred CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House, accusing them of spreading "fake news".
After their reporters had their passes confiscated and were denied access to the building, the three outlets jointly launched legal action, calling the move unconstitutional.
On Wednesday, a judge is set to decide whether to issue an order temporarily lifting the ban, pending a full hearing.
According to a court filing by the Justice Department in a District of Columbia court, the three outlets were issued with a list of "reporting incidents" by the White House ahead of the ban.

The filing cites a number of stories about construction at the White House - including about a security bunker and the building of a new ballroom, as well as a report on an internal information leak investigation.
It goes on to say that "access to the White House is a privilege, not a right".
The three media organisations have argued that the ban breaches their rights under the First Amendment, which forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press.
In a joint statement confirming legal action against the government, they said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting.
"Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."
Major TV networks have withdrawn from a media-sharing arrangement of video and images of the president, known as the pool, in protest over the ban.
Shortly after, the White House launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV, which operates a 24/7 feed of clips of the president.

articles.title: Angus Taylor pledges to repeal swathe of climate policies, saying ‘Australia has done its bit’
articles.summary: Several measures were previously introduced or supported by Coalition, prompting claim Liberals and Nationals would ‘let climate change rip’
articles.byline: Sarah Basford Canales and Petra Stock

blocks.text: Angus Taylor has vowed to repeal a raft of emissions reduction and renewable energy policies, including several measures supported by or introduced under past Coalition governments, within a month of being elected prime minister, prompting accusations he would “let climate change rip”.

On Wednesday, Taylor’s energy spokesperson, Dan Tehan, announced a new bill would be introduced to parliament within 30 days after a Coalition win at the next federal election to ensure affordable, reliable and secure energy to Australians.
The bill, which contains a package of eight previously announced opposition policies, would remove safeguard mechanism and nuclear prohibitions, both introduced by previous Coalition governments.
It would also:

items: Scrap vehicle emissions standards.
Remove the legislated net zero by 2050 target.
Revoke four of six offshore wind energy zones due for completion by the late 2030s: the Hunter, Illawarra, Southern Ocean and Bunbury regions.
Introduce a renewable energy code of conduct for developers.
Require energy funding provided to states and territories prioritises energy affordability and reliability.
Change the Australian Energy Regulator’s main focus to affordability and reliability.

blocks.text: “Australia has done its bit,” Taylor said at a press conference when asked why it wanted to reverse laws driving down emissions.
“What we will continue to see is technologies emerging with lower emissions that Australians want to choose. That is fine, and that is great.”
The energy minister, Chris Bowen, said the plan would take a “chainsaw to the economy and household budgets” and “make Australia poorer, weaker and less secure from global shocks”.
“They want to take choice away from Australians – remove your ability to take control of your energy bills with a cheaper home battery, and pick a cheaper to run car,” he said.

Bowen said the Coalition’s plan to “stop renewables and household batteries” and extend the life of existing coal power stations would mean households would be “left to pick up the bill of global shocks”.
The energy policy reversal was similarly criticised by Kooyong MP, Monique Ryan, and acting Greens leader, Mehreen Faruqi, for taking the country backwards.
“The Coalition’s plan is dumb, dangerous, and desperate climate denial which would make energy more expensive and unreliable,” Dr Ryan said.
Faruqi also took aim at Labor after its resources minister, Madeleine King, marked the opening of the Beetaloo basin with smiles.

“Australians deserve a safe climate future, but we won’t see that while the Labor government is capitulating to fossil fuels and the Coalition’s energy policy is written to prop up corporate profits,” she said.
Environment groups have condemned the Coalition’s announcement, with the Australian Conservation Foundation’s head of political advocacy, Gavan McFadzean, saying Australians deserved better.
after newsletter promotion

“You can’t be anti-renewables and pro-energy reliability, because renewables with storage is the most reliable and affordable form of energy, while nuclear is the most expensive and would need to be publicly funded,” McFadzean said.
“To commit to slow the renewables transition is a breathtaking act of economic self-harm that would increase climate pollution and abandon jobs and investment in the future low carbon economy.”
The chief executive of the Climate Council, Amanda McKenzie, described the energy announcement as “pure ideology” underpinned by years of climate denial.
“The Coalition’s plan is to let climate change rip. It’s deadly negligence that would leave Australians facing more fires, floods and heatwaves,” she said.
“The Coalition wants to force Australians back into the most polluting cars in the world and increase our dependence on foreign oil.”
Farmers for Climate Action, a group representing more than 8,000 farmers across Australia, said they were “extremely disappointed”.
Harden sheep and crop farmer and FCA spokesperson Peter Holding, said giving up on pollution reduction was crazy.

“We are extremely disappointed in the Coalition today. You can’t say you’re looking after farmers while you axe pollution reduction policies, when we know more pollution means more fires and droughts, more climate change, and higher insurance costs,” he said.

articles.title: Marie June Adriano gives PH another karate bronze in Asian Games
articles.summary: Filipina karateka Marie June Adriano triumphs in the kumite category a day after teammates Rebecca Cyril Torres, Ysabielle Arrogante, and Samantha Emmanuelle Veguillas also won bronze in the kata…

blocks.text: FEARSOME. The Philippines' Marie June Adriano (left) in action during her bronze-medal bout against Taiwan's Chung Ya-chi in the karate women's kumite -50kg class in the 2026 Asian Games.
Andrew Couldridge/REUTERS

Filipina karateka Marie June Adriano triumphs in the kumite category a day after teammates Rebecca Cyril Torres, Ysabielle Arrogante, and Samantha Emmanuelle Veguillas also won bronze in the kata event

MANILA, Philippines – Another Filipina karateka delivered a medal in the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, as Marie June Adriano bagged the bronze in the women’s kumite -50kg division on Wednesday, September 23.

Adriano claimed a convincing 10-3 win over Chinese Taipei’s Chung Ya-chi in the bronze-medal bout at the Toyohashi Gymnasium to give the Philippines its fifth medal in the 20th edition of the continental showpiece.
Her victory came a day after karate teammates Rebecca Cyril Torres, Ysabielle Arrogante, and Samantha Emmanuelle Veguillas also won bronze in the women’s kata event.

“I still cannot believe it,” Adriano told Cignal in Filipino. “They told me to just enjoy because this is my first time — just feel the crowd, feel the moment, let go of the negative and feel the positive energy.”
Adriano, 22, fell short of a spot in the gold-medal match after a narrow 5-4 loss to Hong Kong’s Tsang Yee Ting in the semifinals.
But Adriano refused to go home without a medal as she dominated Chung in the battle for bronze.
In the earlier rounds, Adriano opened her campaign with a 4-3 victory over Cambodia’s Srey Phea Chonn then scored a 4-0 triumph over South Korea’s Yang Yewon in the quarterfinals.
The karate team missed out on another medal on Tuesday, September 22, as Alwyn Batican lost his bronze-medal bout to Kazakhstan’s Nurkanat Azhikanov, 10-1. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Senate court lowers conviction voting threshold in Duterte impeachment trial
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court overturns the July ruling of impeachment court presiding officer Chiz Escudero setting the conviction threshold at 16 votes

blocks.text: IMPEACHMENT TRIAL. The Senate impeachment court in session for the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Senate of the Philippines Facebook page
The Senate impeachment court overturns the July ruling of impeachment court presiding officer Chiz Escudero setting the conviction threshold at 16 votes
MANILA, Philippines – The Senate impeachment court on Wednesday, September 23, voted to lower the voting threshold for the conviction of Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial.

With 13 affirmative votes and one negative vote, senator-judges approved the September 8 appeal of Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo seeking to overturn the July 6 ruling of impeachment court Presiding Officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero.
The court ruled that the voting baseline should include only senator-judges who are “legally and factually capable” of participating in the trial.

This excludes those who are detained, suspended or otherwise restrained from legally exercising their functions; those being sought by authorities whose whereabouts are unknown; those suffering from physical or medical incapacity; those beyond the coercive processes of the Senate; and others similarly situated.
Six members of the Senate minority bloc — Senator-judges Alan Peter Cayetano, Pia Cayetano, Robin Padilla, Cynthia Villar, Imee Marcos, and Bong Go — were absent from the afternoon proceedings.
Marcos, in an ambush interview, said they decided not to participate in the voting, reiterating their position that the impeachment court’s interpretation of the voting threshold is unconstitutional.

Before the court went on a lunch break on Wednesday, senator-judges also rejected a point of order raised by Senator-judge Alan Peter Cayetano, who argued that the Senate impeachment court has no authority to interpret the voting threshold.
The point of order was rejected with 13 votes in favor of proceeding with the issue, six against, and one abstention.
Senator-judge Mark Villar abstained from the vote on Cayetano’s point of order. He later voted in favor of lowering the threshold.
“We are raising a point of order of the power of the impeachment court to raise this issue at this time,” Cayetano said.

To recall, Tulfo sought to reverse Escudero’s July 6 decision and revisit the voting threshold for Duterte’s conviction amid the prolonged absence of four senator-judges — Loren Legarda, Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, Rodante Marcoleta, and Jinggoy Estrada.

Legarda remains on extended medical leave abroad, while Dela Rosa is in hiding due to an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC) over alleged crimes against humanity stemming from the Duterte administration’s drug war.
Marcoleta and Estrada are detained over separate plunder charges.
To guide the court in its decision, Escudero had invited four retired Supreme Court justices last week to serve as amici curiae, or “friends of the court,” and provide their legal views on the issue.

Retired Chief Justices Reynato Puno, Hilario Davide Jr., and Artemio Panganiban took the position that the number of votes needed to remove an impeached official is not fixed at 16, while retired associate justice Adolfo Azcuna maintained that the voting basis should be anchored on the entire membership (24) of the Senate.

“The framers of the Constitution of 1935, 1973, and 1986 would never have intended to include in ‘all members’… those who cannot participate in the hearings and deliberations on the impeachment, such as those outside the jurisdiction of the Philippines, or whose whereabouts are unknown or are in hiding to avoid arrest,” Davide stated in a written position read by the Senate secretary on September 16.
Puno and Panganiban shared Davide’s view, while Azcuna maintained that the voting threshold should remain at 16.

Under Article XI, Section 3(6) of the 1987 Constitution, the Senate has the sole power to try and decide impeachment cases. Conviction requires the concurrence of two-thirds of all the members of the Senate. – Rappler.com

blocks.text: Here are the biggest headlines from India on Wednesday, September 23:

September 23, 2026
El Nino-driven heat could kill thousands in India by February: report

This year's powerful El Nino phenomenon, which is driving global heat to record levels and contributing to severe droughts, wildfires and water shortages, is likely to cause 15,800 deaths in India by the end of February, according to a research report released on Wednesday.

The warning, released by the University of Chicago-based Climate Impact Lab, said as many as 451,000 more deaths between June and February of next year could be attributed to El Nino, when compared to typical heat-related deaths in a year.
El Nino is a natural climate phenomenon that occurs every two to seven years, toward the end of the year. It comes in various strengths — depending on the prevailing conditions.

El Nino patterns are considered strong if the surface temperature of the water off the west coast of South America is over 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above average. In July this year, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) was already observing temperature increases ofgreater than 3 degrees Celsius in the eastern and central Pacific.

The Climate Impact Lab report said the powerful heat this year was most dangerous in places that are already hot and relatively poor. It projected that the Global South will see more heat-related deaths.
El Nino, regional wars fuel global food crisis
What could help prevent deaths?

Heat warnings, hydration outreach, cooling centers and a plan to cope with the heat are all ways governments can help protect people, the report said, adding that they should also expand hospital capacity and chalk out anticipatory financing.

blocks.caption: New Delhi had several cooling stations across the city in the summer of 2026. However, not all cities and towns have the same resourcesImage: Manish Swarup/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Abhiyant Tiwari, a heat expert at NRDC India who was not involved in the study, said the report's projections should serve as a call to action rather than be another reason for alarm.
But while it's one thing to have well thought-out plans — as India does — implementing these plans remains a challenge, he said.
"The real measure of our preparedness is not how many heat warnings we issue, but how effectively we protect people and reduce preventable deaths," Tiwari said.
Editing:Sean Sinico
