articles.title: Minority senators boycott voting for VP Sara's conviction threshold
articles.summary: Minority senators did not participate in the voting on the threshold needed to impeach Vice President Sara Duterte after the Senate impeachment court rejected Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter…

blocks.text: MARK VILLAR VOTES 'YES'
Published September 23, 2026 2:19pm

Minority senators, except for Mark Villar, did not participate in the voting on the threshold needed to impeach Vice President Sara Duterte after the Senate impeachment court rejected Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano's motion to defer the matter to the Supreme Court.
Thirteen senator-judges voted against Cayetano’s move for the deferment of the scheduled vote on the threshold.
Among the six senator-judges who voted in favor of Cayetano's move were Pia Cayetano, Christopher "Bong" Go, Imee Marcos, Robin Padilla, and Camille Villar.
While on break, reporters asked Cayetano if he would return back to the plenary. He responded, "Depends kung ano po ang ite-take up." (It depends on what will be taken up.)
Meanwhile, Go and Marcos were seen not wearing their red robes.
After the senators took a lunch break, Alan Cayetano, Pia Cayetano, Go, Marcos, Padilla, and Camille Villar did not participate in the voting for the threshold.
Only Senator Mark Villar from the minority participated and voted "yes."
The Senate impeachment court has voted to lower the threshold required to convict Duterte in her impeachment trial.
This came following the presentation of arguments by the House prosecution panel and Duterte’s defense team.
On July 6, Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero ruled that the threshold needed to convict is 16, which is the two-thirds of the 24 members of the Senate.
The Constitution, however, does not state a number but reads “no [impeachable] person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the members of the Senate.”
There are currently four senators who are absent.
Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta are detained on plunder and other related charges due to their alleged involvement in flood control and undeclared campaign donations, respectively.
Senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa, meanwhile, remains at large amid a warrant of arrest from the International Criminal Court in connection to the previous administration's bloody drug war.
Senator Loren Legarda recently extended her medical leave abroad due to a lung condition. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Is Syria's 'new' economy for the rich only?
articles.summary: The Syrian government says it is restructuring the economy and announces prosperity. But ordinary Syrians are not feeling it. In fact, they say their lives are getting worse. Who exactly is likely to…

image.caption: Syria has announced as many as 46 economic agreements worth billions but monitors such as the Karam Shaar Advisory say only around eight have been acted uponImage: Nabiaha al Taha/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Kanan Abdullah has been working as a driver in the Syrian capital Damascus for around 12 years but he, like many others in his trade, is now finding it difficult to make ends meet following recent fuel price rises in Syria.

"You're left with almost nothing at the end of the day" he told DW. "You have enough to buy another tank of gas but how are you supposed to buy food? Or what if you need money set aside to repair the car?" he complained.

His potential passengers feel the same way. "People are starting to worry about how they're going to get to work and get home because transport alone is costing them half their pay," added Kamar Kasoum, a local mother of three.

In mid-September, the Syrian government raised the price of all kinds of fuel, including petrol and diesel. Diesel saw the biggest hike, rising 40%. The energy ministry explained such changes were necessary because of higher global fuel costs — Syria remains dependent on energy imports — as well as local shortages.

blocks.caption: In Damascus, local reporters say fares on public minibuses rose up to 70% almost immediately and taxi rides become 60% more expensiveImage: Monsef Memari/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: Widest protests since dictatorship

The move triggered some of the most widespread protests Syria has seen since thedictatorial Assad regime was toppled in late 2024. While fuel prices are still comparable with other countries in the region, Syrians are struggling because of lower purchasing power, experts say. Demonstrators burned tires, blocked roads and called for the dismissal of politicians they held responsible.
The protests subsided as the Syrian government walked back some changes and announced plans to subsidize diesel for heating, agriculture and industry.

But higher fuel prices are only the latest to add inflationary pressure on ordinary Syrians. In its most recent bulletin on the consumer price index, the Syrian Center for Policy Research, says prices increased almost 25% between July 2025 and July 2026. Worryingly, the highest price increases — around 37% — were on "essential expenditure" such as housing, water, electricity and gas.

blocks.caption: Protests against fuel price rises erupted in September: Experts say lifting subsidies without creating alternatives to help those most in need is what made locals so angryImage: Mahmoud Hassano/REUTERS

blocks.text: "There is no sensible correlation between the income an individual earns in Syria and the prices they're paying," Alaa Sndyan, an architect in Damascus, told DW. "People are starting to feel the pinch, they feel that prices have gotten way too high."

"And these protests and demonstrations didn't just come out of nowhere," Kamar Kasoum added. "We're at the point where we can't even say that we're just cutting back on non-priorities. It's like, let's just stick to eating and drinking. Nothing else."
Economic growth in Syria — but for whom?

All this is happening despite what appears to be a lot of good news about the Syrian economy. There are regular reports about billion-dollar, international investments and projects and, speaking at the Arab Media Summit in Dubai on Tuesday, Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa predicted Syria's economy would be worth around $50 billion (approx. €44 billion) this year, up from around $20 billion in 2024.
But this much-celebrated prosperity somehow doesn't seem to be reaching ordinary Syrians, over two-thirds of whom still live in comparative poverty according to United Nations.
A new Syria for 'the rich'

Damascus architect Sndyan said it was hard to tell who's benefitting from economic development. "With a lot of the projects being announced now, we don't see anything happening on the ground, there's no impact on the real world," she argued. "And I always feel like these projects are aimed at a specific demographic: the affluent class. I am not sure these projects are actually for the people."

Sndyan added that she felt as if ordinary people who lost everything during Syria's civil war were being forgotten in the midst of various grand plans. She said she would also like to see more transparency and better communication from the government around its plans.
She is not the only one. There has been plenty of criticism about the direction of Syria's economic planning as well as concerns it may benefit the already-wealthy most.

More extreme anti-government activists have pointed to the luxury watches some Syrian politicians appear to be wearing, making accusations of "crony capitalism" and suggesting the government is diverting funds into the military in order to secure its own power. None of those accusations are verified.

But criticism has also comes from more moderate quarters. In an August story, Syrian outlet Al Jumhuriya looked into the billion-dollar real estate projects announced around the country. These are mostly comprised of gated communities and luxury apartments, it said. In a country with a major housing crisis, "who will actually be able to live in these projects?" the publication asked.
'Neo-liberal' policies not suitable

There's concern old patterns are being repeated. "As certain pre-existing forms of corruption and extraction change, new channels of privilege are emerging … albeit with new winners and losers," Syrian think tank Etana argued in an analysis this week.

Observers say the neo-liberal style reforms the Syrian government is currently committed to will only worsen this problem and, in the longer run, cause the same kinds of social problems that sparked Syria's revolution in 2011.

When the new Syrian government first took control in late 2024, ordinary Syrians were willing to give them a chance. But monthly polling by the magazine, Syria in Transition, indicates patience is wearing thin. By April this year, "the most serious deterioration was in attitudes toward the economy ... only 13% of respondents now believed the government was doing enough to tackle soaring energy and food prices while 66% said its efforts were insufficient," the magazine noted.

"The country's new leaders have undertaken a shock therapy program of economic liberalization without, it seems, fully accounting for the acute vulnerability and poverty of most Syrians," Sam Heller, an analyst with the New York-based think tank Century International, pointed out in Foreign Affairs magazine this week.

And that's not suitable, researcher Joseph Daher, an expert on Syria's political economy, argued in an analysis for the online bilingual outlet Syria Untold . "In countries emerging from conflict, 'success' cannot be measured solely by fiscal surpluses or price stability," he wrote. "True success is measured by the ability of fiscal policy to rebuild citizenship, justice, institutional capacity and public trust."

To do that, the Syrian government needs to change its policies, Karam Shaar, director of the Karam Shaar Advisory, a New Zealand-based consultancy for Syrian economic affairs, said during an online interview last week. Some of what the new authorities have done was necessary given the post-war situation, he conceded, but now more transparency, expertise and better governance was needed.
"I think they are they are starting to realize that [and] I continue to have a bit of hope that this will indeed happen," Shaar concluded.

articles.title: US and Iran hold first talks since June after Trump's 'annihilation' threat
articles.summary: The talks are the first since a ceasefire collapsed in June, with the sides exchanging fire intermittently.

blocks.text: Top Iranian and US officials have held talks at the UN in New York on a day when the US leader said he could "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if the conflict went unresolved.

No breakthrough has been reported from the meeting mediated by Qatar and involving Iran's foreign minister and US President Donald Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff - the first since a June ceasefire unravelled.
Witkoff said a round of discussions had been completed "that we hope will prove constructive and promising". Iran repeated its demand for the US to end its "acts of aggression".
The US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on 28 February. Iran responded by attacking Israel and US bases in the Gulf and Arab Gulf allies of the US - as well as blocking the Strait of Hormuz.
Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to pass through the strait before the war and its closure has caused wild fluctuations of prices.
It has also increased pressure on Trump to find a way of ending the conflict - particularly as the US heads to Congressional elections in November.

In his address at the annual meeting of the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Trump began by touting his accomplishments on the economy, immigration, the border and tackling violent crime - remarks that sounded more pitched to voters the US midterms than the diplomats in the hall.

He spent much of his address justifying the war with Iran - a huge contrast with remarks earlier by UN Secretary General António Guterres, who warned global divisions were deepening and underscored the "interdependence" of the world's peoples.

The US president argued that the conflict had prevented Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and demonstrated the value of what he described as peace through strength - ultimatums rather than deal-making or compromise.
"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" he said.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?"
Trump said he believed an Iran deal, which has so far eluded him, would come right after November's elections.
The remarks were indicative of his foreign-policy strategy of coercive diplomacy - threatening overwhelming force while keeping negotiations open.
Trump later told reporters that American officials had had a "very productive" three-hour meeting with the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the general assembly.
Iran state TV confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had met Witkoff.

Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei, quoted by state broadcaster IRNA, later said negotiations took part through a Qatari mediator who communicated Tehran's conditions, including an end to the war on all fronts and to US "acts of aggression".

The BBC asked Witkoff how the meetings had gone as he was leaving the UN building and he responded with a thumbs up. Witkoff later confirmed on X that the talks had been held "through the mediators, who shuttled between the two sides throughout the day".
"They successfully completed a round of discussions that we hope will prove constructive and promising," Witkoff said. "The mediators will continue their work."
Since the ceasefire collapsed, both sides have intermittently exchanged fire.
Iran has attacked vessels it says have attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz without authorisation.
The US has attacked Iranian sites in the strait - as well as Iranian tankers off the country's coast.
The US has also maintained a blockade of Iranian ports, causing a huge disruption to the Iranian economy.

In an effort to force Tehran to agree a deal to end the conflict, President Trump has also threatened sanctions against any country that continues trading with Iran. But so far, there has been no indication of a change of course in Iran, which insists the US and Israel end their war, including against the Iran-backed Shia group Hezbollah in Lebanon which Israel has been attacking.
Yemen's Houthis - also allied to Iran - have recently intesified attacks aimed at disrupting oil shipping from Saudi Arabia, promting an escalation of the conflict with the kingdom.

articles.title: South Africa: 11 killed in attack on house party
articles.summary: The motive for the shooting was not immediately clear.

image.caption: Police said some of the victims were known to authoritiesImage: Kristin Palitza/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Gunmen killed 11 people at a home in eastern South Africa, Kwa-Zulu Natal province's premier said on Wednesday.
Three people were injured in the attack.
The motive for the shooting was not immediately clear.
The shooting occurred at KwaMakhutha, a township some 30 kilometers (19 miles) south of Durban, the eastern province's largest city.

"The victims, including a pregnant woman, were gathered at a house shortly before 11:00 pm [2100 UTC] when armed assailants reportedly entered the premises and opened fire," Kwa-Zulu Premier Thamsanqa Ntuli said.
"The incident has left the community in profound shock and grief," he said.
Police said that one of the victims died after being taken to hospital.
"Ten victims, including the woman, died at the scene and four were taken ​to hospital, were one of them succumbed to gunshot injuries," police said.
Some of the victims were known to police, according to the statement. No arrests had yet been made.
Shootings in South Africa
South Africa has one of the world's highest murder rates. Around 60 people are killed each day in the country of around 62 million.
The incident comes as South Africa is still reeling over a series of femicides east of Johannesburg.
Legal and illegal firearms are common in South Africa, as are shootings, which are often fueled by rivalry between criminal gangs or between informal businesses.

articles.title: Impeachment court lowers voting threshold to convict Sara Duterte
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court on Wednesday voted to lower the threshold required to convict Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial.

blocks.text: Published September 23, 2026 2:00pm Updated September 23, 2026 2:19pm
The Senate impeachment court on Wednesday voted to lower the threshold required to convict Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial.

Thirteen senators voted in favor of the motion put forward by Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo who sought reconsideration of the July 6 ruling that the voting threshold is set at 16 which is two-thirds of the 24-member Senate.
This came following the presentation of arguments by the House prosecution panel and Duterte’s defense team.The parties were given 15 minutes each.
Tulfo sought consideration since four of their colleagues have not been present in the impeachment trial proceedings.

Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta are detained on plunder and other related charges due to their alleged involvement in flood control projects and undeclared campaign donations, respectively.

Senator Ronald dela Rosa, on the other hand, is nowhere to be found amid a standing warrant of arrest issued against him by the International Criminal Court due to his alleged involvement in the drug war deaths.
Senator Loren Legarda, for her part, is on an extended medical leave abroad due to a lung ailment.
The 1987 Constitution states that "no person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate."

In early September, the impeachment court invited retired Supreme Court Chief Justices Artemio Panganiban, Reynato Puno, and Hilario Davide Jr. and Associate Justice Adolfo Azcuna as amici curiae or friends of the court.
Panganiban, Puno, and Davide said that the voting threshold should be based on the number of senator-judges who actively participated in the impeachment trial.

However, Azcuna, one of the framers of the 1987 Constitution, offered a different view that the two-thirds concurrence requirement should relate to the entire membership of the Senate; hence, a conviction by 16 senator-judges is needed. —LDF/AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Marcoleta hints he may skip Sara Duterte impeachment vote
articles.summary: Senator-judge Rodante Marcoleta, who is currently detained while facing a plunder charge, said Wednesday that he no longer saw it fit to participate in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara…

blocks.text: Published September 23, 2026 1:44pm

Senator-judge Rodante Marcoleta, who is currently detained while facing a plunder charge, said Wednesday that he no longer saw it fit to participate in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

In a statement, Marcoleta said that from the onset, he disagreed with Senator-judge Francis Escudero being chosen as the presiding officer of the impeachment court, arguing that it was contrary to the law.

“Hindi ko na nakikitang nararapat pa akong makilahok sa impeachment trial ni Bise Presidente Sara Duterte, kabilang na ang deliberasyon at botohan, kung ang tatahakin ng Impeachment Court ay landas na lalapastangan sa ating Saligang Batas,” Marcoleta said.

(I no longer see it fit to participate in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, including the deliberations and voting, if the Impeachment Court takes a path that violates the Constitution.)
Marcoleta said the Senate should not apply its internal rules in determining the voting threshold when the Constitution itself provides for the requirement.
He issued the statement just as the impeachment court deliberated on the voting threshold needed to convict or acquit Duterte.
Escudero had originally ruled that 16 votes would be needed to convict her, but four senators have since been detained, gone into hiding or been absent from the trial.

“Kung magpapasya ang Impeachment Court na magtakda ng bilang ng boto na salungat sa malinaw na salita at kahulugan ng ating Saligang Batas, at ipagpapatuloy ang paglilitis sa ilalim ng isang namumunong kaduda-duda ang pagkakatalaga, ang dalawang paglabag na ito ay ganap na makasisira sa pagiging lehitimo at integridad ng impeachment trial,” Marcoleta said.

(If the Impeachment Court decides to set a voting threshold that is contrary to the clear words and meaning of the Constitution, and continues the trial under a presiding officer whose appointment is questionable, these two violations would seriously undermine the legitimacy and integrity of the impeachment trial.)
Marcoleta also cast doubt on whatever decision the impeachment court would reach, given what he described as these questionable circumstances.

The senator is currently detained at the Quezon City Jail Male Dormitory. He is facing a P75-million plunder charge over alleged undeclared campaign contributions he received in connection with his 2025 senatorial bid. Marcoleta has pleaded not guilty to the charge.
He has refused to enter a plea to the plunder charges filed against him.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Camille Villar gets emotional, calls for respect for absent colleagues
articles.summary: Senator-judge Camille Villar on Wednesday became emotional as she called on her fellow senators to respect colleagues who are absent from the impeachment trial amid criminal and plunder cases they…

blocks.text: SARA DUTERTE IMPEACHMENT TRIAL
Published September 23, 2026 1:09pm
Senator-judge Camille Villar on Wednesday became emotional as she called on her fellow senators to respect colleagues who are absent from the impeachment trial due to legal and health issues.

Villar stood during the 29th day of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial after Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo reiterated his call for the Senate impeachment court to reconsider its ruling on the absence of several colleagues, which he said could affect the voting threshold needed to convict Duterte.
“The present realities that some of our members are beyond the coercive power or jurisdiction of the Senate, one is on a medical leave abroad, with no definite return date,” Tulfo said.

“Another is in hiding. Two others are under the custody of the Sandiganbayan or the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology. Ito po ang factual circumstances na umiiral ngayon. At hindi naman po ito umiiral o umiral nung tayo po ay nagsisimula pa lamang sa ating proceedings,” he added.
(These are the factual circumstances that exist now. These circumstances did not exist when we were just starting our proceedings.)

He was referring to Senator-judge Loren Legarda, who is currently on extended medical leave, Senator-judges Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta, who are detained in connection with plunder charges, and Senator-Judge Ronald dela Rosa, who remains at large following an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court.

Tulfo said the framers of the 1987 Constitution set the two-thirds supermajority requirement as a safeguard against the possible abuse of the impeachment power, as they did not foresee that senators themselves could face criminal and plunder charges.
“Because it is a fraction, the mathematical baseline dynamically moves or varies depending on structural, operational, situational factors affecting the Senate composition,” he said.
“Ang mga kaso po ng mga senador noon, either subversion, sedition, yun po ang mga kaso. Pero ang mga senador po ay hindi po nakakasuhan ng kriminal, plunder, at kung ano-ano pa,” Tulfo added.
(Senators in the past faced cases involving subversion and sedition. But senators were not being charged with criminal offenses, plunder and other similar cases.)
Villar then interjected, saying the absent senators should not be attacked over their cases.

“While I respect all of my colleagues here, all of you, I think we should be reminded that all of the senators that are detained and who are not here right now, that is not their choice,” she said, becoming emotional.
Villar said the absent senators should not be labelled as criminals because they have yet to be convicted of the charges they are facing.

“And I think it is unfair to call them out that their crimes are plunder and theft because none of those senators have been convicted. There are even a lot of questions why they are not here in the first place,” she said.
“As the youngest member of this august body, can we stop it? With these attacks on each other?” she added.

At the start of the impeachment trial, Senator impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero then stressed that the 1987 Constitution provides that no person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all members of the Senate, or 16 votes.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Sri Lanka: 15 men jailed for life in 2019 Easter bombings
articles.summary: The 15 convicts have been given prison sentences of at least 200 years each, following a long trial in what was among Sri Lanka's deadliest attacks.

image.caption: The 15 men were among a total of 25 defendants accused of aiding and abetting the suicide bombers who hit three churches and three hotelsImage: Ishara S. Kodikara/AFP

blocks.text: A court in Sri Lanka convicted 15 men over the deadly 2019 Easter bombings, sentencing them to 200 to 260 years in prison on Tuesday.

A three-judge bench of the High Court in Colombo found 14 of the defendants guilty on all charges, which included murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism and possessing firearms and explosives under the Prevention of Terrorism Act.
The 15th accused was found guilty only of some charges.
The court also ordered the seizure of the convicts' property and assets.
Nine men were acquitted in the trial. Those convicted have the right to appeal to the Supreme Court.
On April 21, 2019, coordinated suicide blasts struck three churches and three luxury hotels, killing 279 people and injuring 574 more — making it among the worst attacks in Sri Lanka's history.
Investigators had blamed the attack on a local Islamist extremist group.
The 15 defendants were among a total of 25 individuals — all from Sri Lanka's minority Muslim community — accused of providing support to the suicide bombers.
Lengthy Sri Lanka Easter bombing trial
The trial lasted nearly five years with Sri Lankan authorities filing 23,270 charges in 2021 against the 25 suspects. One of the accused died in pretrial detention.
The case listed some 2,300 witnesses.
Mohamed Ibrahim Mohamed Naufer, an Islamic cleric and the alleged leader of the Easter Sunday bombings, was among those sentenced.
Prosecutors said he had radicalized the other defendants with his teachings. He was sentenced to 240 years in prison with hard labor.
'Intelligence failure'
Tuesday's verdict came as a separate probe looks into allegations that elements within the Sri Lankan state may have had links to those responsible for the blasts.
The country's former intelligence chief Suresh Salley was arrested over accusations that he had a role in masterminding the attacks, a charge he denies.
A parliamentary committee had earlier found that police and intelligence officials ignored foreign intelligence warnings of the attacks.
In July, a former police chief and a former senior official of the Defense Ministry were given the death sentence for failing to act despite prior intelligence warnings.
Sri Lanka mourns bombing victims

articles.title: Reports of violence against women in Gaza surge, UN agency finds
articles.summary: The UN Population Fund also says there has been a "severe escalation" in the number of early and forced marriages.

blocks.text: There has been a sharp rise in reports of violence against women and girls in the Gaza Strip, including early and forced marriage, according to a series of recent reports from the UN Population Fund (UNFPA).

One report, which analyses data collected by 10 organisations, says, external the protracted crisis in war-torn Gaza has "created conditions in which women and girls face escalating risks of gender-based violence".

It also warns that there has been a "severe escalation" in the number of early and forced marriage incidents in the second quarter of this year. Both are considered types of gender-based violence (GBV) by the UN.

Another report presenting testimony from 230 women in crowded displacement camps in Gaza City and Khan Younis, external makes for a grim read, describing the violence they have experienced or witnessed.
Some readers may find some of the details in this report distressing

One displaced woman in a school-turned-shelter in Gaza highlights how rape victims are often married to their rapists to avoid shame and scandal. "When rape cases are discovered in schools, you find weddings and celebrations at the school the next day," she says.

Another woman tells how last year, at the time of famine, "a man married off his 14-year-old daughter in exchange for two bags of flour so he and his [other] children could eat". Six women in different displacement camps shared stories of such exchanges - which would have been unthinkable before the conflict between Israel and Hamas began in 2023.

Although data collection to establish actual figures remains tricky, in the second quarter of this year, the UNFPA says the number of reported cases of early and forced marriage had increased by 123% on the first quarter. Early or child marriage involved girls aged 12 to 17.

"The trends are shocking," says Nestor Owomuhangi, the UNFPA representative to Palestine. He says that the extreme circumstances over the past three years - which have seen tens of thousands of people killed, mass destruction and multiple waves of displacement in Gaza - have broken down social structures, so "everything is eroded... there is no system".

While food markets have reopened, many cannot afford the goods on offer, there is still extreme poverty and hunger with reliance on charitable handouts. Nearly all the population of more than two million Gazans have been driven from their homes, leaving most living in squalid tent camps or damaged buildings. Public services have largely collapsed, and Israeli air strikes have continued despite the ceasefire.

Prior to the war, girls in Gaza outnumbered and outperformed boys at every level of education above primary school. Now, with prolonged school closures, many children have dropped out of education. For boys there is pressure to find informal work to help support their families, for girls there are heightened issues around safety.

Living among strangers, without privacy, in a socially conservative society, there are complaints of heightened sexual harassment and abuse - many families see marrying their daughters as a way to protect them and preserve modesty. The UNFPA report - based on research carried out in late 2025 and early 2026 - reveals how girls orphaned during the war are especially vulnerable.
One woman in a Gaza City camp interviewed for the report says she attended the wedding of two girls from her family, aged just 14 and 15.

"Their uncles married them off very young. Do you know why? Because their father and mother were martyred, and their uncles wanted to get rid of the responsibility and expenses," the woman said. "By God, they don't understand what marriage or life is."

The Women's Affairs Center in Gaza - a Palestinian NGO which works with the UNFPA - and other support groups have documented distressing cases of girls who have been married and suffered abuse, often becoming pregnant. They say that those in their early teens are much more likely to have miscarriages and underweight babies than adult women.

"We see adolescent pregnancies going through the roof because of child marriage," says Owomuhangi. "A child who is at an age when the body is not fully developed to sustain another body, who is hungry, in unhygienic circumstances, who doesn't know how to take care of the infant, who doesn't even know how to take care of herself, the consequences of that pregnancy are always really, really bad."

The UN and most humanitarian organisations categorise marriages of girls under 18 as early marriage. Even before the war, this was more common among Palestinians in Hamas-run Gaza than it was in the occupied West Bank, but it was declining.

The law in Gaza allows exceptions to the minimum marital age of 17 with parental consent and authorisation by a judge. Court officials can approve marriage for those as young as 14 years and seven months old, although a local Sharia expert told us that "legal safeguards" had been removed when Islamic courts - which officiate over family matters for Muslims - were closed for a large part of the war.

The BBC has been speaking to some families in which bereaved relatives were married. Zuhair, who is 25, says his uncles pushed him to marry a 16-year-old girl from his extended family after her father - her sole guardian - was killed in an Israeli air strike.
Challenged on why he agreed to go ahead with the plan, he said: "One of the reasons that led me to marry her was that there was no one to take care of her. That's the first point."

"If it were not for the war, she would still be a young girl spoiled by her father. She would be going to school," Zuhair adds. "She still has a child's mindset, not a mature mindset. She misses school, her family, friends. She even misses simply sitting at home."

A couple says they allowed their 17-year-old son to marry his 16-year-old cousin after their older son and the girl's father were killed. The teenager is now pregnant so will not return to school. "She needs to care for her child," her father-in-law says, "her education would be in vain."

Sexual violence in Gaza remains acutely under-reported in large part due to fear of stigma and retaliation. UN safety audits have shown particular risks to women and girls at night, causing them to avoid camp toilets and bathrooms.

The latest analysis report by the UNFPA-led task force stated that incidents of sexual violence, including rape and sexual assault, "have become critical in Gaza". They accounted for 2.7% of total reported incidents of GBV from April to June 2026 - up from 2.1% in the quarter before; this represented a 61% surge in absolute case numbers.

This rise is being linked to efforts to raise awareness and provide better ways to make confidential reports. Demographic data indicated that the majority of survivors were women aged 18-59, followed by adolescent girls at 8% and adult men at 5%.

Women who are widows or have husbands who are detained or missing are at increased risk of sexual abuse and exploitation. Nearly one in four households is now reportedly headed by a woman - double the proportion before the war.

"One widow was looking for a tent, and a [camp] representative told her, "I'll give you a tent, we'll put you in our camp, and you can come stay with me tonight," recalls a woman in Gaza City, interviewed for the UNFPA report.

Aid agencies argue that the dangers for women in Gaza could be greatly eased by improving humanitarian conditions. There are calls for Israel to allow higher quality shelters into the territory as well as equipment to upgrade latrines and sanitation as well as lighting. Israel restricts items it classes as having a potential dual use for military purposes.

There are ongoing efforts to improve education and healthcare and longer-term plans for campaigns to combat domestic violence and child marriage. While the course of so many lives in Gaza has already been permanently changed, women say they hope for a future in which they at least feel safer.
If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available in the UK at BBC Action Line.

articles.title: Senate court rejects Cayetano bid to block impeach threshold vote
articles.summary: Senator-judge Alan Peter Cayetano has lost his challenge to stop the body's decision on whether to lower the math needed for Sara Duterte's conviction.

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 12:50pm

The Senate, sitting as an Impeachment Court, resumes its hearing on Monday, August 3, 2026, on Article I of the case against Vice President Sara Duterte, which concerns the alleged misuse, questionable liquidation and systematic misappropriation of confidential funds.
Senate Social Media Unit / Wendell D. Alinea

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano failed Wednesday to stop the Senate impeachment court from voting on whether to revise the 16-vote threshold for convicting Vice President Sara Duterte. Senator-judges voted 13-6, with one abstention, to reject Cayetano’s challenge and allow the threshold question to proceed.
“With 13 affirmative votes, six negative votes, one abstention, the appeal is lost,” Presiding Officer Chiz Escudero said.

The vote was not yet a decision on how many votes would be required to convict Duterte. Instead, it settled Cayetano’s attempt to prevent the impeachment court from taking up the threshold question at all.
Cayetano had raised a point of order arguing that the issue should have been settled at the start of the trial because it involved the court’s jurisdiction.
He urged the impeachment court to leave the constitutional question to the Supreme Court rather than reinterpret the threshold midway through the proceedings.
Cayetano warned that changing the number of senators used as the base for computing the two-thirds requirement could produce the equivalent of a “mistrial.”
He and Sen. Pia Cayetano had also said they would not participate in a vote on the threshold itself because they believe the Supreme Court should resolve the issue.
Escudero rejected that position and allowed the impeachment court to decide whether Sen. Erwin Tulfo’s motion to reconsider the threshold should proceed.
Thirteen of the 20 senator-judges present backed Escudero’s ruling.
Threshold question still alive
Still before the impeachment court is Tulfo’s bid to exclude four senators who have been absent from the trial from the base used to calculate the two-thirds vote required for conviction.

Escudero had ruled at the opening of the trial that 16 votes were needed to convict Duterte, interpreting the Constitution’s requirement of “two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate” as referring to the chamber’s full 24-member roster.
Tulfo’s motion asks the court to reconsider that interpretation in light of senators who are not participating in the proceedings.
If the court adopts a smaller denominator, the number of votes required for conviction could also fall.
The senator-judges are now expected to vote separately on that question.

The impeachment court had set Sept. 23 for oral arguments and deliberation on the disputed threshold after hearing differing interpretations from retired Supreme Court justices invited as amici curiae, or friends of the court. — with Cristina Chi

articles.title: Marcos admin ‘seriously considering’ absolute pardon for Mary Jane Veloso
articles.summary: Rep. Albert Garcia said the Office of the President will release an announcement regarding the matter in the following days.

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 12:44pm
Filipina inmate on Indonesia death row, Mary Jane Veloso (C) reacts as she arrives at the Soekarno-Hatta International Airport in Tangerang on Dec. 17, 2024, for her repatriation to Philippines.
AFP / Juni Kriswanto

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the President is "seriously considering" granting an absolute pardon on humanitarian grounds to former domestic worker and trafficking victim Mary Jane Veloso, according to a member of the House of Representatives.

House Committee on Appropriations Senior Vice Chair Albert Garcia (Bataan 2nd District) made the announcement during the deliberations on the proposed 2027 budget of the Office of the President on Wednesday, September 23.
It came after Rep. Sarah Elago (Gabriela Women’s Party) inquired about the administration’s efforts on Veloso’s release.

“The Office of the President is seriously considering granting an absolute pardon to May Jane Veloso on humanitarian grounds in support of the government’s commitment to protecting Filipino migrant workers,” Garcia said.
When asked when a decision could be expected, Garcia said the Office of the President will release an announcement regarding the matter in the following days.
Before answering Elago’s inquiry, Executive Secretary Ralph Recto was seen approaching Garcia at the podium.
Veloso’s family continues to call for executive clemency as she remains detained at the Correctional Institution for Women in Mandaluyong following her repatriation from Indonesia in December 2024.
She was convicted of drug trafficking and sentenced to death by firing squad in Indonesia in 2010 after authorities found 2.6 kilograms of heroin in her suitcase.
A last-minute reprieve was granted after the Philippine government informed Indonesian authorities about her recruiters’ surrender.
According to Elago, Veloso’s case was recognized as a human trafficking and forced drug mule exploitation case.

articles.title: Leonen to serve as acting chief justice after Gesmundo's retirement
articles.summary: Supreme Court Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen will serve as acting chief justice, while the post is vacant after the expected retirement of Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo.

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 12:41pm
Photo shows Supreme Court Associate Justice Marvic Leonen.
sc.judiciary.gov.ph

MANILA, Philippines — Supreme Court Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen will serve as acting chief justice, while the post is vacant after the expected retirement of Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo.

In a message to reporters on Tuesday, September 22, Supreme Court Spokesperson Camille, citing Section 12 of the Judiciary Act of 1948, said that “the duties and powers of the Chief Justice shall be exercised by the most senior Associate Justice until a new Chief Justice is appointed and qualified.”

“This is pursuant to Section 12 of Republic Act No. 296, or the Judiciary Act of 1948, which provides that when the position of Chief Justice is vacant, the duties and powers of the Chief Justice shall be exercised by the most senior Associate Justice until a new Chief Justice is appointed and qualified,” Ting said.
Gesmundo is expected to reach mandatory retirement on November 6. His retirement will give President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. his first opportunity to appoint a chief justice.
After his retirement, Marcos should appoint a new chief justice within 90 days from the list of nominees prepared by the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC).
The JBC has invited five senior Supreme Court associate justices, including Leonen, to apply for chief justice ahead of Gesmundo’s retirement.

articles.title: A lot has happened since the B.C. snap election was called. Here's a quick rundown
articles.summary: Cariboo-Chilcotin MLA Lorne Doerkson has become the interim leader of the Conservative Party, and MLAs who quit en masse during Kerry-Lynne Findlay's tenure are rejoining. Meanwhile, some MLAs have…

image.caption: B.C. NDP Leader David Eby is seen outside Government House in Victoria with his wife Dr. Cailey Lynch, after calling the snap election. (Mike McArthur/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New

Cariboo-Chilcotin MLA Lorne Doerkson has become the interim leader of the Conservative Party, and MLAs who quit en masse during Kerry-Lynne Findlay's tenure are rejoining. Meanwhile, some MLAs have announced they won't be seeking re-election next month.
New leaders, election dropouts, and mayors sounding off on back-to-back elections
Eby calls snap B.C. election citing 'existential' Trump threat

On Tuesday, B.C. NDP Leader David Eby put an end to weeks of speculation by calling an early election in B.C., meaning voters will head to the polls to choose their next provincial government on October 24.
Eby said the election, two years ahead of schedule, was required to meet the "existential moment" created by the Canada-U.S. trade conflict.
"We have big decisions to make as a province. And British Columbians, you deserve a say in the direction that we choose," he said in a news conference Tuesday.
But some see it as political opportunism, given the recent turmoil within the B.C. Conservatives.

B.C. Conservative interim leader Lorne Doerkson has characterised it as a "cheap, opportunistic political move," while Greens Leader Emily Lowan called it an unnecessary decision that would bring "yet more instability."
There has been a lot of political movement since the election was called.
Here's a quick rundown to help you make sense of where things are at.
B.C. Conservatives get new interim leader
Before Tuesday, Cariboo-Chilcotin legislator Lorne Doerkson wasn't a well-known name, but he has been chosen by consensus as interim leader of the B.C. Conservatives.
He wasted no time introducing himself to the electorate at a news conference held shortly after the B.C. election was called, flanked by more than a dozen Conservative MLAs.
"We are unified in one simple task, and that is to change governments in this province," he said.
Former CentreBC MLAs join Conservatives
Seven MLAs who quit the Conservative Party en masse during former leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay's tenure, to subsequently join the CentreBC party, have rejoined since she was ousted on Sunday.
Peter Milobar, who departed in mid-August, spent a short time as the leader of CentreBC, but on Tuesday announced he would re-enter the Conservative fold.
Elenore Sturko, who was kicked out of the Conservative caucus in September last year, has taken over from Milobar as CentreBC leader.
She told CBC's On The Coast the Conservative Party did not align with her values.
"I want to be able to represent a portion of the voting public that feels that neither the Conservatives nor the NDP represent them," she said.
MLAs who've decided not to run
So far, three former NDP cabinet ministers have confirmed they will not be seeking re-election.
Among them is Ravi Kahlon, who currently serves as health minister.
He spent nine years as an MLA with the B.C. NDP, and did not give a reason for his departure.
"After three election cycles, I believe this is the right time for the next champion of North Delta to step forward and carry this work on," he said in a statement issued at 4 p.m. PT Tuesday.
Richmond-Steveston MLA Kelly Greene has also decided not to run again.
She was first elected in 2020, and played a key role in B.C.'s wildfire response this summer as minister of emergency management.
"This decision to step down was not made lightly," she said in a post on X.

items: Meet the party leaders running in B.C.'s provincial election

blocks.text: And on Monday, Lana Popham said she wouldn't seek re-election for what would have been her sixth term.
"I am sad to leave this role, but I am not leaving public life without purpose," she said in a statement.
B.C. mayors are not happy
The provincial election will happen exactly a week after civic elections take place in 187 provincial municipalities and regional districts across B.C. on Saturday, Oct. 17.
Local leaders are not happy about the timing, and have argued that dueling campaigns will be confusing for voters and make messaging harder for candidates.
Delta Mayor George Harvie said he was not alone in feeling "pissed off" about the situation, and Vancouver Mayor Ken Sim said it showed a lack of respect for municipalities.

Malcom Brodie, who is not running for re-election after serving 25 years as mayor of Richmond, wondered whether calling a provincial election early would anger the electorate and ultimately backfire on the B.C. NDP.
"I find this to be one of the more cynical moves I've ever seen in political life," he said.
With files from CBC News

articles.title: B.C.'s District of Squamish rejects $142M Woodfibre LNG deal
articles.summary: The District of Squamish has rejected a negotiated 10-year tax settlement that would have seen Woodfibre LNG contributing $142 million to the community in the Sea-to-Sky region.

image.caption: More than 640 Woodfibre LNG workers work at the facility in Howe Sound, about 64 kilometres north of Vancouver. A proposed community contribution deal with the District of Squamish, covering the LNG facility, was rejected on Tuesday. (Woodfibre LNG)

blocks.text: British Columbia
The District of Squamish has rejected a negotiated 10-year tax settlement that would have seen Woodfibre LNG contributing $142 million to the community in the Sea-to-Sky region.
Woodfibre LNG proposed a contribution of at least $142 million over 10 years to the community
The District of Squamish has rejected a deal that would have seen the operators of the Woodfibre LNG project contribute $142 million over 10 years.
During a special business meeting on Sept. 22 at 6 p.m. PT, council voted on the proposed community enhancement payment agreement (CEPA) and revitalized tax exemption (RTE) for Woodfibre LNG (WLNG).
If approved, the agreement would have commenced in 2027. Without the agreement in place, the district says it would continue to rely on regular property taxation on the WLNG property.
Woodfibre LNG is currently the only property in the district that is a Class 4 Major Industry.

The use of the funds would have been subject to council approval, and $117 million would have been used for direct community payments — for wastewater, stormwater system repair and replacements, flood protection, recreation investments, transportation upgrades and climate adaptation and mitigation.
Part of the deal would have been for WLNG to pay $25 million, capped at $2.5 million per year plus inflation, through the RTE.
Woodfibre LNG's floatel plan faces turbulence in Squamish
The agreement would have resulted in the resolution of three existing lawsuits against the district, filed by WLNG in relation to taxation in 2025 and 2026, among other matters.
Coun. Jenna Stoner put forward a motion to decline the agreement.
"I still don't think the deal is quite where I want it to be, and I don't think it's a good enough deal for our community," Stoner said.
She said the CEPA contributions would not be indexed to inflation, and the overall deal put the district at greater risk and liability.

"We know that our costs are only escalating over the next 10 years, and not having those core payments of the Community Enhancement Payments indexed to inflation makes this really challenging at the same time," Stoner said.

items: Woodfibre LNG secures 40-year export licence from feds

blocks.text: Coun. Lauren Greenlaw seconded the motion, and said instead of sticking with the more typical taxation structure, the district was "losing some of our protection" with the CEPA and RTE agreements.
Greenlaw said accepting the agreement would set a precedent for other communities who have LNG facilities planned, and also mentioned the CEPA payments were not subject to inflation.
"We should keep it simple and stick with tax legislation," Greenlaw said.
Canada’s clean LNG pitch — and why not everyone is buying it
Mayor Armand Hurford and councillors Andrew Hamilton and Chris Pettingill also supported the motion to deny the deal.
"It's been clear that this isn't enough for a community, and they'd like to have more control and more visibility into each step of the process," Hurford said.
Councillors Eric Andersen and John French both were in support of the agreement.
French said it was not an easy decision for him, after hearing from community members that did not think it was a good deal.
"The question still remains, how much should Woodfibre LNG pay in taxes? I believe it’s the amount set out in the mindfully negotiated agreement that we had in front of us," French said.
"There is no better agreement out there."
The motion to decline the 10-year deal was passed in a 5-2 vote.
Hurford said that this does not stop future councils from entering into a future deal with WLNG.
"Maybe that’s out there somewhere," Hurford said. "It is clear to me that this is not that."
Advocate relieved
Tracey Saxby, the co-founder of My Sea to Sky, an environmental advocacy group in Squamish that works to defend the Howe Sound, said she is feeling relieved.

“This was a terrible tax deal that Woodfibre LNG was offering our community, and I'm feeling very grateful to council for standing up for residents and for ensuring that we're going to get a better deal than what was on the table,” Saxby said.

items: Carney wants to fast-track LNG expansion in B.C., but can Canadian natural gas compete globally?

blocks.text: She questioned how much Woodfibre LNG should be paying in taxes, and said the proposed deal was not enough.
Saxby argues the proposed CEPA and RTE agreements would have constituted a "below average tax rate" for communities that have major industries across B.C.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

articles.title: Quebec duo Angine de Poitrine wins the 2026 Polaris Music Prize
articles.summary: The otherworldly Quebec duo took home the $30K prize for their second album.

image.caption: Angine de Poitrine's accept the 2026 Polaris Music Prize from last year's winner Jeremy Dutcher. (Jesse Kinos-Goodin/CBC Music)

blocks.text: Polaris·New
The otherworldly Quebec duo took home the $30K prize for their second album.
The otherworldly rock band took home the $30K prize for their second album
Angine de Poitrine, the masked and ornately costumed band from Saguenay, Que., has won the 2026 Polaris Music Prize.
The anonymous duo received the accolade and $30,000 for their second album, Vol.II.

Their manager Sébastien Collin gave an acceptance speech on their behalf since the band members, Khn and Klek, do not speak in their real voices, opting instead to use a made-up language to maintain their anonymity.

"That all this attention is being directed toward music this rock-driven and this complex is unexpected, yet entirely deserved," Collin said at the end of the Polaris Music Prize Concert in Toronto at Massey Hall.
"This artistic project is the result of a lifetime of refinement, collaboration, a drive to push beyond one’s limits, and a refusal to be confined by any established framework."

The Polaris Music Prize goes to the best Canadian album of the year, based solely on artistic merit and voted by a jury of Canadian music experts. The prize has been given out every year since 2006. Past winners include Feist, Kaytranada, Patrick Watson, Jeremy Dutcher, Debby Friday and more.

items: Who is Angine de Poitrine? The masked Quebec band is taking the internet by storm

blocks.text: Angine de Poitrine has had a massive year. The band's dizzying, tension-filled microtonal rock first took the world by storm when they went viral after a performance on KEXP, the Seattle-based radio station, which now sits at 19 million views on YouTube.

Just two years after the release of their debut album, they've sold-out an international headlining tour, opened for Jack White, shared a stage with Shania Twain and made appearances on British and American late-night shows.

items: Get to know the 10 albums nominated for the 2026 Polaris Music Prize

blocks.text: Vol.II was selected from a short list of 10 albums by more than 200 Canadian music critics and journalists who make up the Polaris jury.
Angine de Poitrine beat out previous winner Tanya Tagaq, and previous nominees Les Louanges, Bibi Club, Beverly Glenn-Copeland, Begonia, Peaches, Rochelle Jordan, Charlotte Cornfield and Aquakultre.
Polaris Song Prize and Heritage Prize winners announced

Angine de Poitrine also took home the Song Prize, a joint award from SOCAN and Polaris that goes to the best Canadian song of the year, beating out Charlotte Cornfield, Pup, Charlotte Day Wilson, Patrick Watson and Martha Wainwright.
The band's song Fabienk won the $10,000 prize, as voted by the Polaris jury.
The Song Prize is a new endeavour, only in its second year. Toronto folk musician Mustafa was last year's inaugural winner.

Earlier in the night, the Slaight Family Polaris Heritage Prize winners were announced. The Heritage Prize is Polaris's way of giving nods to albums that were released before they launched in 2006. It is decided in part by a jury of critics and also by a public vote.
Willie Dunn's 1971 self-titled album won the jury selection and the Watchmen's 1992 album, McLaren Furnace Room, won the public vote.

Dunn's widow, Liz Moore and son Lawrence Dunn, took to the stage to honour the late Mi'kmaq singer-songwriter. On behalf of his father, Lawrence reminded the audience of the core message of Willie's album — the historic suffering of Indigenous people at the hands of imperial and colonial forces.

"Willie forces the raw question: Who is served by this suffering? He turns the mythic artifact into embodied grief with sanctity and sovereignty inseparable. Not an easy cure, but an enduring, luminous indictment of the crown."

Shortly after, the four current members of Winnipeg band the Watchmen praised their fans in their acceptance speech, saying, "We really want to thank the fans. It's a fan award. We do have the best fans. I know it's a cliché, but it's true.
"They made it possible, and not only the award, but they make it possible for us to still continue to play in the the greatest country in the world, so we're really grateful for that."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kelsey Adams is an arts and culture journalist from Toronto. Her writing explores the intersection of music, art and film, with a focus on the work of marginalized cultural producers. She is an associate producer for CBC Music.

articles.title: Hurricane Polo intensifies into rare category 5 storm off the coast of Mexico
articles.summary: The storm's sudden intensification is "truly remarkable", the US hurricane monitoring agency said.

blocks.text: Hurricane Polo has rapidly intensified off the coast of Mexico to become one of the most powerful storms of the season in the Pacific Ocean.

A Hurricane Hunter aircraft, operated by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), flew into the storm on Tuesday and recorded sustained wind speeds near 180 mph (285 km/h), with stronger gusts.
NOAA's Miami-based National Hurricane Center called the storm "extremely dangerous" and said its intensification over 24 hours was "truly remarkable".
The slow-moving storm is fuelling up on extremely warm waters caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon and is the season's third category 5 storm, the highest level on the Saffir-Simpson scale.
The storm is predicted to skirt the coast of south-western Mexico, but is not expected to make landfall, a warning from NOAA said.
As it slowly drifts northwest, Polo will drive torrential rainfall in parts of Mexico's south-west coast - which could lead to deadly flooding and mudslides, NOAA said.
Rainfall totals of up to 6in (15cm) are forecast, with 8in possible in some areas. Residents have also been warned of large ocean swells and life-threatening surf conditions for the next few days.

"So far, the information we have is that (Polo) will not make a direct landfall on the coast," Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Tuesday, but she warned residents along the Pacific coast to be vigilant. Sheinbaum highlighted the states of Jalisco, Colima and Michoacan as being at risk.

Data from the Hurricane Hunter aircraft indicated that Polo could still strengthen and would likely stay a category 5 storm for the next few days, because of what NOAA called a "very conducive" environment of extremely warm ocean waters feeding the storm.

articles.title: Trough of tropical depression to bring rains to parts of Visayas, Mindanao — PAGASA
articles.summary: As of 8 a.m. on Wednesday, September 23, PAGASA said that the tropical depression is estimated to be 1,865 kilometers east of southeastern Luzon.

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 10:11am
Satellite image from PAGASA showing a tropical depression located east southeast of Luzon as of 8 a.m. on Sept. 23, 2026.
PAGASA / Released
MANILA, Philippines — The trough of a tropical depression located east of the Philippines may bring rains to some parts of Visayas and Mindanao.
As of 8 a.m. on Wednesday, September 23, PAGASA said that the tropical depression is estimated to be 1,865 kilometers east of southeastern Luzon.
It has winds of 55 kilometers per hour (kph) with gusts of up to 70 kph, moving at 40 kph.
Eastern Visayas, Caraga, Davao Oriental, Misamis Oriental and Camiguin may expect cloudy skies with scattered rains and thunderstorms due to the trough of the tropical depression.
PAGASA warned that residents of these areas may experience possible flash floods or landslides due to moderate to, at times, heavy rains.
Meanwhile, Metro Manila and the rest of the country may expect partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rain showers or thunderstorms due to localized thunderstorms.
