articles.title: Jamaica hails King’s decision to refer slavery reparations petition to privy council as ‘really big deal’
articles.summary:
The move comes after Jamaica’s culture minister Olivia Grange travelled to the UK earlier this month to lodge the historic petition

King Charles has referred a landmark slavery reparations…

blocks.text: King Charles has referred a landmark slavery reparations petition from Jamaica to a high-level UK appeals court for legal advice, Jamaica’s culture minister announced in parliament on Tuesday.

Referring to the move as a “really big deal”, Olivia Grange told Jamaica’s MPs the monarch had confirmed that their legal questions have been passed on to the London-based privy council – the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries.

The petition seeks guidance on three questions: whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful; whether it constituted a crime against humanity; and whether Britain is under an obligation to provide restitution for slavery and its enduring consequences.

“Indeed we went fearless and boldly into this chapter when we petitioned the king on Monday, September 7, 2026 – one day after the 245th anniversary of the commemoration of the Zong massacre, an event that captures the barbarity of chattel enslavement,” Grange said in parliament.

“The king could have ignored us. The king could have delayed responding to us. The king could have made a decision not to refer the questions to the privy council, or he could make a decision to refer the questions,” she said, before adding “King Charles has referred the petition filed on the 7th of September, 2026, on behalf of the people of Jamaica to the Judicial Committee of the privy council.”

Jamaica had activated a rarely used mechanism in the Judicial Committee Act 1833, which allows the king to refer questions of “legal or constitutional nature” to the privy council when they cannot be resolved through ordinary courts, according to the country’s legal counsels.
The minister said that taking the matter to the International Court of Justice, was not an option for Jamaica.

“The United Kingdom has placed specific reservations on the compulsory jurisdiction of the ICJ which prevent the Court from adjudicating on disputes between the United Kingdom and the government of any other country which is or has been a Member of the Commonwealth”.

A privy council opinion would not compel the UK government to pay reparations, but Jamaican officials believe it could shape negotiations and legal options and set a precedent for other Commonwealth nations seeking reparations.

Earlier this month, Grange led a Jamaican delegation to London to officially lodge the petition. While in the UK, the group, lawyers and members of the country’s national council on reparation met diaspora communities, MPs, church leaders and cultural institutions – among them the British Museum, from which Jamaica is seeking the return of artefacts taken during colonial rule.

Tuesday’s announcement follows the Caricom Regional Conference on Reparations, which took place in Barbados last week. Officials at the conference said that Caribbean nations are drawing up a multi-pronged “action plan” with legal options to push the UK into negotiating a decades-long slavery reparations deal.

Leaders in the region are hoping the UK would agree to targeted and constructive negotiation talks at upcoming Commonwealth and UN summits, but they are ready to take the matter to international courts if Britain continues to resist diplomatic options.

Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, the chair of the CRC, said reparations was a matter of justice, adding that countries in the region were forced to create viable democracies “out of the mess” of colonialism, which was still having an impact today.

He said: “When Jamaica took its petition to the UK, we had to surround that petition with the fact that when Jamaica became independent in 1962, 80% of the black people in Jamaica could not read or write. After 300 years of British colonisation, they moved into independence with 80% illiteracy. How do you build a modern nation, not even a competitive economy, with 80% illiteracy?”
Earlier this month, a spokesperson for Andy Burnham reiterated the British government’s long‑held position that “the UK does not and will not pay reparations”.

Grange told parliament that the country is “awaiting directions from the Judicial Committee of the privy council as to the next steps to be taken in the case. And the attorney general is preparing to deal with the case”.

articles.title: Sri Lanka Easter bombings: 15 sentenced to hundreds of years in prison each over deadly terror attacks
articles.summary:
Islamic State-inspired bombings of churches and hotels in 2019 was one of the country’s worst ever attacks

A court in Sri Lanka has convicted 15 men over their involvement in the

blocks.text: A court in Sri Lanka has convicted 15 men over their involvement in the 2019 Easter bombings that killed 267 people, and sentenced them each to at least 200 years in prison, meaning they will spend the rest of their lives behind bars.

Nearly 600 people were wounded in the suicide bomb attacks on 21 April that targeted three churches and three hotels across the country during Easter services and celebrations. The bombings, which were inspired by the Islamic State (IS) group, were among the deadliest attacks in Sri Lanka’s history.
The verdict was delivered on Tuesday by a three-judge high court panel after a trial that spanned nearly five years, and amid tight security, with hundreds of police deployed around the courthouse.
The judges also ordered the property of the defendants, who were all from Sri Lanka’s minority Muslim community, to be confiscated.

In 2021, authorities filed 23,270 charges against 25 suspects whom they accused of planning or inspiring the attacks. The charges included murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism, and firearms and explosives offences under the Prevention of Terrorism Act.
None of those believed to have directly participated in the attacks are alive. Two Sri Lanka-based Islamist militant groups were accused of carrying out the bombings.
In the courtroom, the accused appeared relaxed, chatting and laughing with each other during breaks. They asked for and were granted a prayer break during the lengthy reading of the judgment.

Nine defendants were freed after the court found that the charges against them were not proven. One other died before their case reached trial. Those freed tearfully hugged the rest as they were separated from those convicted, who were later invited to argue for lenient sentences.

blocks.caption: Security personnel inspect St Sebastian’s church in Negombo on 22 April 2019, a day after the church was hit in series of bomb blasts targeting churches and luxury hotels in Sri Lanka.   Photograph: Ishara S Kodikara/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: In total, five defendants were sentenced to 200 years each, five to 220 years, four to 240 years each and one to 260 years, based on their involvement in conspiring and aiding the attacks.

“What I did or didn’t do only God and I know,” said Mohamed Ibrahim Saadiq Abdulla, who was given 240 years in prison with hard labour. “In the end all people will be resurrected and God will judge everyone.”

In calculating the sentences, the court considered all seven blasts: three at churches, three at tourist hotels and one at a motel where an attacker killed himself and two others after aborting his plan to attack a fourth hotel.

Haripriya Jayasundara, who led the prosecution, called for longer prison terms, saying the defendants were part of a well-planned attack carried out with the intention of killing Christian worshippers and tourists, which was proven by a video recording left behind by one of the suicide bombers.

The video, recorded the day before the bombings, showed the attackers with their faces covered, armed with rifles and swords and pledging allegiance to the then IS leader Abu Bakhr al-Baghdadi to make Sri Lanka an Islamic nation and wage war towards that end.

Sri Lanka’s Catholic church has claimed, without providing evidence, that those identified so far as perpetrators are not the masterminds behind the bombings, and that there was a bigger conspiracy behind the attacks.
A parliamentary committee found that police and intelligence officials failed to act on repeated intelligence warnings of the attacks.
In July, a former police chief and a former senior defence ministry official were also sentenced to death for failing to act promptly on foreign intelligence warnings of possible attacks.
Sri Lanka has not carried out an execution since 1976, meaning death sentences typically result in life imprisonment.

articles.title: Texas camp where 27 girls died in 2025 flood investigated for manslaughter, negligent homicide
articles.summary: Camp Mystic faces a criminal investigation that could include manslaughter or negligent homicide charges in the deaths of 27 girls amid devastating flooding in Texas last year, court documents show.

image.caption: A memorial for the victims of the 2025 Camp Mystic flood in Hunt, Texas. The camp is is under criminal investigation which could lead to charges of manslaughter or negligent homicide. (Joel Angel Juarez/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
Camp Mystic faces a criminal investigation that could include manslaughter or negligent homicide charges in the deaths of 27 girls amid devastating flooding in Texas last year, court documents show.
Affidavit suggests Camp Mystic had inadequate emergency plans and training

In applications for search warrants executed last week, investigators sought to obtain the electronic communications of the camp's owners, saying they could provide evidence of manslaughter, negligent homicide, child abandonment or other crimes. No charges have been brought, and a representative of the camp did not immediately return messages seeking comment.

Brant Johnston with the Texas Rangers wrote in an affidavit that Camp Mystic had inadequate emergency plans, failed to conduct emergency drills or training, and in some cabins did not have enough adult counsellors. Its owners neglected to take precautions by relocating children from low-lying cabins despite having monitored late-night flood warnings, Johnston wrote.

"Young campers cannot reasonably be expected to independently recognize a rapidly developing, life-threatening hazard or to organize and execute an evacuation absent direction from an adequate number of adult supervisors," Johnston wrote.
He concluded: "Camp Mystic, LLC was aware of and consciously disregarded a substantial and unjustifiable risk of death to the campers in their care."
Texas flash flood: Why Camp Mystic was so vulnerable

Twenty-five campers and two teenage counsellors at the Christian all-girls camp were killed as the raging Guadalupe River surged beyond its banks before dawn on July 4, 2025. Camp Mystic owner Richard Eastland also died in the flood.

For decades, Camp Mystic was a summer staple and an institution for generations of families, who dropped off their girls at the sleepaway camp to ride horses, canoe, fish and attend Bible studies. The camp did not reopen this year, and it has filed for bankruptcy reorganization.
All told, the destructive flooding killed at least 136 people along a several-kilometre stretch of the river, raising questions about how things went so terribly wrong.
Attorneys for some of the victims' families welcomed the search warrants but said they should not have been necessary.

"For more than a year, families of the 27 angels killed at Camp Mystic have fought, begged, and pleaded with the Eastland family for accountability and answers," Christina Yarnell and Brad Beckworth, attorneys for the family of victim Cile Steward, said in a written statement.
"Instead, the Eastlands have held hostage the information and answers owed to parents who deserve, more than anyone, to know the details surrounding their daughters' final moments."
Steward's body still has not been found.

Johnston wrote in the warrant that he made several visits to Camp Mystic and that he and other investigators have conducted interviews with witnesses, flood victims and people associated with the camp. But several people, including members of the Eastland family and other top camp officials, refused interviews, Johnston wrote.

The Eastland family and other camp leaders have testified in courtrooms and in front of the state legislature in the months since the flood, however, with camp director Edward Eastland offering a tearful apology.

articles.title: Playing loud music on the bus? That will cost you hundreds of dollars in Singapore
articles.summary: Authorities are cracking down on "disruptive behaviours" including eating onboard and putting feet on seats.

blocks.text: Bus passengers in Singapore can now be fined up to $500 Singapore dollars ($391; £293) for placing their feet on seats or playing loud audio, as well as eating, drinking or littering onboard.

A fine of up to $5,000 will be imposed for more serious offences, such as causing obstruction or danger to fellow commuters within bus terminals or "the soiling of any part of a public bus, bus interchange, or terminal".
"These will foster a safer, more considerate and pleasant public transport environment for all," the Land Transport Authority (LTA) said in a news release.
The new regulations, announced on Monday, align with existing rules on Singapore's railway, or Mass Rapid Transit (MRT), network.

But while there have long been punishments for MRT passengers caught eating onboard, for example, rules on buses were typically company policies enforced by drivers, who could ask commuters to alight.
Now these nuisance behaviours have become official legal offences carrying immediate fines.
Authorised bus staff – such as ticket inspectors and bus interchange staff – can issue official notices to passengers who are suspected of committing an offence, according to LTA.

Bus drivers - or "captains", as they are called in Singapore - will not be given the same authority, leaving them to prioritise their duty of safely operating the bus. They can, however, tell commuters to stop disruptive behaviour, and those who refuse to cooperate may be asked to alight the bus or, in severe cases, face police intervention.

Singapore is not alone in trying to make public transport more peaceful. As transit networks grow, cities around the world are actively cracking down on bad behaviour to ensure a peaceful commute for all passengers.

Earlier this year, the Polish city of Kraków introduced similar rules with commuters now facing a fine of up to 200 złoty ($52; £39) for "disturbing the peace and quiet within the vehicle" with their mobile phones and other electronic devices.
In the United Kingdom, existing laws ban "anti-social behaviour" on trains and stations, including using "sound-producing equipment" without permission if it annoys others.
Some politicians have pushed to specifically fine so-called "headphone dodgers" - people who play loud music and videos - across all public transport, including buses, with fines of up to £1,000.
These rules in Singapore, Kraków, and the United Kingdom show a growing trend of transport authorities stepping in to protect passengers.
"Public transport is a shared space, and every commuter has a part to play in ensuring a gracious and pleasant commuting environment," said Singapore's LTA.

articles.title: Indigenous leaders call for change in Sask. health care after woman's death during childbirth
articles.summary: First Nations leaders say a declining health-care system and systemic racism within that system both contributed to Chelsea Bear's death from complications during the birth of her twins last month in…

image.caption: Deb Bear, left, speaks about the death of her daughter Chelsea Bear, pictured on right. She was accompanied by her niece Amanda Bear, centre, and leaders from Flying Dust First Nation and the Meadow Lake Tribal Council at a news conference Tuesday in Saskatoon. (CBC News)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan·New

First Nations leaders say a declining health-care system and systemic racism within that system both contributed to Chelsea Bear's death from complications during the birth of her twins last month in Saskatoon.
Chelsea Bear's family says she was sent home from hospital without proper care
WARNING: This story contains details about death in childbirth.
First Nations leaders say a declining health-care system and systemic racism within that system both contributed to a mother's death from complications during the birth of her twins.

"No matter where you are in life, you should have fair and equitable treatment. Everybody should be treated the same," Meadow Lake Tribal Council vice-chief Richard Derocher said on Tuesday, speaking alongside the family of Chelsea Bear at a news conference in Saskatoon.

Bear, a member of Flying Dust First Nation, went to hospital on Aug. 10 in Meadow Lake, in pain and bleeding, but was sent home without receiving proper care, her family said. She was 36 weeks pregnant and her pregnancy was considered high-risk.

The next day, the pain and bleeding increased severely, and Bear returned to the hospital. She was ultimately taken to Saskatoon, where the first twin was delivered stillborn and the second baby was born very weak, her family said.

Bear died after their deliveries, in the early hours of Aug. 12. She was 36 years old and left behind four other children, in addition to the surviving twin, Gracie, who is still in the neonatal intensive care unit in Saskatoon.
Her family said she died from hemorrhaging blood due to placental abruption — which is when the placenta separates too early from the uterus.
They said that if Bear would have received proper care when she first went to hospital, she and both her babies would still be alive.
"She must have been so scared, I was thinking, just losing all the blood.… It must have hurt her," Chelsea's mother Deb Bear said at a news conference Tuesday in Saskatoon.
"I just don't want this ever to happen to anybody else."
Bear's family is the second Indigenous family to speak out and call for change after the death of a mother during childbirth in Saskatchewan this year.

items: Family seeks answers after Indigenous mother dies in delivery room at Saskatoon hospital

blocks.text: Jaali Sutherland-Weenie, from Beardy's & Okemasis Cree Nation, died on April 26 after first going to the hospital in Rosthern with severe back pain and vomiting, then being sent to Saskatoon. Her family said she was diagnosed with pre-eclampsia, a blood pressure condition. Her baby girl survived.
Sutherland-Weenie's family said they believed she would have been treated differently if she were not Indigenous.
Systemic racism alleged

On Tuesday, near the end of a lengthy news conference, Derocher said that speaking about Bear's death is complicated "because of all the things that are not being said" when people are "trying to be as nice as possible."

He and Meadow Lake Tribal Council Tribal Chief Jeremy Norman both said they were on a conference call with representatives of the Saskatchewan Health Authority that took place after MLTC reached out to them about Bear's death.
They said they expressed frustration that they weren't getting answers and told the SHA they were considering holding a news conference.
Norman said an SHA representative "basically told us, keep quiet, because it's so hard to get doctors in our region, it's so hard to get people to come and work in the north."

Derocher said those words "burnt me hard," and are another example of the systemic racism that happens every day, when First Nations people are asked "to keep silent, do not speak of this issue, do not bring it forth."

He and the other chiefs also spoke about how they have seen the quality of health care declining for everyone in Saskatchewan over the past two decades — in everything from hospital care to long-term care — and how they want to work with the province to make positive changes.
SHA to conduct patient safety review
The SHA declined an interview request, but issued a statement extending their condolences to the family and community for the "profound and tragic loss."

The statement didn't directly answer a question about Norman and Derocher's account of the conference call where they said they were asked to keep quiet. The statement said the SHA met with the MLTC to hear their concerns, but at the time of the meeting, "the SHA had not received consent from the family to discuss the specifics of their case with MLTC."
"We have since received the family's consent and will continue our discussions with MLTC in the coming days," the SHA's statement said.

items: Nurses' union sounds alarm on short-staffing, lack of resources in Sask. maternity wards

blocks.text: The health authority said it would be conducting a thorough patient safety review.

"The SHA acknowledges the complex and dynamic conditions that our maternal health and obstetrical clinical teams operate within, and appreciate their commitment, clinical expertise and professionalism."
Independent investigation called for
The MLTC chiefs and Flying Dust First Nation Chief Tyson Bear are calling for more than a patient safety review.
"We are calling for a thorough, independent, transparent investigation, so Chelsea's family can get the answers they deserve," Chief Bear said.
Chelsea Bear's death was not an isolated incident in the health-care system, the chiefs said.
In a news release, they highlighted that it is the sixth quality-of-care incident that the Meadow Lake Tribal Council has tried to raise with the SHA this year.
"We're here for a better health system. We're here to make change," Tribal Chief Norman said.
"It's unfortunate things like this have to happen before we look at making change, before we really dig in to say, 'What's the problem?'"
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Hannah Spray works as a reporter and copy editor. She began her journalism career in newspapers, first in her hometown of Meadow Lake, Sask., moving on to Fort St. John, B.C., and then to the Saskatoon StarPhoenix. She joined CBC in 2022. Send story tips confidentially via Signal to HannahSpray.10

articles.title: Hamilton-born NHL prospect collapsed after coaches didn't submit workout for review: university
articles.summary: Hockey coaches at Arizona State University didn't submit a plan for review by trainers before an outdoor workout on a hot August day that saw Hamilton-born NHL prospect Matthew Mayich collapse,…

image.caption: Hamilton-born Matthew Mayich, who was drafted by the NHL's St. Louis Blues in 2023, was at an early-morning outdoor workout with the Arizona State University hockey team on Aug. 20 when he collapsed. (St. Louis Blues)

blocks.text: Hamilton

Hockey coaches at Arizona State University didn't submit a plan for review by trainers before an outdoor workout on a hot August day that saw Hamilton-born NHL prospect Matthew Mayich collapse, leaving him in hospital in critical condition, says a review by the Tempe-based school.
Lawyer says Hamilton-born St. Louis draft pick in stable, critical condition, family 'praying for a miracle'

Hockey coaches at Arizona State University (ASU) didn't submit a plan for review by trainers before an outdoor workout last month that saw NHL prospect Matthew Mayich collapse, leaving him in hospital in critical condition.

James Rund, the university official leading the review, wrote that the Hamilton-born 21-year-old collapsed just before 8:30 a.m. during the Aug. 20 training session at Sun Angel Stadium on ASU’s Tempe campus.

The report, which calls for a "a blue-ribbon advisory panel," said the temperature was about 30 C, and the student athletes were involved in "calisthenics, bodyweight exercises such as pushups and planks, and running."

items: Parents of NHL prospect hospitalized after collapse at team workout say he's a 'fighter'

blocks.text: The hockey coaches asked permission for Timothy Zeisel, who was there for the workout and had "spoken with the ASU Hockey team in the 2025-26 season about topics of leadership and teamwork," to speak to the team. However, the coaches didn't "submit a plan of training activities for review by ASU’s strength and conditioning coaches" before training began.

Near the end of the workout, "Matthew appeared to struggle, and then in rapid succession stumbled, dropped the medicine ball and fell to the ground. He attempted to get up and resume running but fell to his knees," wrote Rund, ASU's senior vice-president of educational outreach and student services.
Mayich in stable, critical condition, lawyer says

The Mayich family's lawyer, Rob Carey, said on Tuesday that "Matthew is in stable but critical condition still. The family is still praying for a miracle, but nothing has significantly changed. But even if that happens, we will never have the young man who came to Arizona last month, a hockey star and (by all accounts) a wonderful person."
In an interview last week from Phoenix, Ariz., with CBC News, Mayich's father, John Mayich, said "we know Matthew's a fighter and we're hoping he pulls through this."
Before the workout, Matthew was "perfectly healthy," said his mother, Christina.
Carey said that "when Matthew went down, there was no plan and no preparation, so he was treated in a way that hurt his chances rather than helped them."
"A month later, nobody's been named, nobody's been suspended, nobody's been fired for violating the very policies ASU published today, and the university wants to appoint a committee."

He added that "a committee isn't going to tell us why grown men with a rulebook in their hands let this happen to a young man at his first real workout in the desert. That's what an investigation is for, and it's why we're going to ask the county attorney to do one."
Carey said in early September that based on his own investigation, he believes Mayich endured a "military-style, brutal, gruelling workout" with no breaks and no water for over an hour.

"You have an elite NHL-drafted athlete showing up on the first coach-led workout, the very first day the team could organize formally, and he left the field with no chance of recovery," Carey said. "Obviously there's something wrong."

Rund said ASU would "be undertaking a comprehensive review of its practices to identify and implement best practices regarding the planning, conduct and monitoring of athletic activities. and the response to emergencies that arise during athletic activities."
In early September, a spokesperson for the ASU Police Department said they were investigating what happened to Mayich, which is a "standard procedure" for an incident of this severity.
The report said ASU would have a panel of experts provide best practice recommendations for:

items: Planning and approval of outdoor athletic activities, including strength and conditioning activities, practices and competitions.
Staffing, monitoring and conduct of outdoor athletic activities, including adjustments to address changed conditions or adverse reactions.
Preparation for and response to adverse events or reactions occurring during outdoor athletic activities.
Use of outside consultants in the planning and delivery of strength and conditioning, and practice activities.

blocks.text: Mayich played minor hockey with the Hamilton Huskies between 2016 and 2020. He was selected in the sixth round of the 2023 NHL draft by the St. Louis Blues.

Doug Armstrong, the Blues' president of hockey operations, said in a news release in late August, "The entire Blues organization is keeping Matthew Mayich close to our hearts as we pray for his comfort and recovery while he continues to undergo medical treatment in Arizona."
The organization also extends its "deepest support" to his family, friends and teammates during this difficult time, Armstrong said.
'A tremendous hockey player'

During his six seasons with the Huskies and one as a member of the Hamilton Jr. Bulldogs, Mayich established "himself as a tremendous hockey player and, more importantly, an outstanding person both on and off the ice," the Hamilton Steel Hockey Club, formerly the Huskies, said.

The statement was sent to CBC Hamilton on behalf of the organization, former Huskies president Mike Spadafora and former Huskies head coach Chris Travale. Spadafora is currently the councillor for Hamilton's Ward 14 and running for re-election in the Oct. 26 municipal vote.

"Without fail, whenever [Mayich] is asked, he comes back every year to speak and skate with a new crop of young kids," Travale said. "His message is always about so much more than hockey — it’s about relationships, friendships, and the experiences you have along the hockey journey."

items: Hamilton NHL prospect Matthew Mayich 'needs a miracle' after training collapse, family lawyer says

blocks.text: Mayich's father said Matthew "didn't care if he was at a small rink in Hamilton or a big rink in St. Louis with a lot of people — he just loves the game."
The incident has made waves in the sports world, prompting the Professional Hockey Players’ Association to speak up about the lack of protections for young athletes.

"When athletes feel pressure to remain silent about an injury, illness, exhaustion or concern because they fear the consequences of speaking up, the system has failed them," said PHPA executive director Brian Ramsay in a statement on Sept. 10 that doesn't directly name Mayich.
"Athletes should never have to choose between their health and their careers. Period."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Conrad Collaco is a CBC News producer for CBC Hamilton with extensive experience in online, television and radio news. Follow him on Twitter at @ConradCollaco, or email him at conrad.collaco@cbc.ca.
With files from Julia Wong and Justin Chandler

articles.title: Trump signs 'tremendous' Greenland security deal
articles.summary: Donald Trump strikes a security deal with Greenland and Denmark on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. The deal comes after Trump repeatedly said the US should own the Danish territory.

image.caption: Trump signed the deal after his speech at the UN General AssemblyImage: Brendan Smialowski/AFP

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump on Tuesday signed a security agreement with Denmark and Greenland to strengthen Arctic and North Atlantic security.
Trump, Greenland Premier Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen signed the deal on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday.
The White House released the text of the deal shortly after that.
What's in the Greenland deal?
The deal, which the president first announced earlier this month, bolsters US military and security presence on Greenland.
The US will reestablish a military base in south Greenland in Narsarsuaq and set up the other base on the eastern coast of the island in Mestersvig.

Trump said during his speech at the United Nations General Assembly that the US would "immediately begin the process of developing a significant military presence in appropriate locations and constructing two very important military bases."
He said the deal was "tremendous" for Europe and the US just before he signed it, adding, "And for Greenland, it’s going to be incredible."
Under the agreement, the US will be "allowed to modernize and expand its activities" at the Space Force base.
The deal also reaffirms the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Denmark and Greenland.
Trump has long said he wanted the US to take over Greenland
The agreement comes after months of pressure from Trump,who has long said he wants the US to control Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, a NATO ally.
Behind the scenes, American, Danish, and Greenlandic officials worked many months to address Trump's security concerns regarding the resource-rich island.
The dispute unsettled most Greenlanders and created tensions between the US, Denmark, and the European Union, which quickly increased security exercises and financial support for the Arctic island.
What did Trump really gain from the Greenland deal?
The race for Arctic

Greeland's future has come under the spotlight globally because of trade interests and expectations of future resource development. At least two-thirds of its territory lies within the Arctic Circle, where melting sea ice has opened new maritime routes.
Although the US played a prominent role in Greenland for decades, its military presence on the island has declined since 1945.
From having thousands of troops stationed across 17 bases and installations, only about 200 personnel remain today at Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland.
Jens-Frederik Nielsen, Greenland's prime minister, described the agreement as "a win-win arrangement."

Last year, the Danish Parliament approved a bill allowing US military bases on Danish territory, expanding an agreement it had reached with the Biden administration in 2023. The deal granted US forces broad access to air bases in Denmark.

blocks.caption: US, Denmark and Greenland sign defense dealImage: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: Wide US mobility on Greenland

The agreement grants US military forces broad freedom of movement in Greenland and its territorial waters and restricts non-NATO countries from establishing military facilities in Greenland or maintaining a "permanent" military presence unless the signatories agree otherwise.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte welcomed the signing of the agreement, writing on X that "this agreement, together with NATO's growing role in securing this vital region, enhances our collective security and supports a safer and more stable future for all of us."

Editor's note: We join our media colleagues in objection to the White House barring CNN, MS NOW and Politico. We are not going to use photos or video material produced by the White House and distributed through its official communication channels until further notice.

articles.title: US supreme court declines to intervene in custody fight over baby born via surrogate
articles.summary:
Surrogate who rejected abortion request had asked justices to halt court order recognizing LA couple as legal parents

The supreme court has refused to get involved with a custody dispute…

blocks.text: The supreme court has refused to get involved with a custody dispute between an Alaska surrogate and a California couple whose child was born with a rare and serious heart defect.

On Tuesday, Justice Elena Kagan denied an emergency request from McKenna West, an Alaska nurse and surrogate who had asked the US’s highest court to halt a California court order recognizing the couple, Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar, as the boy’s legal parents.
In recent weeks, the case has garnered nationwide attention, sparking broader discussions about surrogacy and abortion.
In a 9 September filing, West’s attorneys urged the supreme court to intervene in what they described as “extraordinary circumstances”, arguing that “a life hangs in the balance”.

Following a scan that discovered the baby having hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a condition that impedes blood flow and requires extensive surgery, Ahmed and Gilkar asked West to abort the pregnancy. According to NBC, the couple signed a contract last August with West that included a clause stating that the pregnancy could be terminated in the case of a “fetal abnormality”.

However, West refused to terminate the pregnancy and instead traveled to Texas, where abortion is illegal, to give birth. Republican attorney general Ken Paxton intervened, shining a national spotlight on the case. A Dallas judge subsequently issued an order requiring the baby to receive medical care.
Kagan’s refusal to intervene comes just days after the Texas supreme court ruled that the month-old child can leave Texas and relocate to a Los Angeles hospital for treatment.

blocks.caption: Nausheen Gilkar, center, and Omar Ahmed, in court in Dallas last month. Photograph: LM Otero/AP

blocks.text: “Sustaining the life of the medically fragile child is the paramount concern in this time-sensitive matter,” the court said.
West has since argued for custody of the child, claiming that his legal parents will not provide the necessary medical care because they had previously sought an abortion.

West’s attorneys say that because their client “is now completely excluded from the life of the medically fragile infant she brought into the world, much less from the ability to make critical health decisions that protect him, time is of the essence”.
In West’s filing to the supreme court, her lawyers argued that “without relief, she will receive no further information about the child she carried for 37 weeks and fought to save”.

During a court hearing in Dallas last month, the child’s parents said West was “unstable”. Gilkar added: “He’s our child … He’s the most beautiful person I’ve never seen … He’s the love of our lives. He’s suffering a lot.”

articles.title: Kamala Harris returns to Michigan to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed for Senate
articles.summary:
Former VP, who lost state to Trump in 2024 elections, is lending her popularity to unite fractured party

Kamala Harris returned to Michigan on Tuesday to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, lending…

blocks.text: Kamala Harris returned to Michigan on Tuesday to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, lending her popularity among Black voters to a progressive Senate nominee still working to unite a party fractured by a bruising primary – and the former vice-president’s loss to Donald Trump in the state.

Appearing with El-Sayed at a Detroit birth center, Harris used a roundtable on Black maternal health to frame that November’s contest against the Republican Mike Rogers as a fight over women’s access to care.
“Medicaid is the largest funder for maternity care in America. Donald Trump cut Medicaid funding by a trillion dollars,” she said, hammering Rogers for his support of the president’s agenda.

Harris also criticized the Trump administration for halting federal research funding it classified as diversity-related, including studies of fibroids and said the Senate should act as a check on the White House.

“The United States Senate should be a stopgap on the abuses of this administration and I would suggest to you that the fellow sitting to my right would be one of them when elected,” Harris said, nodding to El-Sayed. The crowd murmured in agreement.
El-Sayed, a physician, thanked Harris for “uplifting the issues that we are here to talk about today”, adding his gratitude for her work on them.

The senate seat is open following the retirement of the Democratic senator Gary Peters and holding it is a must for the party’s path to a Senate majority. But even with a win in Michigan, Democrats would need to flip at least four Republican-held seats to control the chamber for Trump’s final two years in office.

El-Sayed, who backs universal healthcare and sits to the left of his party’s leadership, narrowly defeated the congresswoman Haley Stevens in August, following a bitter primary that divided key constituencies. Black voters in Detroit, the backbone of the Democratic coalition in the state, tended to favor Stevens, and Rogers has also been courting them in the city.

The joint appearance also papers over a rift between the Democrats. El-Sayed has called Israel’s military campaign in Gaza a genocide, a sharp break from the Biden-Harris administration’s military support for Israel, but a position that puts him in step with a growing share of the electorate.

A Quinnipiac University poll released this month found 38% of voters more sympathetic to Palestinians and 35% to Israelis, the highest share siding with the Palestinians since the university began asking the question in December 2001.

In Michigan, home to a large Arab American community, that shift has already shown up at the ballot box, and El-Sayed was part of it. In 2024, he backed the “uncommitted” movement, which urged Democrats to withhold their primary votes from Joe Biden in protest at US military aid to Israel. He endorsed Harris when she replaced Biden as the nominee later that year. Many of the movement’s supporters did not follow him and the state narrowly went to Trump.

The trip also comes amid speculation about Harris’s own political ambitions, as she mulls whether to run again for the White House. Michigan is set to hold the fifth contest on the Democrats’ revised 2028 primary calendar and Harris has further campaign stops planned in Nevada and Georgia.
Closing her remarks, Harris urged the room to remind voters “that they have power and voice in the outcome of this election, which will directly impact their lives in many ways”.

articles.title: Spain allows US extradition case against pro-Palestine aid donor to proceed
articles.summary:
Lawyers for James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, wanted over alleged support for Hamas, say client is being persecuted

The Spanish government has decided to allow the Trump administration’s…

blocks.text: The Spanish government has decided to allow the Trump administration’s controversial extradition request to extradite wealthy activist James “Fergie” Chambers to continue in the country’s courts.

Chambers, a US citizen and wealthy donor to leftwing and humanitarian projects, is currently imprisoned in Madrid. It is the first known case of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation tied to money Chambers has donated to support Palestinians, including the Sameer Project, in Gaza.

His legal defense team, an array of Spanish parliamentarians, and some celebrity supporters have publicly opposed the request, calling it political persecution, which would render it illegitimate under Spanish law.

The 22-member council of ministers could have rejected the US petition outright on Tuesday but instead opted to remand the request to the Spanish justice system, beginning a legal process which could now take months.

Meanwhile, Chambers has begun the process from prison of applying for asylum in Spain – which by law makes it impossible for the country to extradite him until the process is concluded, according to attorney Aitor Martínez, part of Chambers’ legal team.

The attorney also told the Guardian that a third request to allow his client to be released on bond while his situation is resolved awaits a judge’s decision, after previous requests have been denied since Spanish police detained him in Ibiza on 10 July.
Elma Saiz, minister of inclusion, social security and migration, devoted less than a minute to announcing Tuesday’s council decision to the Spanish press, calling it “purely procedural”.

blocks.caption: Elma Saiz called the government’s decision ‘purely procedural’. Photograph: Javier Lizón/EPA

blocks.text: Details from the weekly meetings are not public, but sources close to the council told the Guardian: “There was debate, and five ministers from Sumar – including the vice-president – pushed back in the meeting.” Sumar, a leftwing coalition, governs jointly with Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party.
Sánchez’s government has repeatedly expressed support for the Palestinian people, putting him at odds with the Trump administration.
Baltasar Garzón, the international human rights lawyer leading Chambers’ legal team, said that Tuesday’s decision “sets a dangerous precedent regarding the defense of the Palestinian cause”.

“Spain cannot defend international law, the rights of the Palestinian people and the protection of those who provide humanitarian aid while at the same time allowing a request to proceed with an extradition that shows clear signs of political persecution by the US government, as it is directed against an individual because of his political activity and solidarity with Palestine.”

Ione Belarra, secretary-general of Podemos – a progressive party also vital to Sánchez’s interests – said the government “has chosen to keep [Chambers] imprisoned by giving the green light for Trump’s political persecution to proceed to the courts”. Belarra appeared in Parliament on Tuesday afternoon wearing a T-shirt that said “Free Fergie”.

She also noted that Spain must hold a general election by August, and said many of her colleagues in Spain’s Congress “are deeply concerned that by the time Fergie Chambers’ case has gone through the judicial process … Spain could have a more conservative, pro-Israel government”
The possibility of Chambers being extradited “risks opening the floodgates to Trump’s repression reaching into Spain and the rest of Europe and targeting other progressives”, Belarra said.

The US government’s case centers on Chambers allegedly laundering $7.5m he wired several years ago from a US bank account to Tunisia, where he lived at the time, and allegedly using the money to support Hamas.

His partner, activist and actor Stella Schnabel, told the Guardian last month that the $7.5m went to support Club Africain, a Tunisian football club, paying off debt and past-due salaries as well as rebuilding a training center and building youth football fields.

blocks.caption: Ione Belarra of Podemos. Photograph: David Canales/Sopa/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The self-described anti–imperialist’s defense is also asserting that the Trump administration’s charges of “international money laundering” do not hold up because, as heir to one of the richest families in the US, he obtained his personal wealth through legal means.

His money comes from a mid-2023 settlement with his family, owners of Atlanta-based Cox Communications, in which he sold them stock worth about $250m. Members of his family severed contact with him at the time and his donations have gone to about 100 projects in 20 countries.

Chambers’ views and donations have been extensively profiled in US media. He was interviewed on a TV news station in New Hampshire in late 2023 about a direct action against Elbit Systems, an Israeli defense contractor, staged by a group whose legal fees he paid, then called Palestine Action – a group now proscribed in the UK as a “terrorist organization”.
Sealed charges against Chambers were originally filed in New Hampshire.

Chambers’ public comments on Israel and Gaza have previously brought controversy. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/ There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/ No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/ It’s simply genocide/ Like it has been.”
He has also been a staunch critic of the US, telling a reporter in 2024: “I think the most important thing for the prosperity of humanity is the destruction of the US.”

“I am heartbroken,” Schnabel told the Guardian. The two have a young son and Schnabel is just over three months pregnant. “Fergie could spend the first year of our baby’s life unable to hold them, seeing them only through a pane of glass – even though he has not been convicted of any crime,” she said.

articles.title: A new skyline of data centres is rising in rural China
articles.summary: The BBC visits Inner Mongolia, where Beijing's AI infrastructure is progressing at "China speed", says one worker.

blocks.text: ByLaura Bicker
China correspondentReporting fromUlanqab, Inner Mongolia
In the expansive grasslands of Inner Mongolia, farmers are picking plump potatoes alongside new neighbours: huge, rectangular blocks that will fuel China's AI platforms.

Ulanqab, with its steppes and volcanoes, is an unlikely digital frontier. For years, it has been China's official "potato capital". But now its fields have also become construction sites for a slew of data centres, as Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping meet to discuss AI safety among other things.

Hundreds of workers in yellow helmets carry heavy equipment into the building site as welding sparks fly off metal scaffolding. Above them huge cranes move with precision to build rooftops, while men balance on ladders to plaster brickwork.

"This is China speed," jokes one worker. "An infrastructure maniac," is how he describes his country, laughing as he walks away. “There is one phase every year. This is the second phase," explains an electrical engineer. "There will be many more phases afterwards."
Artifical intelligence sits at the heart of China's contest with the United States and the key to it is the computing power inside the data centres here.

To the Chinese Communist Party, these buildings are critical for the country's economic and national security. Once finished, they will help drive its mission to embed AI across 90% of industries and society by 2030.
Watch: Rare look at the remote data centres powering China's AI ambitions

China's not just building the infrastructure. It's also creating a pool of talent: young engineers and researchers who now see their country as a place of opportunity, partly because tensions with the US and Trump's restrictions on immigration have soured the American dream.
"Fewer students and researchers are heading to the US, and more are returning from the US to China. That is very clear," says Jack Zhang from the University of Science and Technology of China.
He himself was recruited by a high-level programme after studying at Yale in the US, and Cambridge in the UK.

"I wanted to take some of the AI work I was doing in the lab and apply it to human health and medicine. That requires more resources, more people and sometimes more government support, which can be difficult to access overseas."

China's expanding AI capabilities are one reason why the US says it doesn't want to hit pause on its AI development, despite stark warnings from inside the industry that the technology was moving too fast.

"Whoever wins AI, wins," President Trump said last week. The CEO of AI firm Anthropic, Dario Amodei, called for keeping the US-led ban on selling advanced chips and equipment to China, while warning that a Chinese lead would "pose grave danger for the US and the world".

This is not what Xi will want to hear when he arrives in Washington on Wednesday. The state-run Global Times, which echoes Beijing, dismissed US fears as part of a "Cold War playbook" to "contain" China's rise.
But China is not just focused on catching up to the US.

It is also touting an alternate model. Xi himself is encouraging Chinese AI firms to develop more affordable, open-source models - which allow people, companies and countries to modify it as they wish.
It also pits Chinese models against those in the US where developers including OpenAI and Anthropic use closed-model approaches, and their design elements are kept a secret.
One reason Beijing is in favour of their approach is that it has worked well for them. By sharing the tech, Chinese AI firms have been able to innovate quickly.
This has helped China overcome one of its biggest challenges: a lack of access to advanced chips, which would help unlock greater computing power.
But Beijing also wants a bigger say in writing the rules that govern AI. Xi has repeatedly called for more regulation and a global framework for others to follow.
With calls for AI safety growing, this week's summit at the White House is especially significant. Can the two sides collaborate on regulating AI? Is any talk of a slowdown even realistic?
It certainly doesn't seem like that in places like Ulanqab, where China's AI ambitions are taking shape.
China is building hundreds of data centres - for Huawei, ByteDance, DeepSeek - in sparsely-populated provinces: Ulanqab, Ningxia and Gansu in the north, Guizhou in the south-west.
It has already built up vast renewable energy capacity - wind and solar - in these regions, land is cheaper and the weather cooler, so there is less demand for water.

blocks.caption: Image caption, These potato farmers' new neighbours are at the heart of China’s AI race with the US

blocks.text: These potato farmers' new neighbours are at the heart of China’s AI race with the US

This doesn't mean there are no concerns or downsides. China wants most of its data centres to be fuelled by green energy by 2030 - but some of its grid is still fed by coal power. Water supply remains a concern in the arid, dry parts of Inner Mongolia.

Entire villages have been relocated, although it's hard to pin down the number or what compensation residents were offered. It's a topic few people will discuss because it can be dangerous to voice concerns too openly.
"This big data has absolutely nothing to do with ordinary people," says one local, speaking anonymously off camera. "What benefits has it brought us?"
He says few locals had found jobs there. Others told us of fears that their land would be taken and they would no longer be able to farm for a living.
But there are optimists too, such as a man who told us his last name was Zhang, standing alongside potato pickers in a field near the data centres.
“China is now at the forefront of the world," he says, adding that his children have managed to find jobs there.
"It's not like the 1960s, when it was relatively backward. China is doing alright now. Whether in economic development or other areas, it is doing well."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Zhang is optimistic about China's embrace of AI, and says his children have managed to find jobs in the new data centres

blocks.text: Zhang is optimistic about China's embrace of AI, and says his children have managed to find jobs in the new data centres

Surveys appear to suggest that there is little opposition to AI or its widespread adoption, compared to so many other countries, but it's hard to evaluate these figures in such a heavily-censored climate.

Beijing has been quite clear that it sees AI as a solution to its ageing workforce, and is rapidly automating manufacturing and production. That is producing anxiety over job losses, which, again, is hard to measure.
But this is also a country that is producing around five million science and tech graduates each year, compared to around half a million in the US.
And as more of them stay in China, they see a growing ecosystem for innovation.
AI developer Dang Ronghao, 27, who works for a leading tech company says Chinese campuses are becoming more open, allowing him to talk to researchers all over the world from his base in Shanghai.
"I've seen research combining AI with nuclear fusion, AI with astrophysics, AI with new materials, and AI with the development of new drugs. I think we are entering a good era."

Even so, some argue that China still rewards conformity over challenge. "It's not as open as I wish," says Professor Liu Jun, Department of Statistics and Data Science at Tsinghua University. He has taught at both Harvard and Stanford.
"I keep encouraging students here to ask more questions, to challenge more, but that's hard to change. I think partly it's culture, partly it's the system."

blocks.caption: Image caption, China sees AI as a solution to an ageing workforce

blocks.text: China sees AI as a solution to an ageing workforce

Far from the labs where Prof Liu and others are wrangling with the AI frontier, many Chinese people are still grappling with more immediate economic troubles: a sluggish economy, rising youth unemployment, low spending and property prices that have plummeted. In rural areas, an ageing population is also a growing concern.
"Big data and all that… pretty good – but it has nothing to do with me," says one farmer in Inner Mongolia, as he trundles on a cart to check on his sheep.
He says he has no use for AI. He hardly even uses the internet.
The screen on his phone is smashed, and wifi comes from a pocket dongle for which he pays just over 40 yuan a month.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Locals like this farmer have little use for AI because they barely use the internet

blocks.text: Locals like this farmer have little use for AI because they barely use the internet
"There haven't really been any changes for me. I don't know about the future," he says.
This kind of scepticism can become a challenge for Beijing.
So much is changing here and everywhere else in the country, but it's hard to know how many people are as invested as their leaders in this tech-charged future.

Artificial intelligence

articles.title: Rare look at the remote engine rooms powering China's AI ambitions

articles.title: Trump flexes 'American power' on UN's biggest stage
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump is vowing to keep using military power to advance his country's interests, including to stop what he calls "hostile foreign adversaries" from gaining influence in the…

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at UN headquarters in New York on Tuesday. (Seth Wenig/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Analysis

U.S. President Donald Trump is vowing to keep using military power to advance his country's interests, including to stop what he calls "hostile foreign adversaries" from gaining influence in the Western Hemisphere.
U.S. won't allow allow adversaries to gain foothold 'anywhere in the Western Hemisphere,' says Trump

U.S. President Donald Trump is telling the world that he will keep using military power to advance his country's interests, including stopping what he calls "hostile foreign adversaries" from gaining influence in the Western Hemisphere.

During his speech to the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump threatened Iran with annihilation, laid claim to Venezuela's oil as the spoils of victory, and justified U.S. strikes on alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean.
He also warned countries that more such interventions could follow.
"We have acted with decisiveness and speed to reshape the world stage and solve problems that have plagued us for far too long," said Trump.

items: Trump says deal struck to boost U.S. military presence in Greenland
As Trump and Zelenskyy talk about potential energy truce, Russia and Ukraine unleash new wave of strikes

blocks.text: "We're reasserting American power, including American military power, where necessary in our region and around the world, to create a safer future for all of us."

Trump's 37-minute speech to the annual gathering of world leaders only briefly touched on Russia's long-running war against Ukraine. He pleaded for an end to the conflict but offered no new initiatives toward peace.
Trump raises possibility of Iran deal — or that he could 'drive them into hell'

He devoted a notable portion of his speech to the Western Hemisphere. That echoes his new national security strategy, published last December before Trump ordered the mission to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and joined Israel in launching the war against Iran.
The official strategy document, which drew praise from the Kremlin, argues for reviving the Monroe Doctrine, the 19th-century declaration of U.S. supremacy over the Western Hemisphere.
'Vicious gangs, bloodthirsty cartels'

Previous U.S. administrations have allowed much of the region to be "dominated by vicious gangs and bloodthirsty drug cartels, destabilized by uncontrolled migration and infiltrated by hostile foreign adversaries — foreign, sick, demented adversaries," said Trump.
"But not anymore," he continued.

items: Trump's Venezuelan oil deal: What we know and how it could impact Canada's oil industry
Venezuelans of all stripes are denouncing Trump's 'biggest oil deal ever'

blocks.text: "Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere, and if necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States."
He boasted about the deal that gives the U.S. control over much of Venezuela's oil productions. "To the victor belong the spoils," he declared.

The speech made clear not only the importance of the Western Hemisphere to Trump's worldview, but also his perception of the region as a potential threat, says Shannon O'Neil, a senior vice-president at the Council on Foreign Relations, a think-tank based in Washington, D.C.
The message sets the U.S. up "to assert control, if not dominance, in this hemisphere," O'Neil told reporters in an online panel discussion Tuesday.
She sees the Trump administration's approach to the governments of Latin America as "really trying to put their finger on the scale to encourage and support those that were ideologically aligned."
Canada gets a pass
The speech did not mention Canada, evidence that the U.S. president has bigger preoccupations than the trade war with his country's northern neighbour.
Trump did, however, take on its southern neighbour, calling Mexico the epicenter of drug cartel violence.

items: Trade 'war' or not, are Canada and the United States now dug in?
U.S. may seek win with Mexico in wake of collapsed trade talks with Canada, says ex-negotiator

blocks.text: "It's unacceptable for the United States to share a 2,000-mile border with a territory controlled by enemy cartels. So Mexico must reclaim control of its soil from the enemies of humanity," he said.
Trump also said his administration is seeking "fundamental change" in Cuba.
Cuban delegation walks out of UN after Trump calls country 'failed state'
"The communist regime is under great pressure," he said. "We'll not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep."
Members of the Cuban delegation walked out of the General Assembly hall as Trump spoke.
'Do I annihilate the Islamic Republic?'
Trump also said he faces a "big decision" on Iran.
He said one option is making a deal that allows Iran to become a "far greater country" than ever before.

"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?"

items: UN mission finds 'grounds to believe' U.S. committed war crimes in strikes on Iranian school, sports centre
Saudi Arabia confirms Yemen's Houthi rebels tried to attack its capital with a ballistic missile

blocks.text: That was Trump's way of laying out both a path for a negotiated solution and the consequences of not following that path, says Mara Rudman, a former U.S. deputy special envoy for the Middle East.
"Fairly clumsy is maybe the kindest word I can use," Rudman told CBC News Network shortly after the speech.
Trump was due to meet the leaders of Gulf countries on the sidelines of the General Assembly on Tuesday.

"My anticipation is that they are urging him, however quietly, to go down the path of negotiation," said Rudman, who served as a national security advisor in both the Clinton and Obama administrations.
Trump predicted that a deal with Iran will happen immediately after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Rudman sees that as evidence that the midterms — which polling suggests put the Republican Party at risk of losing both the U.S. House and Senate — are weighing on the president.
"I think his audience was the American people and not the Iranians or anyone else in the world, despite the fact that he was speaking at the UN," she said.

items: Your guide to the U.S. midterms, and why they're crucial for Donald Trump
Will the U.S. midterm results affect Trump's tariffs on Canada? Democrats think yes

blocks.text: Trump also used the General Assembly podium to call fears over the risks posed by artificial intelligence a hoax and to repeat some of his long-running sharp criticisms of the United Nations, the main theme of his speech last year.

He also called the International Criminal Court a rogue organization. The court was created jointly by 125 countries in the early 2000s to prosecute war crimes and crimes against humanity. The U.S. has never ratified the court's treaty.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Mike Crawley is a correspondent for CBC News, based in Washington. He began his career as a newspaper reporter in B.C., spent six years as a freelance journalist in various parts of Africa, then joined the CBC in 2005. Mike reported on Ontario politics for 15 years. He was born and raised in Saint John, N.B.

articles.title: Iran and US hold talks on sidelines of UN summit, says Trump
articles.summary:
Senior Iranian official indicates willingness to reopen strait of Hormuz if US takes steps to ease pressure on Tehran

Iranian officials held three hours of talks with US special envoy Steve…

blocks.text: Iranian officials held three hours of talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, Donald Trump disclosed on Tuesday.
He said there would a further meeting in the very near future.

Witkoff said he felt very good about the meeting, the first such contact since the US vice-president, JD Vance, met an Iranian delegation to agree a memorandum of understanding in Switzerland in June.
Iranian officials confirmed the meeting with Witkoff involved its foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and was mediated by diplomats from Qatar.

A senior Iranian official also indicated that the country was prepared to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week, so long as the US took reciprocal steps to ease the military and economic pressure it is applying on Iran.

Previously, Iran had set seven onerous preconditions for lifting its blockade on the strait, one of the world’s key oil shipping routes, including an end to the US war “on all fronts” and a commitment by the US to end all aggressive actions against Iran, including sanctions.

blocks.caption: Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, Steve Witkoff and Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, watch on as Trump meets his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the UN on Tuesday. Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

blocks.text: The new position, revealed amid frantic backstage negotiations at the UN general assembly in New York and set out by an Iranian official in Tehran to the Japanese news agency Kyodo and then to Reuters, would involve relaxing some of those preconditions.

The official claimed the position had been approved by Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, and the country’s supreme national security council, although some Iranian media close to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) denied any new position had been adopted, reflecting disputes in Tehran.

Diplomats had been testing the ground for possible talks between the US and Iran, with Qatar’s diplomats in talks with Araghchi. A meeting between Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, and Trump had largely been ruled out as too combustible, however.

Pezeshkian is due on Wednesday to address the UN general assembly, where most of the Iranian delegation left the hall during Trump’s speech on Tuesday after he described Iran as the bully of the Middle East and the number one terror organisation on Earth.

But earlier, the IRGC issued a statement that said there was no contradiction between staging negotiations and waging war at the same time, a position echoed by Iran’s chief negotiator, Mohammad Ghalibaf, in recent remarks delivered online to the Iranian parliament.

The official said Iran was seeking signs from Washington that it was prepared to return to negotiations and take steps toward ending its military blockade of Iranian ports and halting military operations related to the strait of Hormuz. In that case Iran was prepared to reopen the strategic waterway within seven days and return to the negotiating table, according to the official.
Such preconditions are less stringent than those issued by other senior Iranian figures in the previous 48 hours.

blocks.caption: Masoud Pezeshkian, seen departing Iran, is due to address the UN general assembly on Wednesday. Photograph: Iranian Presidency Office/AP

blocks.text: Experience has shown that initially appealing Iranian offers can emerge to be more complex once the small print is revealed, and there is a hardly disguised tussle being played out in Tehran between hardliners and figures like Pezeshkian over the value of any talks. Resolving these disputes is not made easier by the low profile kept by the Supreme Leader, normally the arbiter in such internal ructions.

Trump, in his remarks to the general assembly, said he had a big decision to make: whether to annihilate Iran, or to help it become a great country. “Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he asked, adding he expected Iran to make a deal immediately after the US midterm elections.

Overall, his demeanour, and the mixed signals out of Tehran, suggest the two sides are still too far apart to reach a deal, which would have to start with agreement between Iran and Oman on a new route for commercial shipping in the strait of Hormuz that largely goes through Iranian waters. The Gulf states have not endorsed such a deal.
Saudi Arabia also wanted to be a signatory and authoriser of the route, but Iran insisted it had to be endorsed only by the two countries in which the strait’s waterways pass – Iran and Oman.

Tehran is also under growing pressure as the US blockade of its oil exports plays havoc with its currency reserves and domestic inflation. In his speech, Trump called on other countries to isolate Iran economically, including by demanding that all nations prevent any Iranian civilian planes from landing at their airports. US diplomats have warned Turkey and Iraq to comply or face sanctions.
Many of the Gulf states were also planning to urge Trump to do more to press Israel to meet its commitments under the peace plan to withdraw from Gaza.

The Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, prompted a walk-out by the Israeli delegation when he described Gaza as “the world’s largest graveyard and the most inhumane and shameful concentration camp of our time”.

He added: “Israel refuses to stop the occupation. We are faced with a genocidal mindset that can never get enough of killing. No one with a sense of humanity, mercy, or compassion, no one guided by justice and conscience can possibly remain indifferent to this picture.”

blocks.caption: The Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, was among several speakers at the UN to criticise the Israeli military’s conduct in Gaza. Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPA

blocks.text: Jordan’s King Abdullah, in his address, claimed: “With Israel, resolutions end where they began on paper. This result is a state without restraint. This government’s sense of impunity has reached terrifying levels. It no longer feels compelled to ask: ‘Can we get away with this?’ It already knows the answer.”

He added that what was unfolding across the occupied West Bank was not a series of isolated acts but rather “elements of a single policy to compel an entire population to leave their land. And there is a name for that: forced displacement. And that is a war crime.”

A statement from eight Gulf foreign ministers also called on Israel to immediately fulfil its outstanding commitments under the first phase of the Gaza ceasefire agreement, including by ensuring the immediate, safe and unhindered delivery of humanitarian assistance and early recovery supplies, and facilitating the rehabilitation of critical infrastructure.

The ministers reiterated their categorical rejection of any measures aimed at the expulsion or the forced displacement of the Palestinian people from their homeland or attempts to alter the territorial or demographic character of the occupied Palestinian territory.
